Headline: Parliamentarian troops failed to heed the warnings of their prisoners with explosive results.
Body Text:
In November 1644 Sir Anthony Ashley Cooper’s Roundheads attacked St Nicholas Church and the ancestral abbey house of Royalist Sir John Strangeways.

The thirteen Cavaliers defending the church were quickly discovered and captured.  It took Cooper’s Parliamentarians six hours to fight their way to the abbey’s porch.

Cooper offered terms for surrender but Strangeways refused, and as a result Cooper ordered his men to take no prisoners. The Parliamentarians attacked both sides of the house at once. Intense musket fire from the frontal assault drove the defenders upstairs. At the back of the house windows were forced open, burning faggots were thrown into the building and the Abbey was torched.  As fire and smoke filled the house the Royalist defenders tried to surrender. The soldiers leading the frontal assault killed their prisoners, while those attacking the rear of the house ignored Cooper’s orders and accepted their enemy’s surrender.

The Parliamentarians began to plunder the abbey. Cavalier prisoners, grateful to have been spared, warned their captors that there were still barrels of gunpowder in the burning building. The Parliamentarians plundered regardless. The gunpowder caught fire and the barrels exploded destroying most of the house. Around 50 soldiers from both sides were killed in the blast.

Today little of the abbey survives. Bullet holes can still be seen in the church pulpit.

St. Nicholas Church, Abbotsbury.
“The Church of St. Nicholas” by Spencer Means is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Stormed; No quarter; Churches at war

Headline: In 1645, Charles I ordered soldiers at Abergavenny Castle to destroy their own stronghold to prevent it falling into Parliamentarian hands.
Body Text:
Abergavenny Castle had not been used as a residence for local gentry since the 1400s, but it had always been garrisoned by troops, keen to take advantage of its strength and strategic importance.

During the Civil War, along with many Welsh strongholds, Abergavenny was held for the Royalist cause under the command of Colonel Proger. It withstood a number of attacks from Parliamentarian forces. In 1645 with the tide of the war turning against him and encroaching Parliamentarian troops, Charles took the decision to sacrifice the castle to prevent it falling into enemy hands.

The King ordered his troops to slight the castle, to prevent occupation by enemy forces. Most of the buildings, including the stone keep, were destroyed and their stone used to fortify other buildings against the approaching Parliamentarians.

Abergavenny Castle.
“Abergavenny Castle” by George Redgrave is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Defenders withdrew; Slighted

Headline: Aberystwyth Castle, once a Royal Mint, was attacked on many occasions throughout the war.
Body Text:
In 1637, Aberystwyth Castle was designated as a Royal Mint by Charles I, with the job of manufacturing, or minting, the coins of the United Kingdom. At the start of the Civil War, the operator of the mint Charles Bushell, who had become very wealthy through its operation, pledged his allegiance to Charles I. He lent Charles £40,000 and raised a regiment of soldiers to fight for the Royalists. The mint was closed down during the Civil War, and used instead for the storage of silver and lead.

The castle was garrisoned by the Royalists, under the command of Colonel Whiteley and used as a base for raids. The castle was attacked throughout the war, and later besieged by Parliamentarian forces. Whitely eventually surrendered in 1646, and the castle was destroyed by Cromwell’s troops in 1649 in order to prevent it being used again.

Aberystwyth Castle.

Headline: During the Civil War, Adlington Hall changed hands a number of times, held by both Parliamentarian and Royalist forces.
Body Text:
Adlington Hall was held by the High Sherriff of Cheshire, Colonel Thomas Legh, for the Royalists. The hall was temporarily occupied by Parliamentarian forces in 1642, but then taken back and secured as a Royalist garrison in 1643.

In 1644, the house was again approached by Parliamentarian forces under the control of Sir Thomas Fairfax. The house was besieged by Fairfax’s troops on 16th February and subjected to heavy bombardment. In a desperate attempt to prevent severe damage to Adlington Hall, Legh surrendered the same day.  The hall had a well-stocked garrison of 150 men, 700 arms and 15 barrels of gunpowder. These supplies would have allowed him to hold out longer against the Parliamentarian forces, were it not for his concern for the hall.

Legh was given permission to march out of the house and survived the Civil War.

Sir Thomas Fairfax.
“Thomas Fairfax” by William Marshall, licensed by National Portrait Gallery.
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Sir Thomas Fairfax

Headline: Alcester Church, a base for Parliamentarian forces, was bravely defended by locals when it was attacked by Royalist forces.
Body Text:
The Parish Church of Alcester, St Nicholas, was used by Parliamentarian forces during the Civil War as a base for raiding nearby Royalist troops and strongholds. Although incapable of inflicting severe and lasting damage on the enemy troops, the small garrison proved to be a disruptive and frustrating thorn in the side of Royalist commander Sir Gilbert Gerard.

In an effort to destroy the small garrison once and for all, Gerard led a party of cavalry in a night time attack on the church. The defending garrison, led by two local tradesmen, outmanned and outgunned, sought refuge in the tower. They were forced out when Gerard set alright to damp straw, filling the tower with smoke. The 40 strong Parliamentarian garrison were taken to Worcester as prisoners.
Tags: Stormed; Churches at war; Townspeople

Headline: A desperate defence of the church, led by Colonel Richard Bolle from the pulpit, ended with 867 Royalists taken prisoner.
Body Text:
Sir William Waller set out to attack the Royalist garrison at Alton on the evening of 12th December 1643. He marched through the night to launch a surprise dawn attack. The Royalist infantry under Colonel Richard Bolle were concentrated in buildings around St Lawrence's Church. Waller's infantry regiments occupied hedges to the north and north-west of the Royalist position. The Parliamentarians worked their way around to attack from the west. The Royalist defences were methodically outflanked and overwhelmed and retreated into St Lawrence's church.

From inside the church they continued to resist, climbing scaffolding to fire from the high windows. Hand grenades were thrown in at the windows, while another assault attempted to force open the church door. Dead horse’s bodies were piled up and laid across the aisle of the church to form a barricade. Colonel Bolle is thought to have taken up a position in the church pulpit. He was said to have sworn that he would run his sword through the heart of the first Royalist to call for mercy. Bolle was struck dead by a blow from the butt of a musket. A few desperate Royalists continued to fight after Bolle's death but were quickly overwhelmed.

Sir William Waller lost around 100 men during the attack on Alton. 867 Royalists were taken prisoner, 500 of these are said to have re-enlisted in the Parliamentarian army.

Alton Church.
“P1060815” by Synx508 is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Stormed; Sir William Waller; Churches at war

Headline: Arundel Castle was twice besieged and badly damaged during the Civil War.
Body Text:
In December 1642, in the early stages of the Civil War, Arundel Castle was taken quickly and easily by a small Parliamentarian force, who established a garrison there.

A year later, Royalist troops, led by Ralph Hopton, overwhelmed the occupants after a short siege and installed a large garrison of 1000 men.

Within days of this exchange, on 19th December, Sir William Waller arrived with Parliamentarian troops and cannon to besiege and retake the castle. The forces bombarded the castle, even installing two cannons in the tower of a nearby church. The bombardment inflicted enormous damage to the castle. Fearful of imminent storming, the Royalist defenders surrendered in 1644, and the castle changed hands for the last time in the conflict.

Arundel Castle.

Headline: Plague and starvation finally brought about the downfall of the centre of operations for the Royalists in the East Midlands.
Body Text:
Henry Hastings was the main champion of the Royalist cause in Leicestershire, and was made Colonel-General of the Kings forces in the area. Much of the county supported Parliament including Hastings’ elder brother Ferdinando. Shortly after the battle of Edgehill, Hastings occupied Ashby-de-la-Zouch Castle, the family seat, and placed the garrison on a war footing. He made additional fortifications to the castle and may have created tunnels linking various buildings and parts of the castle.  For over three years it was the centre of operations for most of Leicestershire, Nottinghamshire, Derbyshire and Staffordshire. It became a critical lynch-pin of Royalist operations in the Midlands and strengthened their hold on the port of Chester. Cavalry from the garrison were involved in many actions in the Welsh Marches in 1645-46.

By January 1644, with Colonel Isham Perkins now governor, Ashby housed a garrison of around 400 men. But the tide was slowly turning against the King’s forces. By August that same year Ashby and Newark were the only two Royalist garrisons still holding out against Parliament in the East Midlands.  A Parliamentary newsletter, the Perfect Diurnal of 14th November 1644 describes Ashby’s defences:

?The enemy are very strong, and their works good; they have vaults under the ground, through which they can go from one fort to another at their pleasure; provisions they have good store; hung beef plenty round about their kitchen within, and have lately been killing and salting of more.?

By the end of 1644, Parliamentarian forces were gaining the upper hand in the county, the town was being occupied and the castle closely besieged. For a year the fortunes of the opposing forces fluctuated, but after the battle of Naseby the situation became desperate for the Royalists. The castle was subjected to a prolonged siege from September 1645.  On 27th September, the newssheet, Mercurius Verdicus recorded that Ashby was “closely besieged” the town is much visited with the sickness; and in the garrison or fort is said to be not above 60 men.?

Although the castle proved too strong to be taken by storm, an outbreak of plague and dwindling food supplies took their toll on the garrison, forcing it to surrender on 2nd March 1646. The terms of surrender were remarkably generous, suggesting that the Parliamentarians were relieved to finally hold Ashby. As was usual, the terms of surrender included provision for slighting the castle. One complete wall of each of the outer buildings was destroyed by undermining and gunpowder, however the main castle buildings and towers survived until about 1648, at which point they were largely destroyed by the Parliamentary forces.

Ashby de la Zouch Castle.
“Hastings Tower” by Bvi4092 is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Starved out; Mines and petards; Slighted; After Naseby

Headline: Aston Hall survived as a Royalist stronghold in a strongly Parliamentarian area, until a Christmas Day attack in 1643.
Body Text:
In 1642 King Charles had stayed the night at Aston Hall on his journey to confront the Roundheads at the Battle of Edgehill.  In 1643 Aston Hall’s owner, Sir Thomas Holte, requested his home be garrisoned.  40 musketeers were sent from Dudley Castle and, much to Holte’s displeasure, earthworks were dug in the park grounds.

Aston Hall was attacked on Christmas Day 1643 by a force of 300 Parliamentarian infantry and cavalry. Surrender was offered, and refused. A sustained artillery assault commenced. Cannon fired pounded the walls. A cannon ball smashed its way into the house and punched a hole through the central staircase. After three days of intense fighting the Parliamentarians entered the hall and forced surrender.  Sir Thomas Holte was captured and his precious house confiscated.

Sir Thomas was eventually permitted to buy his house back from his enemies. He repaired most of the wreckage caused by the siege but left some cannonball damage visible as lasting emblem of his defiance.

Aston Hall.
“Aston Hall Domes” by Storkhen is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0

Headline: Although the town was largely Parliamentarian, it took two sieges to dislodge the Royalist garrison from the castle at Banbury.
Body Text:
Despite the people of Banbury's Parliamentarian sympathies, for most of the Civil War Banbury Castle was a Royalist garrison.  The first siege of Banbury began in July 1644. From 19th July Parliamentary forces blockaded the roads around Banbury. But it wasn’t until 25th August that the besieging force of 3,500, commanded by Col. John Fiennes, entered the town. The castle’s defenders numbered 400 soldiers. The defenders were led by Sir William Compton, who was only 19 years old. On 23rd September an unsuccessful attempt was made to storm the castle. Royalists tried to relieve the garrison on 20th and 23rd October but failed. The siege ended on 25th October, with the approach of a Royalist army commanded by William Compton’s brother, James, the Earl of Northampton.

In January 1646 the siege was renewed by Parliamentarian forces commanded by Sir Edward Whalley. On 18th March Sir William Compton rejected the call to surrender. A short while later Parliamentary heavy guns and mortars arrived.  On 8th May the castle surrendered, possibly influenced by news of the King’s surrender on the 6th May.
Tags: Relieved; Oxford's ring

Headline: The Cheshire village of Barthomley suffered one of the most controversial incidents of the Civil War.
Body Text:
On 23rd December 1643 a party of Royalist soldiers, led by Colonel John Connaught visited Barthomley hunting Parliamentarians.  A number of locals sought to escape the soldiers by locking themselves in Barthomley Church. Connaught forced his way in. 20 people retreated up the stairs of the church into the steeple. Connaught offered them quarter and invited them to surrender. They accepted, but as they descended the stairs they were attacked by Connaught and his men at the bottom of the church tower. The prisoners were stripped. Twelve were killed immediately, many of whom had their throats cut. The rest were cut and stabbed and left for dead. Connaught himself fatally struck a man named John Fowler across the head with an axe.

The incident became a byword for indiscriminate brutality during the war. Yet not everyone concurred that the Royalist s had done anything wrong.  Lord John Byron, who had been present at Barthomley, boasted that to kill “these kinds of people” was entirely justified as “mercy to them is cruelty.”

In 1654 John Connaught was put on trial for murder. He was tried by John Bradshaw, who had been chief judge at the trial of Charles I. Connaught was found guilty and hanged.

St Bertoline’s Church, Barthomley.
“Barthomley, St Bertoline’s Church” by Muffinn is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Stormed; No quarter; Churches at war; Townspeople

Headline: The town and castle at Barnstaple changed hands several times during the Civil War.
Body Text:
Barnstaple was strongly attached to the interests of Parliament and was fortified in 1642-43. The castle was refurbished, a trench was dug around the town to the east and three small redoubts and a larger detached fort completed the defences.  It was besieged by Royalists under Colonel Digby in August 1643 and, when the King’s nephew Prince Maurice arrived, the citizens were offered generous surrender terms, including a free pardon. Within a week the decision to surrender had been made. Barnstaple was taken for the King by Prince Maurice, with Digby moving in on 2nd September 1643. In July 1644, the inhabitants rose and took back possession of the town.  The Earl of Essex sent Lord Roberts and Sir Philip Stapleton, with about 500 cavalry, who pushed back Digby and others sent to the relieve the Royalists. The Earl of Essex then garrisoned the town, but it surrendered on honourable terms to General Goring in September following a five day siege that ended on 17th September 1644.

In October 1645, the clubmen of Devon declared for Parliament and killed several Royalists at Barnstaple, where Sir Allen Apsley was then governor. Sir Thomas Fairfax wrote in March 1646:

?It is generally believed that Sir Allen Apsley is willing to surrender the town, fort and castle, but that his desperate brother swears he will cut him to pieces if he offers to surrender the castle?.

Following the fall of Exeter to Parliament on 13th April 1646 Fairfax besieged the town, which surrendered to him on 20th April.
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Townspeople

Headline: Local women joined the desperate defence of Basing House, cursing their enemies and throwing bricks and stones.
Body Text:
Basing House was owned by John Paulet, the Catholic Marquis of Winchester and one of the wealthiest landowners in the kingdom. In July 1643, Basing House was attacked by local Parliamentarians led by Colonel Richard Norton. The Marquis and a few servants succeeded in holding Parliament off until the arrival of 100 musketeers from Oxford. Colonel Marmaduke Rawdon took over as military governor of Basing House. Rawdon supervised the strengthening of Basing's defences, adding an extensive system of earthwork banks, ditches and bastions as well as beefing up the garrison to 400 men. Rawdon transformed Basing House into a formidable fortress that commanded the main road from London to the west.

The second attack on Basing House was led by Sir William Waller. Waller set up his artillery on Cowdrey Down to the north of the house. He called for the Royalists to surrender, but the Marquis courteously declined. At dawn on 7th November 1643, Waller’s guns opened fire. Musketeers advanced to seize a number of farm outbuildings where they shot at Basing's outer defences. The gun battle continued into the afternoon. The Royalists threw grenadoes, trying to set fire to the outbuildings that sheltered the Parliamentarians. Darkness fell and the Parliamentarians fell back to Cowdrey Down. The inexperienced London Brigade, discouraged by the musketeer’s retreat and the cold, wet weather threatened to mutiny forcing Waller to withdraw his troops to Basingstoke.

On 12th November, Waller attempted a second attack. After a two-hour bombardment, the Parliamentarians stormed Basing’s defences from three directions at once. The London regiments mounted diversionary attacks from Basing Park to the south and west of the House. Waller led his main force from Basing village in the east. Two Royalist deserters had told Waller that a section of the eastern wall was weak. Major Strachan led the attack with Waller in support. The Royalists were driven back from the defences and Parliament advanced to the rampart. But the Parliamentarians made a mistake: they attempted to breach a reinforced section of the wall, rather than the weak section they had been told about. They were unable to break through. The Parliamentarians were shot at from a building to the north of the wall.  Women threw stones and bricks at their enemies and insulted them from the battlements. The soldiers Waller held in the reserve refused to fight and the attack faltered. The rest of the attackers were thrown back. As darkness fell a heavy rain set in. Waller abandoned the assault and for a second time ordered a withdrawal to Basingstoke. Colonel Rawdon was knighted for his defence of Basing.

During the siege John Paulet was said to have taken a diamond and scratched his family motto Aymez Loyaulté – "Love Loyalty" – onto every window pane in Basing House.
Tags: Besiegers gave up; Besieged again and again; Sir William Waller; Family homes

Headline: Parliament tried to starve the defenders of Basing House into submission, but a daring raid changed the course of the siege.
Body Text:
Early in June 1644, the Basing garrison was seriously weakened when a raid against a Parliamentarian outpost at Warnborough Mill failed. A Royalist soldier had betrayed them and the raiding party was ambushed by Colonel Norton's cavalry. Nearly 100 men were killed or captured, leaving the Royalists with only 250 men to defend Basing House. A force was quickly assembled from the Southern Association counties to take advantage of the weakened garrison. 3,000 Parliamentarians were sent to blockade Basing House.

Basing House was surrounded and cut off. Parliamentarians began to build siege works and mortars and siege guns were sent down from London. The bombardment began on 29th June and continued on-and-off throughout July and August. Colonel Norton did not want to risk a direct attack. He hoped instead to starve the Royalists into giving in. The Marquis of Winchester rejected all calls to surrender despite narrowly escaping death himself when a cannon ball smashed into his bedchamber. Despite dwindling supplies and an outbreak of smallpox, the defenders refused to give in. They even led several raids against their Parliamentarian enemies.

By early September 1644, supplies were running dangerously low for Basing’s defenders. The Marquis appealed to Oxford for help. The King's army was fighting in the west so few troops could be spared. However, Colonel Henry Gage managed to raise a force of 400 musketeers and 250 cavalry. Gage set off for Basing House on 9th September with supplies of ammunition and gunpowder. The Royalists drove the besiegers back and on 11th September they forced their way through to Basing House. The next day Gage's troops forced the Parliamentarians out of Basingstoke and captured livestock and supplies of wheat, malt and cheese. Gage delivered the food and ammunition to the starving defenders. Almost as soon as he had arrived, Gage and his Cavaliers left, slipping away under cover of darkness and fog. Gage evaded Parliamentarian patrols, returning to Oxford on 14th September. Gage was later knighted for his gallant exploit.

Colonel Norton resumed the siege of Basing for a further two months, but the fresh supplies had boosted the morale and resolution of the defenders to carry on fighting.
Tags: Relieved; Besieged again and again; Turncoats and treachery; Family homes

Headline: Oliver Cromwell showed no mercy during the third and final siege of Basing House.
Body Text:
The third siege of Basing House began in August 1645. Colonel John Dalbier had been ordered to take Basing. At his disposal was artillery sent from London and local forces from Hampshire, Sussex and Surrey. Dalbier, a skilled military engineer, surveyed the defences and planned the deployment of his guns to maximise their effectiveness. The bombardment began in mid-September. By the end of the month, Parliamentarian guns had weakened Basing’s defences in several places. Dalbier experimented with a form of poison gas. He took bales of wet straw and soaked it with arsenic and brimstone. He lit the straw to create a choking smoke. The wind carried the fumes over the house. The gas was effective, reducing the fighting spirit of the defenders, but it made no real difference as Dalbier didn’t have enough soldiers to take fortress.

On 8th October soldiers from the New Model Army under Lieutenant-General Cromwell's command arrived. Cromwell had brought with him some of the most powerful siege guns in existence at that time, including: a canon-royal, which fired a 60-lb shot; two demi-cannons; and at least one mortar. The total strength of the Parliamentarian force was now around 7,000 men.  Basing House was defended by 300 men. By 11th October, Basing was completely surrounded.  Cromwell invited Basing House to surrender, warning them that the defenders would be killed if his demands were rejected. Encouraged by the Catholic priests in the garrison, the Marquis of Winchester said nothing. Cromwell’s canons opened fire on 12th October. Two days later the heavy guns had breached the walls in at least two places. Cromwell ordered his men to attack.

The fight was brief and bloody, lasting less than two hours. The defenders didn’t have enough men to stand against the massive strength of the New Model Army. The Royalists made a last stand at the gatehouse of the house.  They tried to call for a parley but were ignored by the enraged Parliamentarians. Few prisoners were taken. Civilians as well as soldiers were killed along with a number of Catholic priests. Of the 300 defenders, up to 200 may have been killed. The rest were taken prisoner. The Marquis of Winchester is said to have been captured whilst hiding in a bread-oven. The architect Inigo Jones was present among the defenders. He was carried out naked, wrapped in a blanket.

Cromwell let his troops plunder Basing House, stealing jewels, hangings and furniture to the value of £200,000. Having been looted bare, Basing House caught fire. It burned for 20 hours until nothing was left but bare walls and chimneys. Even these ruins were demolished by order of Parliament, the stones and bricks carted away for use in other buildings in the locality.

A wagon load of Catholic books, pictures, rosaries and relics taken from Basing House were sent to London to be publically burned. There is a legend that tells of rich treasure still buried in the grounds today.
Tags: Stormed; No quarter; Slighted; After Naseby; Besieged again and again; Oliver Cromwell; Family homes; Townspeople

Headline: During Civil War the Somerset city of Bath changed hands a number of times.
Body Text:
In the early years of the Civil War Bath pledged its allegiance to the King, despite a strong Parliamentarian presence in the area.  Bath spent £7,000 (the equivalent of £600,000 in today’s money) strengthening their defences.  Yet when a small party of Roundhead cavalry were spotted in the area Bath opened its gates and surrendered.

Sir William Waller, the Roundhead commander, used the city as one of the New Model Army’s main posts. On 5th July 1643, Waller was defeated by Sir Ralph Hopton’s Royalists army at the battle of Lansdown Hill. Parliament abandoned Bath allowing the Royalists to retake the town.

Naturally, Parliament were keen to take back one of their key strategic bases. Over the next few years the forces of Parliament launched a number of assaults on the town. On 30th July 1645 they finally succeeded. In an early morning raid, Colonel Oakley surprised Bath’s 140 man garrison. For the second time the Royalists were forced to flee.
Tags: Taken by surprise; Sir William Waller; Sir Ralph Hopton

Headline: Beachley was supposed to be impossible to capture, but a tough and cunning Roundhead soldier found a way to breach the town’s defences.
Body Text:
The Royalist outpost of Beachley was in an incredibly strong defensive position. It was built on raised ground, surrounded by water on three sides and had a series of trenches at its only entrance. Colonel Edward Massey was given the seemingly impossible task of taking the town.

At midnight on 13th October 1644, Massey left nearby Monmouth with cavalry troops and 100 musketeers. Early the following morning the tide was out. Massey launched his attack from the river side.  20 Royalist troops were killed in the assault and 220 prisoners were taken.  More Royalist soldiers died as they fled the town, drowning whilst trying to get away. Some of them managed to escape to nearby ships, including John Wintour, Beachley’s Royalist commander.

The defenders had been routed. Massey and his forces had taken the town for Parliament.
Tags: Stormed; Ports and the sea; Edward Massey

Headline: The “impregnable” castle at Beeston was taken by daring commando raid (and probable treachery).
Body Text:
Beeston Castle was situated on a rocky hilltop and commanded the crossing through the Peckforton Hills, making it very difficult to attack. In February 1643, a Parliamentarian garrison of between 200 and 300 men was installed, but the defences were in a poor state of repair.  In December 1643, Lord Byron was made Field-Marshal of Royalist forces in Cheshire, Lancashire and north Wales. Byron marched from Chester against the Parliamentarians on 12th December with an army of 5,000 men. Most of his men were tough soldiers who had fought in Ireland. Byron planned to cut off Nantwich, the headquarters of the Cheshire Parliamentarians, before advancing to capture it.  Early morning on the 13th, Captain Thomas Sandford led a daring attack on Beeston Castle.  The castle was thought to be impossible to take, but in a commando-style raid, Sandford and a small company of men climbed the rock face and scaled the castle wall.  When Sandford's men appeared inside the castle, the defenders believed they had been tricked by a larger force and surrendered.  It is highly likely that Sandford was helped by treacherous defenders. The castle’s commander Captain Steele was later executed for cowardice.

The fall of Beeston Castle opened up southern Cheshire to Byron's forces. The nearby Parliamentarian garrisons were quickly taken.
Caption Image 1:
Beeston Castle.
“Beeston Castle” by Giborn_134 is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Taken by surprise; Besieged again and again; Turncoats and treachery

Headline: An attempt to starve the defenders out at Beeston led to some catastrophic eating.
Body Text:
In November 1644, Parliamentarians laid siege to Chester. The nearby Royalist garrison at Beeston Castle was a threat to Parliament’s efforts and therefore had to be taken.

Parliamentary troops built siege works in front of the outer ward of Beeston Castle. In early summer 1645, the Royalists defenders destroyed them. Parliament responded by building a fort for 100 men within musket shot of the gate and tried to starve Beeston into submission. It is said that when the food ran out the defenders ate cats to stay alive.

On 24th September 1645 the King was defeated at the Battle of Rowton Heath, near Chester. The King’s defeat meant that there was little point in the Royalists at Beeston continuing to hold out. They surrendered on 15th November.

When the Parliamentarians entered Beeston they found that: ?theire was neither meate, Ale nor Beere “save only a peece of Turkey pye, Twoe Bisketts, a lyve Peacock and a peahen.”
Caption Image 1:
Beeston Castle.
“Beeston Castle” by Giborn_134 is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Starved out; Besieged again and again

Headline: Parliamentarian troops destroyed a local village in their attempt to win back Belvoir Castle from the Royalists.
Body Text:
Parliamentarian John Manners owned Belvoir Castle, but on 28th January 1643 the Royalists took it and kept for almost four years.

On 6th November 1646, Belvoir Castle found itself under siege.  The Governor of the garrison, Sir Gervase Lucas refused to surrender. On 20th November the village was taken and demolished by Parliamentarian forces command by Major-General Sydenham Poyntz. The church of Woolsthorpe was also burnt down.  The siege lasted four months, until honourable terms for surrender were obtained with the Castle surrendering on 3rd February 1646. The defenders had to give up their arms and ammunition but were allowed to march away with colours flying and drums beating.  Parliament occupied the castle for three years, but in 1649 the order was given to demolish it. Manners was paid compensation for the inconvenience.
Caption Image 1: “Belvoir Castle” by Brett is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Slighted; Newark's ring

Headline: Cannon fire from the nearby church roof forced the garrison at Berkeley to surrender.
Body Text: Berkeley Castle was first occupied by Parliament in 1642, before being evacuated in 1643 when the Royalists marched towards Gloucester. The Royalists held Berkeley until after the battle of Naseby. Sir Thomas Fairfax sent a Parliamentarian siege expert, Colonel Thomas Rainsborough to take Berkeley. The Royalist garrison was made up 500 men and 11 cannon and was commanded by Sir Charles Lucas, one of Prince Rupert’s cavalry generals.  Lucas was unimpressed by Rainsborough’s summons to surrender, saying he would eat his horses first.  Within three days the Parliamentarians had brought cannons into the churchyard that joined the castle. Cannon fire battered breaks in the walls of the castle keep. Lucas was forced to ask for terms for surrender.  On 26th September 1645, his garrison was allowed to march out after laying down their arms. The Berkeley family was allowed to keep ownership of the castle so long as they never repaired the damage to the Keep and Outer Bailey. To this day the law forbids any repairs to them.
Caption Image 1: “Berkeley Castle” by Giborn_134 is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Surrendered on terms; After Naseby; Sir Thomas Fairfax; Churches at war

Headline: Its position on the border between England and Scotland made Berwick on Tweed extremely valuable to both the King and Parliament.
Body Text:
During the 1500s, the border town of Berwick was valued for its important strategic location in the fight between England and Scotland. Its extensive Elizabethan defences posed a serious challenge to anybody wanting to attack the town. Although Parliament controlled Berwick, the King was keen to take it. He gave the task to William Cavendish, the Earl of Newcastle. A staunch Royalist, Cavendish had used his wealth to help fund the King’s armies. He was made a general and tasked with fighting the Parliamentarian forces in the North of England.

In 1643 Cavendish and his forces attacked Berwick but were successfully resisted. Parliament held the town until the Scots army was disbanded in England in 1645. The town proved highly useful to the Roundheads who then used it as a base for mustering troops to fight the Royalist forces in Scotland.
Tags: Besiegers gave up

Headline: The town of Beverly’s closeness to Hull meant that it was much fought over by Cavalier and Roundhead forces.
Body Text:
The town of Beverly found itself the focus of national attention, thanks to its proximity to the Parliamentarian stronghold of Hull. Before the start of the Civil War, King Charles marched to Hull to drum up support for his cause. He was refused entry. After being turned away, Charles turned his attention to nearby Beverly where he was welcomed with the ringing of church bells.

When war began, Beverly declared its support for the King.  However, Roundhead troops from Hull soon took the town. Once Parliament had occupied Beverly they repaired the medieval walls that surrounding the town.

In July 1643 the Royalist forces of the Earl of Newcastle attacked Beverly. The town’s recently improved defences made little difference. The Earl of Newcastle defeated the Roundhead general Sir Thomas Fairfax and re-took Beverly for their King. Now that Beverly was back under Royalist control, the Cavaliers used it as a base from which to launch the Siege of Hull.
Caption Image 1: “Thomas Fairfax” by William Marshall, licensed by National Portrait Gallery.
Tags: Stormed

Headline: Beverstone Castle should have been impossible to capture., but one man’s stupidity caused the fortress to fall into enemy hands.
Body Text:
Beverstone castle was a Royalist stronghold. It was a much sought after prize by the Parliamentarians and difficult to capture. The Roundhead commander Colonel Massey besieged the fortress twice without success.

In 1644, the castle was attacked for the third time. Despite the strength of the Parliamentarian attack, the Cavaliers withstood the fierce assault. A Royalist victory looked likely until the Castle’s governor made a critical mistake. His mistress lived in a nearby village and he decided to pay her a visit. He was captured. With such an important prisoner in their clutches Parliament was able to force the Royalists to surrender.
Caption Image 1: “Beverstone Castle” by Hugh Llewelyn is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Edward Massey

Headline: The enthusiastic destruction of Bickleigh Castle was a spiteful act of vengeance on the Royal family and their supporters.
Body Text:
Bickleigh Castle was held by the Royalist Sir Henry Carew. During the Civil War, Queen Henrietta Maria stayed at the castle. When Thomas Fairfax’s Parliamentarian troops marched on Bickleigh the Queen fled to France. Fairfax bombarded the castle and forced the Carew family and their troops to surrender.

Once Bickleigh had been captured, Parliamentarian forces were ordered to slight the fortress. They flattened many of the buildings on the property but left the gatehouse and the chapel alone. In this instance slighting the castle held an added benefit for the Parliamentarians. Not only had the Queen stayed at the castle, but the Carew family were also well known Royalists. By destroying their family home, the Parliamentarians were sending a clear message to other Royalist sympathisers. Their intention was to intimidate and spread fear amongst their enemies.
Caption Image 1:
Bickleigh Castle.
“2001-D113 Devon” by Gerry Labrijn is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Slighted; Sir Thomas Fairfax

Headline: The siege of Biddulph Old Hall saw members of the same family fighting against each other.
Body Text:
The Tudor manor house of Biddulph Old Hall was held for the King during the Civil War. The Biddulphs were a staunch Catholic family. John Biddulph was killed at the battle of Hopton Heath. Before going north to fight for the King, John Biddulph’s son, Francis, entrusted the defence of the family home to Lord Brereton.

In 1644, Parliamentarian forces besieged the Hall. The commander of the attacking forces was Lord Brereton’s uncle, Sir William Brereton. The Manor was bombarded, first by muskets and later by the cannon known as the Roaring Meg. Huge damage was done to the property’s stained glass windows.

Unable to persuade the family to give in, the Parliamentarians occupied higher land to the east of the hall. Continuous firing shook the walls. When the family eventually surrendered, Biddulph Old Hall was demolished to prevent it being re-garrisoned.

Francis Biddulph was captured at the fall of Chester. He was released, only to return and find his family’s ancestral home in ruins.
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Slighted; Sir William Brereton; Family homes

Headline: Sometimes two or three weaker towns would join together to form one stronghold in an attempt to ward off attacks.
Body Text:
Bideford formed part of a Parliamentarian stronghold alongside nearby Barnstable and Appledore. The River Torridge ran through the town and forts were built on each side to ward off enemy attacks.

In the autumn of 1643, despite the strong fortifications, the defenders were unable to withstand an attack by Colonel Digby’s Royalists. According to Lord Clarendon: “the swords of the Royalists were blunt with slaughter, and that they were overburdened with prisoners.” The forts collectively surrendered to Digby soon after, on 2nd September 1643.
Tags: Surrendered on terms

Headline: The fire and slaughter on the streets of Birmingham stood as a warning to rebellious Parliamentarian towns and cities.
Body Text:
Birmingham was a deeply puritanical place. During the Civil War, the city became renowned for its “hearty, wilful, affected disloyalty” towards the Royalist cause. It had a strong iron industry, which supplied the Parliamentarian army with blades. Both of these elements made it a key target for the Royalist troops of the King’s nephew, Prince Rupert.

Prince Rupert arrived on 3rd April 1643 with 1,200 cavalry and 700 infantry soldiers. Birmingham had no walls or natural defences. In place of walls were hastily erected earthworks defended by a force of 200 Parliamentarians commanded by Captain Greaves. The Parliamentarians found themselves outnumbered but put up a strong defence. The defenders fired on the Royalist troops from their makeshift earthwork defences. They barricaded roads and upstairs windows. Rupert's troops were twice driven back by heavy fire. On the third attempt they were temporarily halted by a Roundhead counter-attack during which the Royalist Lord Denbigh was mortally wounded. When the Parliamentarians were finally driven out, the Royalists plundered and burnt the town before marching on. Not only did this help supply the King’s troops and prevent reprisals from Birmingham’s population, it sent out a clear message to other Parliamentary strongholds to surrender or suffer the consequences.
Caption Image 1:
Prince Rupert.
“Prince Rupert, Count Palatinate” by Gerrit van Honthorst, licensed by National Portrait Gallery.
Tags: Stormed; Prince Rupert; Townspeople

Headline: A man of God was so desperate to escape certain death during this Hampshire siege that he covered himself in dung.
Body Text:
The medieval Bishops Waltham Palace housed 200 Royalist soldiers commanded by Colonel Bennett. Initially the palace was attacked by a small force of Parliamentarians. When reinforcements arrived the attacks became more intense. Serious damage was inflicted on the magnificent building. Parliamentarian troops surrounded the property. The bishop, Walter Curle, was hiding in the palace at the time. Recognising that defeat was certain, Curle realised that his only hope for survival was to escape.  He dressed as a common labourer and hid in a manure cart, making his escape on 6th April 1644.

The recent defeat of the King’s forces at the Battle of Cheriton strengthened Parliament’s position. On 9th April 1644, Waltham Palace surrendered to Major-General Sir Thomas Browne. After the siege parts of the palace were destroyed so that the building would have little strategic value if it was ever recaptured. The palace became a private residence, before finally falling into ruin.
Caption Image 1:
Bishops Waltham Palace.
“Bishops Waltham Palace” by Neil Howard is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Slighted

Headline: Cutting edge Tudor technology proved useless against 17th century cannon fire.
Body Text:
Strengthened by Sir James Hamilton in the mid 16thcentury, Blackness Castle had one of the most advanced artillery fortifications in Scotland of its time. No Tudor cannon was capable of knocking down Blackness Castle’s walls.

A century later, the fortress was besieged in the Second Civil War as part of Oliver Cromwell’s invasion of Scotland. In 1650 the New Model Army, led by General Monck, surrounded the castle and began a heavy bombardment. 17th century artillery technology had improved beyond anything that Hamilton’s original defences could withstand. The garrison soon surrendered under bombardment from land and sea.
Caption Image 1:
Blackness Castle.
“Blackness Castle, built 15th c.” by Beth is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Ports and the sea; Scotland and Ireland

Headline: Oliver Cromwell’s crafty tactics ended a siege peacefully, but the consequences for surrender would be serious for one Royalist soldier.
Body Text:
Bletchingdon House was a strategically important outpost in Oxford. It was held by the Cavalier officer Colonel Windebank. In 1644 Royalist cavalry were defeated by Oliver Cromwell at the Battle of Islip Bridge. Survivors of the battle rode to Bletchingdon House and took refuge there. Cromwell followed. On 24th April 1645 Cromwell demanded that Windebank surrender. Colonel Windebank refused.

Cromwell only had cavalry troops and not enough men to conduct a successful siege. Instead of launching an attack, Cromwell decided to use a new tactic. By shouting commands within earshot of the house, Cromwell managed to deceive the defenders into thinking he had a large body of foot soldiers with him. Fearful of being outnumbered, the Royalist forces surrendered after a four hour standoff.  Cromwell allowed his enemies to march out with honours.

Windebank’s ordeal was not over. Allowed to return to his Royalist commanders, Windebank had to justify why he had surrendered Bletchingdon House without putting up a fight. Windebank claimed that fighting in the presence of his wife and female friends would have been inappropriate. The Royalist commanders in Oxford were not impressed with his excuse and Colonel Windebank was shot a week later. His execution was intended to discourage others to fight and not give up so easily.
Caption Image 1:
Oliver Cromwell.
“Oliver Cromwell” by Robert Walker, licensed by National Portrait Gallery.
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Oxford's ring; Oliver Cromwell

Headline: A Manor House on the border of Roundhead and Cavalier territory changed hands three times.
Body Text:
Positioned between Royalist Oxford and Parliamentarian Aylesbury the Manor House of Boarstall was the centre of heavy fighting as both sides tried to occupy the property.

At the beginning of the war Boarstall Manor declared for the King. It served as a garrison to protect Oxford, led by the Cavalier soldier Sir William Campion. In April 1644 the house was taken by Parliament, only to be retaken in June and held for two years by Royalists. In May 1645 the house was unsuccessfully attacked by the Parliamentarian forces of Sir Thomas Fairfax.

Knowing how keen Parliament were to take the manor, the Royalists considerably re-strengthened the fortifications. The house was besieged for the final time in 1646. Campion and his men withstood a 10 week bombardment before surrendering on 10th June. Campion might have fought on had he not heard that Oxford, the King’s last outpost, was about to surrender. The surrender of Boarstall Manor was watched by several hundred spectators. Campion and his men were allowed to leave with their colours flying and their heads held high.
Caption Image 1:
Boarstall Tower.
“Boarstall Tower” by David Sheldon is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Oxford's ring

Headline: A Lincolnshire castle’s thorough preparations for a siege proved useless once the enemy turned up.
Body Text:
Surrounded by Parliamentarian forces in Lincolnshire, Bolingbroke Castle was a key Royalist garrison.

At the beginning of the Civil War Bolingbroke Castle was run down and unfit for use. Fortifications were repaired, supplies were brought in and 200 Royalist soldiers were garrisoned in the castle. Bolingbroke was now a serious threat to Parliament. The defenders prepared for a siege.

In September 1643, the castle was attacked by the Earl of Manchester.  After a month of attacks and bombardment Bolingbroke Castle surrendered.

In 1644, the castle was recaptured by the Royalists. The Royalists then suffered a number of defeats in Lincolnshire and the castle passed back into Roundhead hands.  In 1652 Parliament demolished the castle walls. They destroyed the castle’s towers and threw the rubble into the moat.
Caption Image 1:
Bolingbroke Ruins.
“DSCN3411” by Jon is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Slighted

Headline: The wealthy owner of Bolsover Castle abandoned his beloved home after being defeated in battle.
Body Text:
From early 1643, the mansion at Bolsover was a Royalist garrison. Run by Sir William Cavendish, the house had hosted King Charles I and his wife, Queen Henrietta Maria, underlining the family’s Royalist status.

After the Parliamentarian’s decisive victory at Marston Moor, Cavendish immediately announced his intention to abandon Charles and leave England. Soon after, he set sail from Scarborough with his sons.

Once he was gone, Bolsover Castle was besieged by Parliamentarians in August 1643. Despite a hard fought defence, without Cavendish to lead them the house soon fell to the Parliamentarians. The castle’s fortifications were destroyed and the castle became a ruin. It remained a ruin until Cavendish returned from exile after Charles II’s Restoration in 1660.
Caption Image 1:
Bolsover Castle.
“Bolsover Castle” by DncnH is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: After Marston Moor

Headline: The siege of Bolton was the sight of one of the worst massacres of the Civil War.
Body Text:
During the Civil War, Bolton was known as the "Geneva of the North" because it contained many strict Puritans like the Swiss city. The town was defended by 4,000 soldiers, led by Colonel Shuttleworth.

The Royalists wanted to take Bolton.  The task was given to the King’s nephew Prince Rupert. On 28th May 1644 despite heavy rain, Rupert ordered four regiments to attack immediately. They were beaten back. 300 men were killed or wounded. Colonel Russell, the commander of Rupert's own regiment of foot, was one of the wounded. Shuttleworth hanged a Royalist prisoner who he thought was an Irish Catholic. The hanging provoked the Royalist troops to murderous rage.

Rupert ordered a second attack. The Royalists successfully stormed Bolton’s walls and carried the fight into the streets of the town. Royalist hatred made certain very few prisoners were taken. It was thought that up to 1,600 of Bolton’s defenders and inhabitants were slaughtered during and after the fighting. The rules of war meant that the people of Bolton should have expected harsh treatment as they hadn’t surrendered quickly, but the viciousness of the massacre was shocking. The Royalist soldiers showed no restraint and were allowed to kill and plunder their way through the town. Prince Rupert did nothing to stop them.
Caption Image 1:
Prince Rupert.
“Prince Rupert, Count Palatinate” by Gerrit van Honthorst, licensed by National Portrait Gallery.
Tags: Stormed; No quarter; Prince Rupert; Townspeople

Headline: Even when the war was lost, Royalist John Scrope refused to surrender until the last scrap of food had been eaten.
Body Text:
Bolton Castle was a Royalist stronghold, held for the King by John Scrope and his teenage son, Richard. After the decisive Royalist defeat at the battle of Marston Moor the castle found itself exposed and vulnerable.

In autumn 1644, Bolton Castle was besieged by Parliamentarians. A heavy bombardment damaged the fortifications but, despite the strength of the attackers, the castle held out. In June 1645 the Royalists lost the Battle of Naseby. With the King’s cause in tatters no one was coming to rescue the defenders at Bolton, yet John Scrope still refused to surrender.

It was not long before Scrope and his defenders ran out of food and were forced to eat their horses. Only when the last horse had been eaten did the defenders finally give in. On 5th November 1645 Scrope surrendered Bolton Castle. The castle was held for two years by the Parliamentarians, who destroyed the fortifications.
Caption Image 1:
Bolton Castle.
“Bolton Castle” by UncleBucko is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Starved out; After Marston Moor; After Naseby; Family homes

Headline: Lady Brilliana Harley held out against the Royalists but died of pneumonia during the second siege of Brampton Bryan.
Body Text:
When war broke out, Parliamentarian Sir Robert Harley remained in London, but he insisted that his wife Lady Brilliana and her daughters were left at Brampton Bryan. Their home was an island of Parliamentary support in a sea of Royalists.

On 26th July 1643, Brampton Bryan was surrounded by 700 soldiers commanded by Sir William Vavasour.  Brilliana and three of her children had about 50 civilians and 50 soldiers with which to defend the castle. She refused to surrender, saying: ??my dear husband hath entrusted me with his house but according to his pleasure, therefore I cannot dispose of his house but according to his pleasure? The village was destroyed. The castle suffered heavy bombardment but casualties were surprisingly light. A personal offer of terms of surrender from the King himself did not move Brilliana. She played for time knowing that the Earl of Essex would soon be heading to Gloucester to relieve the siege there. Essex’s presence in Gloucester would mean that the soldiers besieging her home would be needed there. After seven weeks, on the 9th September, the siege was lifted. Lady Brilliana set about replenishing stores within the castle. By early October the Royalists were back. The siege began again.

On the 9th October 1643 Brilliana wrote to her son, Ned:

??I have taken a very great cold, which has made me very ill these two or three days, but I hope that the Lord will be merciful to me, in giving me health, for it is an ill time to be sick in. My dear Ned, I pray God bless you and give me the comfort of seeing you again?

She was never to see her husband or sons again. She died of pneumonia on 31st October.

On 17th April 1644 the castle fell to the Royalists, after a siege of three weeks. The lives of the defenders were spared. 67 prisoners were taken, including three Harley daughters, Dorothie, Margaret and Elizabeth, (aged 13, 12 and 9). The fame of Lady Brilliana Harley spread, earning her the “admiration and applause even of her enemies”.
Tags: Besiegers gave up; Besieged again and again; Family homes

Headline: A personal feud made a bad situation worse in Derbyshire during the Civil War.
Body Text:
Bretby was the home of Philip Stanhope, 1st Earl of Chesterfield. The Stanhope’s mansion was garrisoned for the King and defended by 40 musketeers, 80 cavalry and seven small cannons, known as drakes.

The house was besieged in late summer 1642 by forces commanded by Major Molanus. The Parliamentarians used saker cannons to bombard the house, but the sakers did no significant damage. Changing tactics, Molanus attacked the house with 400 foot soldiers. Vastly outnumbered, Stanhope and many of his soldiers abandoned the house and fled to nearby Lichfield. With the house deserted, the Parliamentarians captured the valuable guns and the house was savagely plundered by the troops. Sacking a captured house was normal, but the viciousness with which the Bretby house was plundered can be partly traced to before the war and a bitter feud between Stanhope and Sir John Gell, one of Derbyshire’s most prominent Parliamentarian Colonels.
Caption Image 1:
Bretby Hall.
“Bretby Castle” by Melbourne Footpaths Group is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Defenders withdrew

Headline: Royalist forces burned down their own town to save their castle. It didn’t work.
Body Text:
Bridgnorth stood as a key Royalist stronghold in the Midlands. In 1642 it housed a strong garrison under the command of Sir Robert Howard. Towards the end of the First Civil War, Oliver Cromwell sought to take this key stronghold. On 31st March 1646 he arrived in the town and stormed the North Gate.

The Royalist troops immediately retreated to the relative safety of the castle. In an attempt to slow down the Parliamentarians’ approach, they set fire to houses in the High Street on their way. The fires spread quickly through the wooden buildings, reaching St Leonard’s church, where Cromwell had been storing gunpowder. The fire ignited the gunpowder and caused a huge explosion that reduced most of the High Street to ashes.

The garrison in the castle held out for almost a month and finally surrendered on 26th April. Cromwell had the castle slighted so badly that almost nothing was left of the structure, except the great tower which remains standing. As a result of the damage the tower leans at a 15 degree angle, four times that of the Leaning Tower of Pisa.
Caption Image 1:
Bridgnorth Castle Ruins.
“England, Shropshire, Brignorth” by Brian Yap is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Slighted; Oliver Cromwell; Townspeople

Headline: Parental guidance advised. This story contains nudity.
Body Text:
Bridgwater was garrisoned for the King by 1600 men under the command of Colonel Francis Wyndham. The castle in Bridgwater, which was defended by an impressive moat, was an important fortress for the Royalists. Keen to take the stronghold, Fairfax and Cromwell arrived at Bridgwater in July 1645. They carried out a spying mission to see how well the castle was defended. As the two men looked towards the castle, they were spotted by Lady Christabella Wyndham. She took a loaded pistol and went to the ramparts of the castle. She pulled the top of her dress down to expose one breast, and fired a shot at Cromwell. The musket ball narrowly missed Cromwell, but killed one of his soldiers. Lady Wyndham later sent a messenger to Fairfax asking if he had received her “love token”.

The Parliamentarians began bombarding the Royalists, forcing them back into the castle. Fairfax called twice for their surrender. Both times he was refused. The following day, Fairfax’s troops prepared to storm the castle once more.  Fairfax offered safe passage to the women and children, 800 of whom, including Lady Wyndham, took the opportunity to escape. In order to reach the castle, the Parliamentarians brought several 40 foot portable bridges with them. They used the bridges to mount a surprise night time attack. On waking to find Roundhead soldiers swarming into his castle, Wyndham realised the futility of his position. On 23rd July he surrendered.

The castle was destroyed the following year. Wyndham survived and would go on to play a key role in the Third Civil War, making arrangements for Charles II to flee to France following the Battle of Worcester.
Caption Image 1:
Oliver Cromwell.
“Oliver Cromwell” by Robert Walker, licensed by National Portrait Gallery.
Tags: Stormed; After Naseby; Sir Thomas Fairfax; Oliver Cromwell

Headline: The unlucky village of Brill found itself inconveniently positioned between the Cavaliers and the Roundheads.
Body Text:
Brill, sitting between Parliamentary Ayesbury and Royalist Oxford, found itself a target for both sides in the Civil War. Both sides needed an extra line of defence for their strongholds. After the Battle of Edgehill, Charles I ordered Royalist troops under the command of Sir Gilbert Gerard to secure the village.

On 27th January 1643, one month later, Roundhead troops led by Arthur Goodwin arrived to take the village for themselves. Their task was not easy.  The Royalists had been hard at work, transforming the old castle earthworks into a complicated network of ramparts and ditches. The Parliamentarians bombarded the garrison with cannon fire for around two hours. Royalist troops set fire to damp straw, creating so much smoke that their attackers were forced to abandon the assault. Exact casualty numbers from this fight are not known. Roundhead sources suggest 10 dead.  Royalist reports (probably in exaggeration) say about 80 men were killed and 40-50 wounded.

It wasn’t until late winter 1644 that Brill was finally occupied. 1,000 Roundhead soldiers stationed themselves in Brill after Royalists abandoned the place.
Tags: Besiegers gave up; Oxford's ring

Headline: Prince Rupert and his men fought like devils to take the crucial port of Bristol.
Body Text:
Parliamentarians seized control of Bristol in November 1642. Colonel Nathaniel Fiennes became its commander in February 1643. He strengthened Bristol's medieval defences. Despite the city's apparent strength, he didn’t have enough troops to man the fortifications.  2,000 trained troops and a number of poorly-armed town militia were not enough to defend Bristol’s five-mile circuit of walls and forts.

The Royalist Oxford and Western armies met in front of Bristol on 23rd July. The following day, Prince Rupert asked the city to surrender. Colonel Fiennes refused. Rupert was convinced that Bristol's defences could be taken by direct attack rather than a long siege. It was decided that four infantry brigades, would attack at the same time at different points. Once the attackers were inside the outer defences, they were to tear down the walls and fill in the ditches. Once they had accomplished this the cavalry would enter Bristol. The attack was planned for daybreak on 26th July 1643. Three brigades of the Oxford army would approach Bristol’s northern defences. The Cornish brigade would attack from the south.

On the morning of the attack, the Cornish brigade began their attack before the signal guns were fired. Carts were driven into the ditch around Temple Gate to make a temporary bridge. The ditch was deeper than expected. The Cornish were forced to fill the ditch with brushwood before ladders could be brought up to scale the walls. They fought for half-an-hour to reach the walls. They were thrown back by heavy gunfire from the defenders, losing three hundred men during the attack.  On the northern side, Lord Grandison's brigade launched an unsuccessful assault. Colonel Belasyse's brigade attacked Colston's Mount fort without success. Lord Grandison was mortally wounded and Prince Rupert's horse was shot from under him. The vital breakthrough was made by Colonel Henry Wentworth's brigade. Once inside the defences, the Royalists began to tear down the wall. By the time Colonel Fiennes counter-attacked, 300 Royalists were inside the wall. Rupert established a command post at the breach. Wentworth and Belasyse fought on towards the inner defences. The fight raged for a further two hours. The arrival of further reinforcements allowed the Royalists to finally break into the city itself.  Colonel Fiennes called for a parley at about 6.00pm and promptly surrendered. He marched his troops out the following day, leaving his weapons, ammunition and artillery. When he reached London, Fiennes was court-martialled for incompetence. He was sentenced to death, but the sentence was overturned by the Earl of Essex.

The capture of Bristol was an important victory for the Royalists. It provided the King with ships and control of a major port.  Bristol produced three hundred muskets a week, ensuring a regular supply of firearms for the war effort. Because of this the use of pikes was gradually abandoned in the Royalist armies.
Caption Image 1:
Prince Rupert.
“Prince Rupert, Count Palatinate” by Gerrit van Honthorst, licensed by National Portrait Gallery.
Tags: Stormed; Ports and the sea; Besieged again and again; Prince Rupert

Headline: Prince Rupert’s desperate defence of Bristol nearly cost him his reputation.
Body Text:
On 18th August 1645, Sir Thomas Fairfax marched towards Bristol to retake it, arriving three days later. Prince Rupert, who had captured the city in July 1643, returned to defend it. Rupert faced similar difficulties to those encountered by its previous Roundhead defender Colonel Fiennes. Rupert didn’t have enough troops to defend Bristol's five miles of walls and fortifications. The Royalist garrison had strong cavalry and artillery, but the infantry were mostly inexperienced Welsh recruits. Plague had also broken out in the city and most of the leading citizens had fled. There was little enthusiasm for a siege amongst the civilians who had stayed behind. A plot by the townspeople to surrender the city was discovered. In spite of all of this Rupert believed that he had enough stores, guns and ammunition to withstand a long siege. He wrote to the King assuring him that he could hold Bristol for several months.

With artillery carefully placed to defend the walls, Rupert's cavalry raided and harassed the Parliamentarians as they set up the siege. The Parliamentarians proceeded to surround the city. A naval squadron in the Bristol Channel blockaded the Royalists by sea. Despite these advantages, Fairfax was not confident that his army was strong enough to lead a full siege of a major fortress like Bristol. He was concerned that either Lord Goring or the King might send a relief force to help Prince Rupert.  On 4th September, Fairfax called on Rupert to surrender. Rupert entered into talks with Fairfax. But he was playing for time, hoping to hear from the King. On 9th September, Fairfax broke off the talks and prepared to attack. In the early hours of 10th September, Parliamentarian siege guns opened fire on the defences at five different points. The infantry prepared to storm the breaches. The well-placed Royalist guns made the assault dangerous and bloody. The New Model Army fought back with zeal and determination. Within an hour, the outer walls were breached. The infantry attacked, breaking through the defences at several points. After a further two hours of ferocious fighting, Prior's Hill Fort was taken by Colonel Rainsborough.  Its defenders were massacred and Rupert abandoned the outer walls. He fell back towards the strongpoint of Bristol Castle, but as the Royalists withdrew, Cromwell's cavalry charged in. Rupert knew his position was hopeless. His forces were split. Some of his best troops were cut off at various points along the walls. The well in the castle had been damaged. He had no water supply. Hoping to save at least a part of his army, Rupert called for a treaty.

Fairfax accepted Rupert’s surrender. The Royalist army was allowed to march out of Bristol with colours flying. They had to leave their artillery and ammunition behind. The loss of Bristol enraged King Charles. Encouraged by Lord Digby into believing that Rupert had betrayed him, Charles dismissed Rupert and his officers from his service. Rupert rode to Newark to confront the King and defend his reputation.
Caption Image 1:
Sir Thomas Fairfax.
“Thomas Fairfax” by William Marshall, licensed by National Portrait Gallery.
Tags: Stormed; No quarter; After Naseby; Ports and the sea; Besieged again and again; Prince Rupert; Sir Thomas Fairfax; Oliver Cromwell; Townspeople

Headline: A Scottish castle was passed back and forth between different fanatical religious groups.
Body Text:
Brodick Castle changed hands many times over the course of the First Civil War, caught in a battle between warring religious factions. The castle was originally run by James Hamilton, the King’s advisor in Scotland. Hamilton detested the Covenanters who had rejected Charles I’s religious reforms, describing them as being "possessed by the devil". Many in Scotland did not agree with Hamilton’s religious views. Even his own mother disagreed with him and is alleged to have threatened to shoot her own son dead if he ever landed his Royalist forces in Scotland.

The Presbyterian and friend of Covenanters, Archibald Campbell, Marquis of Argyll, took Brodick Castle early in the war. Hamilton recovered the Castle, only to lose it to Parliamentarians again, towards the end of the War.

In 1650, after the war was over, Hamilton died. The castle passed back to his only surviving child, his daughter Anne. Two years later Brodick Castle surrendered to the English Parliamentarian troops of Oliver Cromwell during his invasion of Scotland.
Caption Image 1:
Brodick Castle.
“Brodick Castle bei Brodick” by Sodele is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Scotland and Ireland

Headline: Royalists destroyed their own castle rather than let the Roundheads have it.
Body Text:
The Royalist garrison at Broncroft was held through much of the war, until it was evacuated in the spring of 1645. As the defending soldiers left, they took apart most of the castle’s defences hoping to limit its use to the Parliamentarians. The Roundheads took control of the stronghold in June 1645. Their commander Lord Calvin made significant repairs to the defences.

Soldiers from the castle were attacked in a skirmish with Cavalier forces outside the castle walls. Many of the castle’s defenders were killed and wounded, yet they managed to hold on to the stronghold. In July 1648, Parliament gave the order to, “demolish Broncroft Castle and make it untenable.”
Tags: Defenders withdrew; Slighted

Headline: A Devonshire Abbey became a crucial base for launching raids against the Roundheads.
Body Text: Buckland Abbey was a key strategic stronghold for the Royalists. When they launched the siege of Plymouth, Cavalier troops used the Abbey as a base for launching attacks. The house remained in Royalist hands until spring 1646 when it was stormed and captured by Fairfax.
Caption Image 1:
Buckland Abbey.
“Buckland Abbey” by Tudor-rose is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Stormed; Sir Thomas Fairfax

Headline: Viscount Camden was more concerned for the state of his house than defending the Royalist cause.
Body Text:
Burghley House was taken into Royalist control on 19th July 1643 when the Royalist commander Viscount Camden retreated there after suffering defeat in Peterborough. The retreating soldiers had been followed by Parliamentarian troops under Oliver Cromwell’s command.

On 24th July the siege of Burghley House began. It didn’t last very long. A short bombardment was enough to spur Camden into action. Realising he was heavily outnumbered and fearing damage to his house, Camden surrendered the following afternoon. Half a dozen officers and several hundred troops were taken prisoner.
Caption Image 1:
Burghley House.
“Burghley House” by Airwolfhound is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Oliver Cromwell; Family homes

Headline: Royalists and Roundheads disagreed on whether or not prisoners were killed at Burton-on-Trent but both sides agreed on the looting.
Body Text:
The river crossing at Burton was so important it changed hands many times during the Civil War. In April 1643, Captain Thomas Sanders set up a Parliamentary garrison.  Three months later in July, Queen Henrietta Maria with her convoy and guard, set out from Newark to Ashby-de-la-Zouch. They travelled to Burton-upon-Trent on their way to join the King.  On 4th July the Royalist cavalry, led by Colonel Thomas Tyldesley, charged across Burton Bridge to fight the Parliamentarians. Although damage was done to St Modwen's Church, most of the fighting centred on the bridge. According to Sir John Gell, leader of Parliamentarian forces in Derbyshire, the town was "most miserably plundered and destroyed".  Henrietta Maria recorded that so much loot was taken that her men "could not well march with their bundles".

The Royalists claimed that they had requested the surrender of the town twice before they attacked and that the Queen had forbidden any violence against people of the town. The Parliamentarians claimed that 30 of their men were forced into the church. They offered to surrender but had their throats cut. The Royalist account admits to plundering Burton-upon-Trent but insisted that they showed mercy to anybody who surrendered.  The town would change hands several more times before being finally taken for Parliament in early 1646.
Caption Image 1:
Queen Henrietta Maria.
“Queen Henrietta Maria” by Sir Anthony van Dyck, licensed by Royal Collections Trust.
Tags: Stormed; No quarter; Churches at war; Townspeople

Headline: Its position on the Derwent made Buttercrambe Castle important to anybody wanting to raise hell in the North.
Body Text:
Buttercrambe Castle held an important position overlooking the main bridge on the River Derwent.
This made it a key part of the Royalist defences of York. As keen as the Royalists were to keep control of the Castle, the Parliamentarians were equally keen to take it. On their way to attack York in May 1644, Covenanter forces took the stronghold to strengthen their position for the major siege that was about to take place in the Royalist capital of the North.

Headline: A gallant defence by Mrs Purefoy and her household left a dent in Prince Rupert’s forces.
Body Text: MP for Coventry and staunch Parliamentarian Colonel William Purefoy owned Caldecote Hall. On 28th August 1642, Prince Rupert and his brother Prince Maurice planned to capture Purefoy at his home. Purefoy was not there and a day long siege took place. The house was defended by Mrs Joane Purefoy, her son in law George Abbott and a handful of servants, four men and six women. The maids repeatedly loaded muskets. Three of Rupert’s officers and 15 of his men were gunned down.  When the shot ran out, the defenders melted down pewter plate to make more bullets.  Only when the outbuildings were set on fire did Mrs Purefoy surrender. Out of respect for the gallant defenders, Rupert prevented further damage to the hall.  The original door of the hall, bearing marks from musket fire, can still be seen in the local church.
Caption Image 1:
Prince Rupert.
“Prince Rupert, Count Palatinate” by Gerrit van Honthorst, licensed by National Portrait Gallery.
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Prince Rupert; Family homes

Headline: A quick siege ended in a bloody act of revenge.
Body Text:
The 15th century manor house, Canon Frome Court, was garrisoned for the King by Colonel Sir John Barnard and 120 men. The garrison wasn’t attacked until the arrival of a Scots army under the command of the Alexander Leslie, Earl of Leven, on 22nd June 1645.

Leslie invited Barnard to surrender. Barnard refused. Barnard’s garrison was forced to demolish a nearby medieval church in order to build defences for the oncoming siege. Leven and his troops stormed and captured the stronghold that same day. Once inside Leslie’s men savagely ransacked the house. In revenge for Scots who had been killed at Leicester recently, Leslie’s men executed Barnard and 70 of the Royalist garrison
Caption Image 1:
Alexander Leslie.
“Alexander Leslie” by Sir Anthony van Dyck, licensed by University of Leicester Fairclough Collection.
Tags: Stormed; No quarter; Churches at war

Headline: Roundhead tax collectors got a royal roasting at Canons Ashby.
Body Text: Canons Ashby was a key Parliamentarian raiding base for the area. It managed to survive much of the Civil War relatively unscathed. However, in August 1644, a group of Royalists attacked a group of Parliamentarian tax collectors, forcing them to take shelter in a local church. The Royalists used a small explosive device, known as a petard, to blow the church door in. Faced with the threat of being burnt alive, the tax collectors surrendered.
Caption Image 1:
Canons Ashby House.
“Canons Ashby House” by Jeroen Francois is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Mines and petards; Churches at war

Headline: The people of Cardiff took the law into their own hands and humiliated the King.
Body Text:
Cardiff Castle was initially held by a Royalist garrison, but a sneak attack using a secret passageway gave the castle to Parliamentary forces early on in the war. The Royalist commander William Seymour, the Marquis of Hertford, attacked the castle in another surprise assault, retaking control of the stronghold. His victory was short lived. Parliamentary forces and local troops immediately besieged the castle, retaking it once again after only five hours of fighting.

Later in the war, the Royalist position in Wales weakened. In July 1645, King Charles I visited the castle to meet with local Welsh leaders. Upon leaving the castle Charles was confronted by a small army of angry Clubmen – armed locals whose main concern was protecting their own region. The Clubmen declared themselves the "Peaceable Army."  They demanded they be given control of the castle and regional independence from the Royalists. Charles negotiated with the Peaceable Army. He allowed a local force to take over the garrison in exchange for £800 and the promise of 1,000 men to fight for the King. When Charles returned in September, he went back on his agreement and disbanded the Peaceable Army. Without the military strength to carry out his wishes, Charles was forced to watch the disgruntled locals cross over to the Parliamentary side, forcing the surrender of the Castle.

Unlike many castles, after the war the Cardiff Castle’s fortifications were not destroyed. In fact, they were strengthened in response to Parliamentarian fears of a Scottish invasion.
Caption Image 1:
Cardiff Castle.
“Cardiff Castle” by Michael Day is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Townspeople

Headline: Cardigan Castle was passed backwards and forwards in a series of bloody sieges.
Body Text:
Cardigan Castle started the war in Parliamentarian hands. In June 1644, the castle was taken for the Royalists by Colonel Gerrard. 200 Roundhead soldiers were killed defending the castle.

The Royalists held the castle for five months. They strengthened their defences using guns recovered from a local shipwreck. On the 21st December, Major-General Laugharne approached Cardigan with a Parliamentarian force of 500 cavalry and 200 infantry. Although the town surrendered immediately, the castle under the command of Major Slaughter remained defiant. Laugharne sent for artillery.  By the end of the year Laugharne had succeeded in storming and capturing the castle. Around 200 Cavaliers were killed in the siege, many more were taken prisoner.

Three days later, on 4th January 1645, Colonel Gerrard returned to Cardigan with 1200 cavalry and 1300 infantry soldiers. He easily recaptured the town and captured boats carrying supplies for the Parliamentarian soldiers in the castle. Despite losing 150 men in his initial attempt to besiege the stronghold, Gerrard’s men eventually retook the castle.

Before the year was out the Royalists would lose the castle to the Parliamentarians for the last time. Roundhead troops destroyed some of the stone buildings and burnt the rest, making the stronghold useless for defence.
Tags: Stormed; Slighted

Headline: The castle at Carew changed hands several times over the course of the war.
Body Text:
Despite strong Parliamentarian support in south Pembrokeshire, Sir George Carew chose to fight for the King and strengthened the castle against expected attacks. The first attack came in early 1644 when Parliamentary forces from Pembroke seized a number of Royalists strongholds. Carew was taken prisoner after a short but damaging siege.

The castle changed hands three times over the course of the war, eventually falling into Parliamentarian hands. The Roundheads pulled down the south wall of the castle, making it indefensible to the Royalists.

Following the Civil War, the castle was occupied for some years but eventually abandoned in 1686.
Caption Image 1:
Carew Castle.
“Carew Castle” by The Bridge Family is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Slighted

Headline: Carlisle’s starving defenders resorted to eating anything they could find rather than surrender.
Body Text:
In 1642, Carlisle was a Royalists stronghold commanded by James Graham, 1st Marquis of Montrose. Its first siege took place in 1644 when Scots Covenanters tried unsuccessfully to take the city.

Following the catastrophic Royalist defeat at Marston Moor in July 1644, and the storming of Newcastle in October 1644, Carlisle stood as the only significant Royalist stronghold in the north. The former Governor of York and King’s Commander in Chief in the north, Sir Thomas Glenham, took refuge in Carlisle. The north of England was occupied by Scots Covenanters on the side of Parliament. The Covenanters were command by General David Leslie.  In October Leslie besieged Carlisle with around 4,000 infantry and cavalry. The roads were blocked by earthworks which provided gun platforms. Leslie’s plan was to starve the defenders out.  The defending garrison was made up of around 700 men, which included many of the townsmen who had been given weapons to defend Carlisle. As the inhabitants’ food supplies ran out, Leslie tightened the ring around the city.  The defenders ate their horses, then dogs and rats.
