After the Royalist defeat at the Battle of Naseby in June 1645, there seemed no more hope of relief. On 25th June, Carlisle surrendered on honourable terms.  Following the surrender Leslie’s troops ransacked the cathedral, using some of the stone to strengthen Carlisle’s defences.

During the final stages of the siege the defenders had minted their own coins called “siege pieces.” The values of the coins were a shilling and three shillings.
Tags: Starved out; After Marston Moor; After Naseby

Headline: Clan loyalties and swapping sides defined the confusing siege of Castle Campbell.
Body Text:
During the First Civil War, Clan Campbell fought with the Covenanters. Their decision made a powerful enemy of James Graham, 1st Marquis of Montrose. Montrose was not only a Royalist, but also commanded an army made up of soldiers from Clan MacLean, long standing enemies of the Campbells. After the Battle of Inverlochy in 1645, Montrose’s men besieged Castle Campbell but were unable to take the stronghold.

In 1648, the Castle was placed under the command of Archibald Campbell, 1st Marquis of Argyll and an important member of the Covenanters. Despite fighting against the Royalists, many Covenanters were horrified by the execution of Charles I. Campbell switched sides and supported Charles’ son, Charles II.  Argyll opposed Charles’ invasion of England during the Third Civil War. In 1652, he switched sides to support Oliver Cromwell allowing the Parliamentarians to set up a garrison in the Castle.

In July 1654, in retaliation for the castle’s support of Cromwell, Royalist rebels attacked the stronghold and burned it down.
Caption Image 1:
Castle Campbell.
“Dollar Glen” by Vanessa is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Besiegers gave up; Scotland and Ireland; Turncoats and treachery

Headline: A Roundhead Colonel kept his distance but still managed to force a Royalist surrender.
Body Text: Caus Castle was one of the best defensive sites along the whole of the Welsh border. Surrounded by steep slopes and formidable ditch systems, the castle proved a challenge to any army that tried to take it. The Parliamentarian forces commanded by Colonel Mackwork understood this. In June 1645, Mackworth decided not to risk the lives of his soldiers in a direct attack. Instead he kept a safe distance and used cannon fire to successfully bombard the castle, leaving the fortress in ruins and forcing the Royalists to surrender.
Tags: Surrendered on terms

Headline: A besieged manor house didn’t even put up an effort.
Body Text: Caverswall Castle, the fortified manor house that belonged to the Craddock family, didn’t make a particularly good fortress. Built in 1615, the house had been created with luxury in mind, and was even described as being “indefensible”. In spite of this the house was still garrisoned by Parliamentary forces during the war.  When Royalist forces attacked in 1645, the defenders didn’t waste any time and surrendered straight away. The house survived undamaged.
Tags: Surrendered on terms

Headline: Despite a Royalist owner, Chatsworth House became a Parliamentarian stronghold.
Body Text:
William Cavendish, the owner of Chatsworth House, was a staunch Royalist. At the start of the Civil War, Cavendish and his family paid for the raising of armies for King Charles I. Unfortunately for Cavendish, this led to him being expelled from the House of Lords. Fearing for his life, he escaped abroad in 1642. In his absence, his estates were taken for Parliament and garrisoned under Sir John Gell.

On 29th November 1643, Chatsworth House was retaken by Royalist forces after a short siege. Parliament would take Chatsworth back the following year. The house was slighted but not completely. Throughout the war Chatsworth would remain an important target for Royalists. In 1645 the house was retaken by Colonel Shalcross who established a garrison of 300 men. This was the last time the house would change hands by force. It wasn’t until Charles II was crowned King that William Cavendish would return to his ancestral home.
Caption Image 1:
Chatsworth House.
“Chatsworth-004” by Andy Moore is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Slighted

Headline: During the Second Civil War a Royalist commander’s refusal to surrender proves to be a fatal mistake.
Body Text:
At the outbreak of the Civil War, Chepstow was a garrison for the Royalists. In April 1643, the Parliamentarian general, Sir William Waller, tried unsuccessfully to take Gwent’s castles. In October 1645, Parliamentarian artillery finally forced Chepstow’s garrison of 64 defenders to surrender to Waller.

In 1648, during the Second Civil War, the castle was seized by a local Royalist, Sir Nicholas Kemeys.  Oliver Cromwell, on his way to take Pembroke, demanded the castle’s surrender.  When Kemeys refused, Cromwell left Colonel Ewer’s regiment to take Chepstow.  The siege began on 23rd March. Ewer’s four cannon shot away the parapets of the towers, making life difficult for the defenders.  Even after the walls had been breached Kemeys wouldn’t surrender. On 25th May 1648 Ewer was forced to take the castle by direct attack. During the fight Kemeys was killed and 120 prisoners were taken.

Following the Restoration of the Monarchy in 1660 Henry Marten, one of the Commissioners who signed the death warrant of Charles I, was imprisoned in one of Chepstow Castle’s towers.  The tower currently bears his name. A plaque commemorating Sir Nicholas Kemeys’ death can still be seen today.
Caption Image 1:
Chepstow Castle.
“Chepstow Castle” by Ed Webster is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Stormed; Oliver Cromwell

Headline: The prospect of spectacular rescue came to nothing outside the wall of Chester.
Body Text:
The city of Chester was a Royalist stronghold from the beginning of the war. Sir William Brereton's Parliamentarian forces attacked the city in February 1645. They attempted to climb the walls, but the attack was forced back and the city was blockaded. In March the siege was disrupted when Prince Maurice arrived with a relief force. When Maurice left the following month he took 1,200 soldiers with him, leaving only 600 troops and a number of armed locals to defend the city.  On 20th September 1645, Colonel Michael Jones led a determined Parliamentarian attack on Chester's outer defences. The Parliamentarians moved artillery into a newly captured area and began blasting Chester's inner walls from close range. Two days later the artillery opened a breach in the walls.  At this critical point in the siege Lord Byron, one of Chester’s Royalist commander’s, received word that the King was marching from Wales to Chester’s aid with 4,000 cavalry.

The King arrived at Chester on 23rd September.  Sir Marmaduke Langdale took the main body of Royalist cavalry across the River Dee south of Chester. The plan was to trap the Parliamentarians between Langdale’s cavalry and the Chester garrison.  On the afternoon of 24th September at nearby Rowton Heath a Parliamentarian force, led by Colonel General Sydenham Poyntz with reinforcements from Colonel Michael Jones?, defeated the Royalists. King Charles I was said to have watched the disaster unfold from Chester's walls, accepting with strange calmness the defeat of his best remaining cavalry. On 25th September 1645, the King fled Chester.

Lord Byron refused to surrender Chester. The Parliamentarians built siege works around the city and maintained a constant bombardment. Conditions grew worse as the siege carried on into the winter and many of Chester’s citizens were by now dead or dying of starvation. Chester’s Mayor convinced Byron to surrender in January 1646. On 3rd February Sir William Brereton's forces finally occupied Chester.
Caption Image 1:
King Charles I.
“Charles I” by Sir Anthony van Dyck, licensed by Royal Collections Trust
Tags: Starved out; Sir William Brereton; Townspeople

Headline: Chichester faced an internal squabble over which side to support.
Body Text:
On 16th August 1642, shortly after the King had raised his standard at Nottingham, local MP William Cawley declared Chichester’s support for Parliament. Cawley’s decision was disputed by the Mayor of Chichester Robert Exton, who called upon Chichester’s citizens to fight for the King. The disagreement led to fighting between the two sides.  Cawley and his supporters were driven from the town and Chichester officially declared for the King. Chichester installed a garrison under Sir Edward Ford. Unfortunately for Chichester, this placed the town directly in the sights of the Roundhead Colonel William Waller, who sought to secure the entire south of England for Parliament.

On 21st December 1642, Waller arrived at Chichester with an army of 6,000 men. Waller immediately began to construct battering rams. He called for the surrender of the town. The Royalists refused, instead offering to give up any Roman Catholics within the city walls. Waller didn’t want Chichester’s Catholics. Parliament opened fire the next day. Setting up guns in the civilian buildings that surrounded the town walls, the Parliamentarians bombarded the Royalists for five days. Realising that defeat was certain, on 27th December Sir Edward Ford surrendered Chichester. Waller’s Roundheads looted the town, vandalising Chichester Cathedral in the process.
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Sir William Waller; Townspeople

Headline: Both Royalist and Parliamentarian garrisons struggled to retain this Dorset castle.
Body Text: Chideock Castle started out as a Royalist stronghold but it was taken by Parliamentarians, under the command of Captain Thomas Pyne, in March 1644. A few months later Royalist soldiers managed to retake the manor, only for it to be taken back by Parliamentarian soldiers less than a year later. This time the Parliamentarian soldiers, under the command of Colonel Ceeley, destroyed the Castle, leaving it in ruins.

Headline: Fighting was not the only way to end a siege and take a castle.
Body Text:
Chirk Castle, home to the Myddelton family, was secured for Parliament at the start of the First Civil War in 1642. The head of the house, Sir Thomas Myddelton, was Sergeant Major General of Parliament’s forces and frequently away from home. In January 1643, when Sir Thomas was fighting in Powys, Royalist troops took advantage of his absence. A force led by Colonel Ellis attacked the Castle and took the stronghold for King Charles I.

Sir Thomas made a number of attempts to retake his home by force. All ended in failure. It wasn’t until February 1646 that Sir Thomas Myddelton successfully retrieved his castle. He didn’t fight for it this time. He bought his castle back with a £200 bribe to the garrison’s Royalist governor, Sir John Watts.
Caption Image 1:
Chirk Castle.
“Chirk Castle” by Andrew and Annemarie is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Turncoats and treachery

Headline: A Welsh town’s ancient defences provided Prince Rupert with a quick but bloody victory.
Body Text:
When the Civil War began, Cirencester was held by Parliament. Its strategic location made it an important target for the Royalists. King Charles was confident of Welsh support but needed a safe route to get there. Falling halfway between the King’s base in Oxford and the Welsh border, Cirencester promised to be an excellent supply base for the King’s soldiers travelling to and from Wales. Cirencester’s old ruined Roman walls meant that the town would be easy for an attacking force to capture.

King Charles sent Prince Rupert, one of his best generals, to capture the town. On 3rd February 1643, at midday, Rupert attacked Cirencester with artillery fire. Rupert’s soldiers entered Cirencester. There was fierce fighting in the town’s streets. 300 were killed and 1,200 were taken prisoner. The town fell to the Royalists with the garrison of 1,000 men surrendering. The attack had only taken four hours.
Caption Image 1:
Prince Rupert.
“Prince Rupert, Count Palatinate” by Gerrit van Honthorst, licensed by National Portrait Gallery.
Tags: Stormed; Prince Rupert

Headline: Cromwell was tricked and the New Model Army suffered its first defeat at Clonmel, but the Irish celebrations didn’t last for long.
Body Text:
Oliver Cromwell besieged the town of Clonmel on 27th April 1650 with a force of 8,000 infantry, 600 cavalry and twelve field guns.  Clonmel was defended by the Royalist commander Hugh Dubh O'Neill. Cromwell planned to take Clonmel by direct attack. In early May Cromwell's gunners bombarded Clonmel's northern wall but little damage was done. Cromwell waited for heavier cannon to be brought to him which arrived on 16th May. This time the cannon fire caused an opening in the town wall. Cromwell planned to attack the following morning, sending his infantry into the break in the wall to fight their way into the town from there and capture the North Gate. Cromwell and his cavalry would wait to enter the town as soon as the gate was opened.

What Cromwell didn’t know was that Clonmel’s defenders had built a V-shaped inner fortification of earth and timber behind the point where the gunners were battering the wall.  The Irish fortification was about six feet high and lined with musketeers. When the English soldiers entered the breach, they were trapped in an enclosed area with no protection from the Irish musket and cannon fire. They couldn’t go forwards because of the fortification and they couldn’t go backwards because their own soldiers were pouring into the breach behind them. Up to 1,000 of Cromwell’s men were killed in the attack.

Cromwell’s foot soldiers refused to enter the breach a second time. They asked Cromwell to send in the cavalry, who were better protected by their iron helmets and body armour. At around 3.00pm, Cromwell’s cavalry attacked on foot. The defenders were quickly driven back. Fierce hand-to hand fighting continued for three hours, but the English couldn’t penetrate the Irish defences. Many of Cromwell’s officers were killed during the second attack. Cromwell’s men retreated. It is thought that between 1,500 and 2,500 English soldiers were killed during the assault. It was the first serious defeat suffered by the New Model Army and the greatest loss of life it sustained in a single action. Cromwell was now faced with the lengthy prospect of starving the town into surrender.

Several hundred of O'Neill’s men were dead and their ammunition was gone. Almost no food remained. The night after the assault O'Neill decided to evacuate his troops. The Irish soldiers slipped away under cover of darkness. The next day, John White, the Mayor of Clonmel, sent a message to Cromwell asking for terms for the town’s surrender. Cromwell was anxious to bring the messy siege to an end but had not realized that O'Neill and his soldiers were gone. Cromwell promised that the lives and property of the townspeople would be spared if they surrendered. Although Cromwell was furious when he learned that he had been tricked, he kept his word to the town’s people.
Caption Image 1:
Oliver Cromwell.
“Oliver Cromwell” by Robert Walker, licensed by National Portrait Gallery.
Tags: Defenders withdrew; Scotland and Ireland; Oliver Cromwell; Townspeople

Headline: A ditch in time?
Body Text:
The Parliamentarian garrison of Cockermouth Castle found itself under siege by Royalist troops in August 1648. The castle had strong defences including a series of ditches. They were able to hold out against the attackers for a month, by which time they were relieved by Parliamentarian soldiers.

At the time, Charles II had amassed armies in Scotland. Fearing that the castle might be used as a base for an invasion of England, Parliamentarian forces filled in the castle’s defensive ditches to render them useless.
Tags: Relieved

Headline: The torture of messenger boys, the desecration of graves and the use of poisoned bullets all occurred in the bloody siege of Colchester
Body Text:
During April 1648, rioting broke out in several places around the country. The rioters demanded the return of King Charles to full power. The Cavalier war veteran Sir Charles Lucas took command of the rebel Royalists in Essex. On 12th June, Lucas’ Royalists occupied Colchester, hoping to recruit more troops before marching on to persuade Norfolk and Suffolk to fight the King. The New Model Army, under the command of General Fairfax, marched quickly up from Kent. The following day Fairfax was at the outskirts of Colchester.

Fairfax tried to take Colchester by direct attack. Between 500 and 1,000 of his men were killed and Fairfax resigned himself to a long siege. Roads leading to Colchester were secured to prevent the Royalists breaking out. Parliamentarian warships blockaded the mouth of the River Colne. Throughout June the Parliamentarians built a ring of forts around the town where siege guns were mounted to batter Colchester’s walls. On 2nd July the siege works around Colchester were completed. The siege grew bitter and brutal. Fairfax's troops committed a number of war crimes.  They tortured a messenger boy and destroyed graves in the Lucas family vault. On the other side, the Royalists were accused of using bullets that they had roughened and rolled in sand to increase the chance of infecting the wounds of their enemies. By August, Colchester’s food had almost run out. The defenders were starving, but Sir Charles Lucas fought on. On 24th August, news came of the Royalist defeat at the Battle of Preston. Realising that their cause was lost, Colchester began negotiations for terms of surrender.

Fairfax's terms were harsh. Although Junior officers and the lower ranks would not be killed, the lives of Senior officers depended on the whim of their victorious captors. On 27th August 1648, Fairfax sentenced Sir Charles Lucas, Sir George Lisle, Colonel Farre and a mercenary Sir Bernard Gascoigne to death by firing squad.  Farre escaped and Gascoigne was allowed to live because he was a foreign national. On the evening of 28th August 1648, in Colchester Castle, Lucas and Lisle were shot dead. Fairfax justified the harshness of the punishment on the grounds that they had caused unnecessary bloodshed by attempting to defend a useless position. Lucas and Lisle died courageously.  They were soon regarded as Royalist martyrs by supporters of the King. Pamphlets appeared within days condemning their death as acts of murder committed by General Fairfax. According to legend, the grass never again grew on the spot where Lucas and Lisle were killed. The area is now paved over and marked by a memorial obelisk.
Caption Image 1:
Sir Thomas Fairfax.
“Thomas Fairfax” by William Marshall, licensed by National Portrait Gallery.
Tags: Starved out; Sir Thomas Fairfax

Headline: Parliamentarian soldiers made a fortune when they looted this Warwickshire manor house.
Body Text:
Compton Wynyates was the ancestral home of the Compton family. Spencer Compton, was a close friend of Charles I and a staunch Royalist who fought for the King at the Battle of Edgehill. The house was a useful base for raiding parties, which made the Parliamentarians even more keen to take the manor.

On 12th June 1644, Compton Wynyates was besieged by Parliamentary forces under the command of Colonel William Purefoy. The manor house fell two days later. One of Spencer’s sons hid in the attic tending to the garrison’s wounded. He managed to stay undetected and eventually made his escape. Others were less lucky. During the capture of the Compton Wynyates, the attackers took 120 prisoners, £5,000 (£450,000 in today’s money), 60 horses, 400 sheep, 160 head of cattle, 6 earthen pots of coins recovered from the moat, and most of the house’s furnishings.

Keen to regain their ancestral home, the Comptons attempted to recapture the house on 29th January 1645, attacking with over 1,000 cavalry troops. Despite managing to take several of the Manor’s outbuildings, the Royalists were beaten back after four hours of fighting. The Compton family fled into exile abroad. They did not return home until the Restoration of the Monarchy in 1660.
Caption Image 1:
Compton Wynyates.
“Compton Wynyates” by Rupert Parsons House is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Family homes

Headline: A Welsh Royalist changed sides but never lost his loyalty to his home town.
Body Text:
Born and raised in the Welsh town, the governor of Conwy Castle was the Royalist Archbishop of York John Williams. Williams was keen to see his hometown protected, spending his own money refortifying Conwy. The town was at risk from Parliamentarian attacks as it had become a rallying point for Royalist support in North Wales. Despite his loyalty, Williams was replaced as governor of the Castle by Sir John Owen in 1645, creating a bitter dispute between the two men. Williams’ changed sides and went over to Parliament soon after.

The town of Conwy was besieged in August 1646, but it was allowed to surrender thanks in part to John Williams’ good relations with the Parliamentarian commander. The castle, however, did not surrender. It took a three month siege force the garrison to surrender, after which the castle was slighted to prevent Royalists ever using it again.

There is strong evidence to suggest that John Williams’ decision to change side was made, in part, to protect his beloved hometown.
Caption Image 1:
Conwy Castle.
“Conwy castle rear view” by Ashley Perkins is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Slighted; Turncoats and treachery

Headline: Lady Bankes and her children managed to inflict staggering casualties on the Roundheads that tried to take her home.
Body Text:
Sir John Bankes, the owner of Corfe Castle, died in December 1644. By 1645, Corfe Castle was one of the few remaining Royalist strongholds in southern England. In late 1645 the castle was besieged by a Parliamentarian force, under the command of a Colonel Bingham. One of the castles defending officers, Colonel Pitman, plotted with Bingham. In February 1646, Pitman proposed that he would go to Somerset and bring back 100 reinforcements. He returned with 100 Roundhead soldiers disguised as Royalists who were welcomed inside as reinforcements. Once inside the castle, Pitman’s men waited until the defending force attacked before launching their own assault. The defenders were attacked from within and without, forcing the castle’s governor to surrender.

On 27th February, the defenders were allowed to leave. In March 1646, Parliament voted to destroy the castle’s fortifications. The stone from Corfe Castle provided a ready supply of building material that was reused by the villagers.  After the Restoration of the Monarchy in 1660, the Bankes family regained their properties. Rather than rebuild or replace the ruined castle they chose to build a new house at Kingston Lacy on their other Dorset estate near Wimborne Minster.

Legend has it that because Lady Bankes had showed such enormous courage defending her home, she was allowed to keep the keys of the castle. However, recent research has challenged whether Lady Bankes was actually at Corfe at all during the final siege.

Headline: King Charles I made an enemy of Coventry before the war even began.
Body Text:
Although, Coventry had traditionally been loyal to King Charles, his controversial “ship money” tax proved a step too far. At the outbreak of war, the city chose to fight for Parliament and proved to be a valuable stronghold.

Charles responded quickly, sending 6,000 cavalry troops to retake the town in late August. The King’s soldiers were beaten back the same day by the Parliamentarian garrison and Coventry’s townsfolk. Over the course of the war, the city became a key Roundhead outpost and was used to house Royalist prisoners.

After Charles II was crowned in 1662, he ordered the destruction of the city walls as revenge for the city taking up arms against his father.

Headline: A bizarre and creative use of hostages kept the Roundheads out of Crowland, but the demon drink let them in.
Body Text:
The fenland town of Crowland was fortified by the Royalists in March 1643. When it became known that Captain Welbie planned to declare Crowland for the King, Mr Ram, a Parliamentarian minister from Spalding, wrote to the townspeople of Crowland seeking to change their mind.  Welbie travelled to Spalding and kidnapped Mr Ram, John Harrington and two 60 year olds named Horn and Slater.  The prisoners were taken to Crowland.

Three weeks later a Parliamentarian force from Spalding attacked Crowland. The four prisoners were taken to the ramparts and tied to stakes.  It was only luck that stopped the prisoners from being shot by the attackers.  Once the attackers realised the identity of the four prisoners they broke off the assault.  The four prisoners were taken away.  The Spalding men advanced. The four men were brought out once again and placed in front of the attacking soldiers as Crowland’s cannons hurled missiles over their heads. Captain Harrington of Spalding took a musket from a soldier and shot three times at his own father without knowing who it was. When the attackers realized what was happening they aimed their muskets well to the right of the hostages. The Crowland men instantly moved the four hapless men into the line of fire. The men continued to suffer in this way for three hours or so. Rather than kill their own men, the Spa’ding force withdrew. The prisoners were removed. The attackers renewed their assault on a heavy scale. The defenders produced the prisoners once again, and the attack failed.

The Crowland garrison believed that they had won. A priest named Jackson had the prisoners brought from their cells and performed a short ceremony in celebration of victory.  The garrison troops spent the rest of 28th April getting drunk and mocking the Parliamentary forces surrounding the town.  While the defenders were intoxicated the Parliamentarians, commanded by Colonel Sir Miles Hobert, Colonel Sir Anthonie Irbie, and Colonel Oliver Cromwell who had come to their assistance, stormed Crowland from three different directions, entering the town before anybody could realize what was happening.

Headline: The King’s nephew was given the task of besieging this Devonshire town.
Body Text:
The town of Dartmouth declared itself for Parliament in the early days of the First Civil War. A year later the King’s nephew Prince Maurice turned his attention to Dartmouth. In September 1643, shortly after his capture of Exeter, Maurice marched on the town. Hampered by bad weather, the siege dragged on for longer than expected. Rather than suffer the bombardment, Dartmouth surrendered on 5th October 1643. The main defences had already been taken and 17 defenders had been killed. Once inside Dartmouth the Royalists set about reinforcing the defences they had just overcome to establish the town as a stronghold for the King.

The town was held for three years until 19th January 1646, when Thomas Fairfax stormed Dartmouth. The defenders fled or surrendered. Fairfax’s men quickly removed the defences that the Royalists had spent so long fortifying.
Tags: Surrendered on terms

Headline: Three rebel castles supported each other in their fight against Parliament.
Body Text: Deal Castle was one of the three “castles of the Downs” that had initially supported Parliament but later turned to the Royalist cause. Deal had been taken by Kentish rebels in May 1648. Three months later, at the beginning of August 1648, Parliamentarian commander Colonel Rich set about retaking all three castles. Despite a strong artillery force of four cannons, the Deal rebels, supported by troops from the other two castles, held out for three weeks. By 25th August, the damage done to Deal Castle was so great that the defenders were forced to surrender.

Headline: A Royalist garrison that once hosted the King refused to surrender until they were ordered to.
Body Text:
Denbigh Castle was garrisoned for the King at the start of the First Civil War by William Salisbury. He invested much of his fortune into repairing the castle and raising and maintaining a garrison. The castle was a useful stronghold in the region, even hosting King Charles I after his heavy defeat at the Battle of Rowton Heath on 24th September 1645.

The following year, Parliamentarian forces under General Mytton laid siege to the Castle for six months. Despite heavy cannon bombardment, the Royalists refused to surrender. Defeat only came after a special order from the King to lay down their arms. The Royalists were able to negotiate an honourable surrender and on 26th October 1646, the castle was handed over to Mytton’s men who slighted it and used it as a prison for the remainder of the war.

Headline: Events elsewhere prevented a Parliamentarian force from taking Devizes Castle.
Body Text:
Devizes supported the King at the beginning of the First Civil War, making it a target for nearby Parliamentarian forces. Barely a year later on 10th July 1643, Parliamentarian troops under the command of Sir William Waller led an attack against the castle. The attackers might have succeeded, but three days later, Waller’s crushing defeat at the nearby Battle of Roundway Down forced him to retreat and the attack was abandoned. The castle and town remained in Royalist hands, and Colonel Charles Lloyd was made governor in 1644. Recognising the town’s vulnerability, Lloyd fortified the castle and established a garrison of 400 men.

In September 1645, Cromwell invaded the town and besieged the castle. Cromwell called for Lloyd and his men to surrender, but his offer was refused. In response, the Parliamentarians bombarded the Castle with mortar fire, killing several of the defenders. Realising they had no real chance against the overwhelming artillery power, the Royalists negotiated surrender. A few years later in May 1648 the castle was slighted, making it useless for future Royalist occupation.
Tags: Relieved; Slighted; Oliver Cromwell; Sir William Waller

Headline: Troublesome Royalists were given no mercy when their stronghold was finally captured.
Body Text:
After Oliver Cromwell defeated Royalist forces at the Battle of Dunbar on 3rd September 1650, he established control in a large part of southern Scotland. This pushed remaining Royalists in the area to band together at Dirleton Castle. From this stronghold, the Royalists launched raids on English supply routes causing great inconvenience for Cromwell’s forces.

In retaliation, on 9th November of the same year, Cromwell ordered General Monck, General Lambert and their 1,600 troops to capture Dirleton Castle. An artillery bombardment destroyed the drawbridge and inner gate, as well as badly damaging much of the building. The Royalist forces surrendered a day later and in a fury, Parliamentarian commanders ordered for the defending Captain and two of his deputies to be hanged from the castle walls. The castle was slighted and used as a field hospital for a short time, before it fell into disrepair.

Headline: A Royalist soldier’s stubbornness led to a two year siege and a knighthood.
Body Text:
Donnington Castle was strategically important. It commanded the roads from London to the west of England and the roads from Portsmouth to Oxford and the north. After the first battle of Newbury in September 1643, Donnington was garrisoned by Royalist troops commanded by Colonel John Boys. Boys strengthened Donnington’s defences by building an extensive system of earthworks around the castle. In late July 1644, around 3,500 Parliamentarian cavalry, commanded by Lieutenant-General Middleton, approached Donnington. On 31st July Boys rejected Middleton's invitation to surrender. Middleton attacked, but had no siege artillery so instead commanded his forces to climb the castle walls but the Parliamentarians were driven back and 300 of Middleton’s men were killed. Shortly after his unsuccessful assault, Middleton was ordered to reinforce the Earl of Essex and soon after left Donnington and marched away to the west.

On 29th September 1644, the siege began again with Colonel Jeremy Horton leading the attacking force this time. He had more soldiers than Middleton. He also had siege guns. Horton bombarded the castle for 12 days, shattering three towers and destroying part of the walls. Still Boys refused to surrender. On the 4th October the Earl of Manchester arrived to take over the siege. Once again Boys refused to surrender. The Earl of Manchester resolved to storm the castle. Over a three week period 1,000 cannonballs were fired at Donnington. Despite inflicting structural damage to the castle the attackers were no closer to taking it when King Charles and his army approached. Manchester withdrew.

On 22nd October 1644 Boys was knighted by the King for his loyalty. After the second Battle of Newbury on 27th October, the King set out to join Prince Rupert in Bath. He left his crown and great seal at Donnington. The following day Sir William Waller and the whole Parliamentarian army surrounded the castle. For the fourth time Boys was invited to surrender. Once again he refused.  On 9th November King Charles returned to Donnington. He relieved the castle and retrieved his crown.

By the close of 1645 Parliament was on the verge of winning the war but Donnington still stood for the King.  Cromwell gave Colonel John Dalbier the task of destroying Donnington Castle. Unfortunately for the Parliamentarians, Sir John Boys had not only provisioned the castle, he had also set fire to the village of Donnington and other nearby villages to deprive the besiegers of cover. On 30th March 1646, with the King’s cause lost, Dalbier wrote to Boys telling him that he could not expect any relief and advised him to surrender. Boys was allowed to send messengers to the King at Oxford for instructions.  The King advised Boys to negotiate the best terms he could. On 1st April 1646, after years of fighting, Donnington Castle finally surrendered.

Headline: Despite a strong Royalist legacy, the actions of a small group of local men secured the castle at Dover for Parliament.
Body Text:
Before the Civil War, Dover Castle had a long history of housing English Royalty. Having previously hosted Henry VIII, Elizabeth I and King Charles I’s Queen Henrietta Maria, it was no surprise that the Castle supported the King at the outbreak of the First Civil War.

In the town of Dover there was a great deal of Parliamentary support, in particular a local tradesman named Richard Drake. Knowing the castle defences were weak and that it was garrisoned by only 20 men, Drake and ten of his Parliamentarian friends decided to take the castle themselves.

On the night of 20th August 1642, Drake and his friends began their attack. Half of them scaled the cliffs and the other half climbed straight over the castle walls. They quickly overcame the four watchmen, and the remaining 16 defenders who thought they were being attacked by a much larger force of professional soldiers, quickly surrendered.

As news of Drake’s actions spread, the Royalists immediately decided to retaliate and sent an army of 2,000 soldiers to take the castle back. By the time they arrived though, Sir Thomas Fairfax had already garrisoned the castle with a 500 strong Parliamentarian army. The Royalists fired over 500 cannon balls at the castle but were unable to take it and the stronghold remained in Parliamentarian hands for the rest of the war.

Headline: The massacre at Drogheda made Cromwell one of the most hated Englishmen in Irish history.
Body Text:
Drogheda was an important town because it guarded the most direct route from Dublin into Ulster. Following an earlier Parliamentarian attempt to take the town, the one legged soldier Sir Arthur Aston was appointed Governor.  Drogheda was one of the best-fortified towns in Ireland and Aston boasted that anyone who could take Drogheda could capture Hell itself.

On 3rd September 1649, the Parliamentarian army under the command of Oliver Cromwell arrived at the south side of Drogheda. Cromwell wasted no time in deploying siege guns to blast openings in the walls. On 10th September, Cromwell invited Drogheda to surrender. Aston rejected the offer and the bombardment started as soon after.  By noon on 11th September, breaches had been blasted in the southern and eastern walls. At around 5.00pm, Cromwell ordered the attack to begin. Cromwell’s Roundheads forced their way into the town. Cromwell himself was there, rallying the wavering Parliamentarians. The defenders fell back as the Roundheads poured through the breach and overran the Royalist entrenchments. Aston and about 300 of his men fell back on Mill Mount, which was protected by a bank and ditch and a timber barricade. The defences were soon broken down and many defenders were killed. Cromwell ordered that no mercy be shown. Aston was beaten to death with his own wooden leg by Roundhead soldiers who believed that the false limb was filled with gold coins. By late evening, up to 6,000 Parliamentarians had entered the town. They overwhelmed all resistance, slaughtering officers and soldiers. Catholic priests and friars were treated as if they were soldiers and killed on sight. Many civilians died in the carnage. A group of defenders who had barricaded themselves in the steeple of St Peter's Church were burned alive when the Roundheads set fire to the building. Around 2,000 people died in the massacre. A number of prisoners had surrendered before Cromwell had given the order for no mercy. The prisoners were murdered in cold blood. Some of the surviving defenders were captured the following day and transported to Barbados. Parliamentarian losses were around 150.

According to the customs of 17th century warfare, a city under siege that refused to surrender could expect no mercy if taken by direct attack. Cromwell regarded the massacre at Drogheda as God’s righteous judgment on the Catholics who had slaughtered Protestant settlers during the Irish Uprising of 1641. Cromwell’s view was probably shared by most Protestants at the time. Cromwell also considered that the example of Drogheda would serve as a warning to other garrisons in Ireland. The message was to surrender or risk a similar fate, preventing further bloodshed in the long run. But the massacre of Drogheda left an indelible stain on Cromwell's reputation. It has lived on in Irish folk memory, making Oliver Cromwell’s name one of the most hated in Irish history.

Headline: Surrendering at Dudley Castle proved to be a smart move for an unpopular Royalist Commander.
Body Text:
A Royalist stronghold throughout the Civil War, Dudley Castle was thought impossible to destroy by mining or bombardment.  On 10th June 1644, Lord Denbigh and an army of 3,500 men arrived to disprove this notion. Denbigh placed the castle under siege. He had brought with him a 32 pounder cannon, known as the “Stafford Great Piece”. A Royalist attempt to relive the siege, led by Prince Rupert, resulted in a skirmish fought in Tipton Green. Although both sides claimed victory it was technically a Royalist win. The Cavaliers had succeeded in driving off Denbigh’s Roundheads and held the Castle for the next two years.

On 27th April 1646, with Royalists were losing ground in Worcestershire, another siege began. The garrison of 340 decided to resist so they burned all the buildings around the castle, including St Edmunds Church. But their resolve soon gave way. The governor Colonel Thomas Leveson surrendered to Sir William Brereton on 13th May 1646.  With the castle now in Parliament’s hands they discovered it contained a year’s supply of food, ample water, beer, 20 barrels of powder and firearms for 400 men. Colonel Thomas Leveson’s premature surrender was not popular with the local people, whose homes and livelihoods he had wrecked. If he not been protected by Parliamentarian troops he might well have been lynched.

Headline: The imposing castle at Dumbarton was a much sought after prize during the British Civil Wars.
Body Text:
Sitting on top of the 73 metre high Dumbarton Rock, Dumbarton Castle presented a formidable challenge to any attacker. Its natural strength made it a much sought after prize and the castle changed hands multiple times. The stronghold was first taken during the Bishops’ Wars in 1639 when Covenanter supporters forcibly took the keys from the governor while he was at Church. At the end of the First Bishops War later in the year, the Castle was returned to the Royalists as part of the Treaty of Berwick.

In 1651, during Cromwell’s invasion of Scotland in the Third Civil War, the castle was besieged by General Monck and eventually fell to the Parliamentarians. Later, it was retaken by Royalists who in turn surrendered it back to General Lambert’s forces in 1652 in order to avoid being attacked. The castle changed hands for the last time in 1654, when Royalist forces took it in a surprise attack.

Headline: Women played a prominent role when valuable objects belonging to Charles II were smuggled out of a besieged Scottish castle.
Body Text:
Charles II was crowned King of Scotland on 1st January 1651, using Scottish royal clothing and ornaments (or regalia). But with Cromwell's troops in Scotland, the regalia could not be returned to Edinburgh where they belonged. In June the decision was taken to place them at Dunnottar Castle. Hidden is sacks of wool, the regalia was brought to Dunnottar by Katherine Drummond.

Sir George Ogilvy of Barras was appointed Governor of the castle. On November 1651 Cromwell's troops called on Ogilvy to surrender. He refused. During the siege of the castle, plans were made to spirit away the royal regalia and papers belonging to the King. The King's papers were removed first. Anne Lindsay walked through the besieging force with the papers sewn into her clothes. Two stories are told about the removal of the regalia.  Christian Fletcher, a minister’s wife, claimed that during February and March 1652, over the course of three visits to the castle, she carried away the crown, scepter, sword and sword-case, hidden among sacks of goods. Another account, given in the 18th century, records that the regalia were lowered from the castle onto the beach, where they were collected by Fletcher's servant and carried off in a basket of seaweed. Having smuggled the regalia from the castle, Fletcher and her husband buried them under the floor of the Old Kirk at Kinneff.

In May 1652, Parliamentary commander Colonel Thomas Morgan took delivery of the heavy artillery necessary to break down the castle’s walls.  Within days, holes had been punched in the keep and seven of the 70 defenders had been killed.  Food was running out. Ogilvy surrendered on 24th May, on the condition that the garrison could go free.

In 1660, at the Restoration of Charles II, the regalia were removed from Kinneff Church and returned to the King.

Headline: A change of allegiance meant the Luttrell family had to endure both Royalist and Parliamentarians attacks.
Body Text:
At the beginning of the First Civil War, Thomas Luttrell and his family declared Dunster Castle for Parliament. Knowing the Royalists were keen to establish themselves in the south west William Russel, the Parliamentarian commander for the area, ordered the garrison to be strengthened.

Russel’s fears were confirmed in 1642 when the Royalist commander William Seymour attacked the castle. Seymour was driven back by the garrison, led by Thomas' wife, Jane. On 7th June 1643, as the war in the south west turned in favour of the King, the Royalists gathered forces to attack the castle again. This time Luttrell surrendered, switching sides to support the Royalists until his death the following February.

As the fortunes of the Royalist forces reversed towards the end of the war, Colonel Robert Blake set out to retake Dunster in November 1645. Blake set up his artillery in Dunster village and started to dig tunnels to undermine the walls.  Legend claims that at one point Blake threatened to stand Wyndham’s mother in the line of fire unless he surrendered.  When the spirited old lady urged her son to just do his duty, Blake backed down.  The castle was briefly relieved by reinforcements in February 1646, but the siege resumed and by April the Royalists’ situation was desperate.  An honourable surrender was negotiated on 20th April 1646. A few years later in August 1650, Parliament decided to slight the castle’s medieval defences. It took 300 workmen 12 days to demolish the walls.

Headline: A vicious bombardment prevented a besieged garrison from burying their dead.
Body Text:
At the outbreak of the First Civil War, Eccleshall Castle was the home of Bishop Robert Wright. A close friend of Charles I, the Bishop had previously made a speech in support of the King in the House of Lords but fearing reprisals from Parliament, had fled to the safety of Eccleshall Castle. Parliamentarian forces attempted to take the castle by siege in early 1643, but after the Battle of Hopton Heath in March, nearby Royalists came to the castle’s rescue and beat off the attackers.

In June of the same year, Sir William Brereton arrived to retry the attack. Artillery was installed in a nearby church tower and churchyard, bombarding the castle and causing considerable damage to the walls. The castle was finally taken on 30th August. When Parliamentarian soldiers entered the buildings, they discovered that the Bishop had died of a heart attack during the siege, but the heavy bombardment meant the household had been unable to bury him. Most of the defenders were found to have escaped and of those that remained, many were drunk. The castle was slighted to prevent further use as a fortress, but the main building was preserved and used as a prison for Royalist gentry.
Tags: Slighted; Sir William Brereton; Churches at war

Headline: Besieged three times over 10 years, Edinburgh’s final surrender may have been due to an act of betrayal.
Body Text:
In March 1639, at the beginning of the First Bishop’s War, a Covenanter army, led by Alexander Leslie captured Edinburgh Castle after a short siege.  The castle was restored to Charles I after the Treaty of Berwick in June 1639. The peace was short lived. The following year, during the Second Bishop’s War, Leslie laid siege to the castle again.  Leslie’s forces bombarded Edinburgh’s east front. The city’s governor, Lord Ettrick, conducted a determined defence, but the garrison ran out of supplies. On 15th September 1640, after a three month siege, starvation eventually forced Edinburgh’s surrender.  The defenders were allowed to march out with full honours.

In May 1650, the Scots crowned Charles II, supporting the Royalist cause they had fought against previously. In September, following Cromwell’s defeat of the Covenanter army at the Battle of Dunbar, the city of Edinburgh was taken by Parliament, but Edinburgh castle remained in Covenanter hands. The castle was bombarded with cannon fire. A mine was dug under the castle to undermine the wall.  On 24th December, the castle surrendered after a three month siege. The governor, Colonel Walter Dundas, surrendered to Cromwell despite the castle having enough supplies to hold out for a longer siege. After the siege Walter Dundas changed sides and joined Parliament which led many people to suspect that Dundas might have deliberately betrayed Edinburgh Castle when he surrendered it to the Roundheads.

Headline: A valuable strategic position was overwhelmed by quick thinking and clever tactics.
Body Text:
Situated directly between the Royalist strongholds of Oxford and Gloucester, the town of Evesham was a communication route. This made Evesham a significant target for Parliamentarian forces. The town was garrisoned for the King by William Legg. Despite strong natural defences, the town had very few fortifications, with only a network of ditches to deter attackers.

Colonel Edward Massey seized his chance to besiege the castle on 26th May 1645. The Parliamentarian troops easily overcame the defensive ditches by using bundles of brushwood to fill them in. Once close enough, Massey split his force, attacking from several directions and overwhelming the Royalist defence. Eyewitness accounts recorded that the attack “lasted almost an houre with great fury on both sides” before the Royalists surrendered. Over the course of the siege, Massey lost seven soldiers, while 11 of the defenders were killed and 548 taken prisoner. On top of this, the Parliamentarians took 200 horses, 20 barrels of powder, 700 firearms and two tonnes of match.
Tags: Stormed; Edward Massey

Headline: A city changed hands, a royal baby was born and a siege ended in a civilized fashion.
Body Text:
From the outbreak of the First Civil War in 1642 Exeter was controlled by a pro-Parliamentarian group.  In December a Royalist army under Sir Ralph Hopton approached the city, which was reinforced by Parliamentary troops from Plymouth.  Hopton issued a demand for the defenders to surrender.  The city sent a force to Cowley where a small, fierce skirmish forced the Royalists to fall back. Winter weather halted hostilities and Hopton withdrew to Cornwall. On the 6th January 1643, the Earl of Stamford arrived with Parliamentary reinforcements and was made Governor.

By June 1643, Exeter was once again surrounded by the King's army commanded by Sir John Berkeley. In July the Royalists besiegers sank five ships across the River Exe to prevent relief from the sea. A strong Royalist following in the city undermined the defender’s morale. On the 27th August 1643, Prince Maurice arrived with reinforcements enough to swell the ranks of the besieging army. On 3rd September an artillery barrage set fire to buildings and damaged Exeter’s walls. There was a lull in the fighting. Terms of surrender were offered but they were refused. A second assault quickly began. The Royalist troops had captured Roundhead artillery and fired on Parliament with their own guns. Generous terms of surrender were offered by Prince Maurice and on 7th September 1643, Stamford and his men marched out on Exeter after a 16 day siege.

Sir John Berkeley became governor of the new Royalist garrison and repaired the defences damaged during the siege.   Following the Royalist defeat at Naseby, Parliamentarian forces began to take Royalist strongholds in the south west.  In October, Exeter was cut off from Royalist support by a blockade established by Fairfax.  In January 1646, an invitation to surrender was rejected by Berkeley, who believed relief from Oxford was still possible.  Fairfax gradually squeezed Exeter, taking outlying Royalist strongpoints and establishing his own.  Just as preparations to storm the city were almost complete, news arrived that a Royalist force, led by the Prince of Wales and Lord Hopton, was gathering in North Devon. On 10th February, Fairfax set out for North Devon to neutralise the new threat and the attack on Exeter was postponed. Fairfax pursued the Royalists into Cornwall.  On 15th March the Prince of Wales fled to France and his forces surrendered. By the 29th, Fairfax had returned and two days later he delivered terms of surrender to Berkeley. After six days of negotiations, on the 9th April, an honourable agreement to surrender was reached.  The King’s youngest daughter, Princess Henrietta, who had been born in Exeter in 1644, was allowed to leave with her household. The garrison were free to leave. Those left inside Exeter were guaranteed safety from plunder.

Headline: A son held back when ordered to attack his father. But was it family loyalty or something more mercenary that stayed his hand?
Body Text:
Faringdon House was the home of the Pye family and owned by Sir Robert Pye, a Royalist supporter. Pye’s son, also called Robert, left the house after declaring his support for Parliament, splitting the family. On the 28th April 1645, Sir Robert received a summons from Oliver Cromwell who was nearby with his army. The summons read:

?Sir,
I summon you to deliver into my hands the house wherein you are, and your ammunition, with all things else there, together with your Persons to be disposed of as the Parliament shall appoint: which, if you refuse to do, you are to expect the utmost extremity of war.
I rest your servant. April 29, 1645 O. Cromwell?

Sir Robert refused, only to be sent a further message from Cromwell:

?Sir,
I understand by forty or fifty poor men whom you forced into your House that you have many there whom you cannot arm, and who are not serviceable to you. If these men should perish by your means, it were great Inhumanity. Surely Honour and Honesty requires this, that you be prodigal of your own Lives, yet not be so of theirs. If God gives you into my hands, I will not spare a Man of you, if you put me to a Storm.
Oliver Cromwell.?

The Royalists again refused the request, and unwilling to give them any more chances, Cromwell attacked at 3.00am on the morning of 30th April. Despite putting up a strong fight, the attackers could not breach the walls and after 14 of his men had been killed, Cromwell decided that the attempt was too costly and abandoned it.

The Parliamentarian forces were not finished, and decided to attack again in June 1646. This time though, the task was given to Sir Robert’s son. Robert made little effort to attack Faringdon house, partly because he was still due to inherit the house after his father’s death, but also because the King had announced the surrender of nearby Oxford and nearby garrisons were expected to soon follow. The surrender was negotiated and on 24th June, Sir Robert and the garrison marched from the house.

Headline: A shot fired by one of his own men narrowly missed William Waller, but he went on to capture many valuables.
Body Text:
Sir William Waller was ordered to secure the south-western approach to London by capturing Farnham in Surrey. Farnham occupied a strategic position mid-way between London and Winchester. Though initially supporting Parliament, the original garrison had fled on hearing the King's army approaching and the town was taken by Royalists. When Waller's forces arrived in November 1642 the castle was defended by a Royalist garrison of 100 men under the command of Sir John Denham, the high sheriff of Surrey.

Realising that the Parliamentarians had no artillery, Denham refused Waller's summons to surrender on 26th November. Undeterred, the Parliamentarians blew in the main gate of the castle with an explosive charge, known as a petard, and then rushed in to kick down a barricade of stacked logs and overwhelm the garrison. The Royalists threw down their weapons and cried for quarter, which was granted. In the chaos Waller, leading the attack, was just missed by a shot fired by one of his own men.  The Parliamentarians captured a good amount of animals, provisions, weapons and gunpowder at Farnham, as well as money and valuable tableware. From then on Waller used Farnham Castle as his headquarters whenever he was in the region.

Headline: Caught up in the Siege of Chester, Flint Castle was subjected to multiple Parliamentarian attacks.
Body Text:
During the First Civil War, Flint Castle supported the King. Garrisoned by Sir Roger Mostyn, the stronghold was used as a base to support Royalist defenders at the siege of Chester. As a key Royalist holding, the castle was attacked several times, most significantly by Colonel Brereton in November 1643, but was not taken.

In spring 1646, a final attack was mounted by General Mytton, who besieged the castle for three months before the garrison finally surrendered on 24th August. To prevent it being reused, Cromwell ordered the castle to be slighted.

Headline: An important Royalist prisoner was accidently killed by his own side in the siege of Gainsborough.
Body Text:
On 20th July 1643, during their capture of Gainsborough, Robert Pierrepont, Earl of Kingston was caught by Lord Willoughby’s Parliamentarians. Pierrepont had retreated to the strongest house in the town but was forced to surrender. He was placed in a boat to be transported up the River Trent to Hull. Before they could set off though, Royalists fired a cannon at the boat accidently killing Pierrepont.

Willoughby’s capture of Gainsborough disrupted the Earl of Newcastle's communications with Newark and blocked an expected Royalist advance from Yorkshire. Parliament ordered Sir John Meldrum and Colonel Oliver Cromwell to reinforce Lord Willoughby, whose position at Gainsborough was threatened by Royalist cavalry commanded by Sir Charles Cavendish.

On the morning of 28th July, the Parliamentarians encountered Cavendish's advance guard a few miles south of Gainsborough. A fierce battle was fought. Cromwell’s cavalry gained the upper hand and Charles Cavendish was killed. Later that day news came of another Royalist force approaching from the north. The advance guard of the Royalist cavalry was beaten back. But on reaching the top of a nearby hill, the Parliamentarians were astonished to find themselves facing Newcastle's main northern army on their way to lay siege to Gainsborough. The Parliamentarians were unable to hold out against Newcastle's forces and Lord Willoughby abandoned both Gainsborough and Lincoln and retreated to Boston. On 20th December 1643 the town was retaken for Parliament by Sir John Meldrum.
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Newark's ring; Oliver Cromwell

Headline: Strong ties to the King placed Gaunt House squarely in Parliament’s sights.
Body Text: The moated Gaunt House belonged to Samuel Fell, the Dean of Christ Church Cathedral in Oxford. A staunch Royalist, Dell had the house garrisoned with troops to defend against Parliamentarian attacks. An attack came in late May 1645, when Colonel Rainsborough besieged the house, bombarding it with artillery fire until the garrison surrendered. Afterwards, the house was garrisoned by Parliamentarian troops who used it as a raiding base against the local Royalist presence.
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Oxford's ring

Headline: Gloucester’s defenders fought to their last few barrels of gunpowder in this pivotal siege.
Body Text:
Gloucester was the last Parliamentarian stronghold between Bristol and Lancashire. On the 1st August, King Charles arrived in Bristol. His council took the decision to separate the Royalist forces. Some marched south to Dorset and Devon. The rest marched with the King and Prince Rupert to Gloucester.

The Parliamentarian governor of Gloucester was Colonel Edward Massey. Defending Gloucester were about 1,500 infantry. They had insufficient artillery and only forty barrels of gunpowder.  As the Royalist army approached, Massey ordered the suburbs outside the city walls burned to remove cover for the enemy.

The Royalist army arrived on 10th August. Massey, despite weak defences, refused to surrender. Prince Rupert recommended attacking, but Charles did not wish a repeat of the heavy losses suffered at Bristol. He ordered a formal siege, which was to be directed by the Earl of Forth. Reinforcements from Worcester and Oxford increased the strength of the besieging army to roughly 25,000 men.  The main Royalist cannon were placed on Gaudy Green and began bombarding the south walls. Sappers started work on siege trenches. Miners were brought in from the Forest of Dean to undermine the east gate. Steps were taken to cut off the city's water supply. Elaborate siege engines were designed to provide cover for musketeers once a significant break in Gloucester’s walls had been made. The siege proceeded slowly. The artillery bombardment proved ineffective. The mining operations were hampered by underground springs and counter-mines. Frequent raids were mounted by the defenders on the Royalist lines disrupted operations and killed as many as 1,000 besiegers. By contrast Gloucester’s defenders lost a mere fifty during the entire siege.

On 19th August, the Common Council of London agreed to authorise a brigade Parliamentarian troops to march for Gloucester alongside the Earl of Essex's regular army. Essex’s army and the London Brigade set out for Gloucester on 26th August, meeting up at Brackley, Northamptonshire on 1st September. Prince Rupert, with most of the King's cavalry, fought a series of delaying actions around Stow-on-the-Wold, but Rupert’s efforts didn’t stop Essex reaching Prestbury Hill, ten miles from Gloucester on 5th September. Rather than risk becoming trapped between Essex's army and Gloucester, King Charles ended the siege and withdrew to Painswick, covered by Rupert's cavalry. Essex occupied Gloucester on 8th September. The relieving army had arrived in the nick of time – Massey's garrison was down to its last three barrels of gunpowder.

In failing to take Gloucester the Royalists had let a crucial opportunity to cement their advantage slip through their fingers. The siege marked a turning point in fortunes for both sides in the conflict.

Prince Rupert.
“Prince Rupert, Count Palatinate” by Gerrit van Honthorst, licensed by National Portrait Gallery.
Tags: Relieved; Mines and petards; Prince Rupert; Edward Massey; Townspeople

Headline: The Royalists at Goodrich Castle were introduced to “Roaring Meg”.
Body Text:
Goodrich Castle was abandoned by its Parliamentarian garrison just before the siege of Gloucester. For nearly three years the castle was occupied by Royalists, under the command of Sir Henry Lingen.  When the war began to go badly for the Royalists, the south west of England became one of the few remaining Cavalier strongholds.  Lingen had 200 men and 90 horses. He conducted raids on Parliamentary forces in the region, but Lingen made no attempts to strengthen the castle's old fashioned defences.

In 1646, the Roundhead Colonels John Birch and Robert Kyrle marched south from Hereford with the intention of besieging Goodrich Castle.   Birch wanted to prevent any further attacks being launched by Lingen. On 9th March, in a surprise night time assault, Birch burned the weakly defended stables, driving away the Royalist horses. Over the next few months Lingen succeeded in replacing some of his horses and resumed attacks on Parliamentary forces.

On 19th June 1646, Colonel Birch invited the castle to surrender.  Lingen refused and Birch commenced a heavy bombardment.  The Roundheads had brought a powerful mortar that they had named “Roaring Meg” able to fire a gunpowder-filled shell 187’198lb in weight. Roaring Meg threw 22 grenadoes into the castle, damaging every part of it including the stone water cisterns, cutting off the water supply and forcing the garrison to rely on the castle well.  Mines were cut through the rock. In response Lingen’s defenders dug counter mines. A night time bombardment brought the castle’s north west tower crashing down on the counter mines.  The Roundhead’s created a breach and an attack was ordered. The Roundhead assault was successful. Down to their last four barrels of gunpowder and last thirty barrels of beer, the Royalists surrendered.  The Royalists were allowed to leave alive and 170 men marching out of Goodrich Castle singing “Sir Henry Lingen’s Fancy”

Roaring Meg can still be seen today in the courtyard of Goodrich Castle.
Caption Image 1:
Goodrich Castle.
“Goodrich Castle” by Andrew and Annemarie is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Mines and petards

Headline: Royalists took the town of Grantham, but left it vulnerable by refusing to leave a garrison.
Body Text:
A Parliamentarian town, Grantham’s proximity to the nearby Royalist strongholds of Newark and Belvoir meant it was incredibly vulnerable. The attack they feared came in March 1643. Royalist forces under the command of Sir Charles Cavendish and Sir John Henderson captured the town in a surprise attack. Despite the significance of the victory, the Royalists didn’t garrison the town and instead marched on to Boston.

Already keen to take Newark and now with the opportunity to retake Grantham, Parliament ordered Lord Willoughby to march on the towns. His forces arrived on 11th May and advanced on Grantham, retaking it easily in the absence of a Royalist garrison. Willoughby remained in the town for two more days, until Cavendish and Henderson attacked the Parliamentarian troops in a surprise attempt to retake the town, killing 70 and taking 40 prisoners. Despite this the Parliamentarians, led by Oliver Cromwell in his first independent action as a cavalry commander, were able to defeat the Royalists, driving them from the area.

Oliver Cromwell.
“Oliver Cromwell” by Robert Walker, licensed by National Portrait Gallery.
Tags: Taken by surprise; Newark's ring; Oliver Cromwell

Headline: Parliamentarians sought to capture the Great Fulford estate as part of their plan to retake Exeter.
Body Text: The Fulford family who lived on the Great Fulford estate were committed Royalists and declared for the King at the start of the First Civil War. Keen to retake the nearby Royalist stronghold of Exeter, Parliamentarian troops had the estate in their sights. Sir Thomas Fairfax was given the task and led his troops to besiege the house in December 1645. After 10 days of bombardment, severely damaging the house, the Royalists surrendered. Fairfax garrisoned the house and it remained in Parliamentarian hands until the end of the war, with the family eventually able to return after the restoration.
Caption Image 1:
Sir Thomas Fairfax.

Tags: Surrendered on terms; Sir Thomas Fairfax

Headline: An enormous explosion ended the siege of Great Torrington and nearly killed Sir Thomas Fairfax.
Body Text:
After Lord Wentworth’s defeat at the Battle of Bovey Heath, the Prince of Wales appointed Lord Hopton as commander of the Royalist western army. The army could only muster 2,000 Cornish infantry and 3,000 badly-disciplined cavalry. In early February 1646, Hopton advanced into north Devon in an attempt to draw the New Model Army away from the siege of Exeter. On 10th February, he occupied Torrington and took up a defensive position. He built a circuit of earthworks around the town and barricaded the approach roads. General Fairfax learned of the manoeuvre and marched with 10,000 men towards Torrington.

During the evening of 16th February 1646, the Parliamentarians approached Torrington from the east. A group of Royalist dragoons posted at Stevenstone Park were driven back by Fairfax's advance guard. There was fighting to the east of Torrington as Royalist cavalry and infantry came up to support the dragoons' withdrawal. It rained heavily. Night fell. Fairfax decided to wait until the next morning to survey Royalist defences before attacking, but when Oliver Cromwell came to inspect the Parliamentarian outposts, he heard noises from the town which suggested that the Royalists were attempting to move out. Cromwell sent a patrol of dragoons to test the defences. The Dragoons were shot at from the Royalist barricades. A gun battle developed as more troops were ordered forward in support. Fairfax abandoned his decision to wait for daybreak and ordered an attack.

The fight at the barricades lasted for two hours. Men fought hand-to-hand with pikes and the butt-ends of muskets. The Cornish infantry were overwhelmed and retreated into Torrington, pursued by the Roundheads. Royalist cavalry counter-attacked.  Bitter fighting continued in the streets of Torrington. As the battle raged, a stray spark ignited the Royalists' stores of gunpowder that were stored in Torrington Church. Eighty barrels of gunpowder exploded, blowing the roof off the church. A host of Royalist soldiers and around 200 Parliamentarian prisoners were killed in the explosion and falling debris narrowly missed hitting Thomas Fairfax. The explosion effectively ended the battle. In the resulting confusion, Lord Hopton and the survivors of the Royalist western army withdrew from Torrington and escaped into Cornwall.

Sir Thomas Fairfax.
“Thomas Fairfax” by William Marshall, licensed by National Portrait Gallery.
Tags: Stormed; Sir Thomas Fairfax; Oliver Cromwell; Sir Ralph Hopton; Churches at war

Headline: One of the last Royalist strongholds in Lancashire, Greenhalgh withstood attacks for over a year before surrendering.
Body Text: During the First Civil War, Greenhalgh Castle was garrisoned for the King by James Stanley. By late 1644, it was one of only two Royalist garrisons in the whole of Lancashire, so was a key target for the Parliamentarians. The house was besieged in 1644 and managed to withstand attacks for over a year until May 1645, when the castle eventually surrendered under the provision that the garrison were allowed to return to their homes unharmed. Once empty, Parliamentarian forces slighted the castle, rendering it unusable as a defensive position.

Greenhalgh Castle.

Headline: The Royalist garrison closest to London was reduced to rubble in this vicious siege.
Body Text:
In 1642, at the outbreak of war John d’Oyley, a staunch Royalist, offered his house as a Cavalier stronghold. Two miles from Henley, on the River Thames, Greenlands House was strongly fortified. Greenlands occupied an important site for disrupting Parliamentarian communications both by road and by river. It was also the nearest Royalist garrison to London.  Greenlands House was commanded by Sir Stephen Hawkins and protected by 300 defenders with seven cannon.

In May 1644, after the fall of Reading, Greenlands was vulnerable to attack from Henley.  A Parliamentarian force of 400-500 infantry and cavalry and two cannon laid siege to the house.  Although the besiegers didn’t have enough troops to attack Greenland’s strong defences, they were able to put a stop to their raiding activity.  Parliamentarian reinforcements arrived from Windsor, with a further six guns. The bombardment of Greenland increased in intensity. On 7th July Major-General Browne's London brigade, consisting of 7,000 men and heavy cannon marched to attack Greenland House.  News of their approach forced a relieving Royalist force to pull back to Oxford.  Browne’s forces arrived on 10th July and began a renewed bombardment.  Hawkins knew that the house could not survive for long under the continued battering from Parliaments guns.  Browne was willing to grant favourable terms for surrender, and these were gratefully accepted by Hawkins.  On 11th July 1644, the garrison marched out to Oxford, fully armed with colours flying.  Royalists later claimed that the gunpowder magazine had exploded during the bombardment, accounting for their hasty surrender.  The house was completely destroyed by Parliament.
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Oxford's ring

Headline: One the last Royalist garrisons standing, Guernsey faced a huge challenge from Parliamentarian troops.
Body Text:
The Medieval fortress of Castle Cornet chose to fight for the King at the outbreak of the First Civil War, defying the rest of Guernsey which supported Parliament.  From 1642 onwards, Parliamentarian forces on the island attempted to take the castle. Regular skirmishes took place between the two sides. The nearby town of St Peters Port launched bombardments at the castle and the Royalist forces retaliated. It is thought that some 10,000 cannon balls were fired during the siege. Although the defenders had little support from Guernsey, its coastal position meant that the nearby Royalist island of Jersey was able to ensure that the castle was supplied well enough to withstand the siege.

In March 1651, Parliamentarian forces launched a huge surprise attack to take what had become one of the last remaining Royalist strongholds. The attack was met with fierce resistance. Cannon fire had destroyed part of the west wall. As the attackers tried to enter, Royalist troops used iron forks to push their ladders over and throw rocks at them. On 17th December 1651, with hope of relief diminishing, the governor of the castle Colonel Burgess surrendered. Nine years after the start of the war and two years after the execution of Charles I, the penultimate Royalist stronghold in the country had finally given in.

Castle Cornet.

Tags: Surrendered on terms; Ports and the sea

Headline: Fearing the might of Rupert’s army, Parliamentarians surrendered Halton Castle without a fight, but the tables were soon turned on the Royalists.
Body Text:
Halton Castle chose to fight for the King at the beginning of the First Civil War. The castle was commanded by Captain Walter Primrose. Parliamentarian forces under the command of Sir William Brereton besieged the castle in 1643. The Roundheads bombarded the castle heavily and in the face of overwhelming opposition, the garrison surrendered a few weeks later.

Parliamentarian forces garrisoned the Castle. But on hearing of the approach of Prince Rupert’s army, knowing that could not win, they abandoned the Castle and it was returned to Royalist hands. In 1644 a second siege was cut short. Realising there was little chance of relief, the Royalists surrendered. The castle changed hands for the final time.
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Sir William Brereton

Headline: A ruined castle was made ready for war.
Body Text: In 1642, at the outbreak of the First Civil War, the castle in Harlech was in a state of disrepair having been badly damaged in a siege almost 200 years before. In 1644, Prince Rupert appointed Colonel William Owen to oversee repairs to the fortifications. Two years later in June 1646, his work was put to the test when the garrison was besieged by the forces of Major-General Thomas Mytton. The castle held out until 15th March 1647, when the 44 man garrison surrendered. To prevent it being used to mount a counter attack, the castle fortifications were destroyed.
Caption Image 1:
Harlech Castle.

Tags: Surrendered on terms

Headline: A generous bribe ended the siege at Hartlebury without any bloodshed.
Body Text:
The fortified bishops’ palace at Hartlebury was held for the King during the First Civil War. It was garrisoned with 120 foot soldiers and 20 cavalry soldiers under the command of Colonel William Sandys. The Royalist garrison held out for four years until 14th May 1646, when a Parliamentarian army under the command of Colonel Thomas Morgan approached the castle. Morgan’s troops didn’t attack and not a single shot was fired. Two days later the Royalist garrison surrendered. It later transpired that Sandys had surrendered in exchange for £3,000 and a promise that his own estate at Ombersley would be safe. King Charles had already surrendered and Sandys was aware that as a known Royalist his future was at risk. He took the opportunity to ensure his own and his family’s safety.

The Roundheads established a garrison at Hartlebury and used the buildings to house Royalist prisoners.
Tags: Turncoats and treachery

Headline: 120 men held out against 3,000 for as long as they could in the siege at Hawarden Castle.
Body Text:
Hawarden Castle was taken by Parliamentarian troops on 11th November 1643, much to the annoyance of Royalist commanders. Holding North Wales was important for the Royalists since the Royalist port at Conwy facilitated the arrival of reinforcements from Ireland that could be sent all over the country. Knowing that Hawarden Castle would be essential to holding the north of the country, the Royalists immediately launched a counter attack. 3,000 Irish troops were sent to retake the castle, but the 120 man garrison refused to give in. The castle was besieged. As more Royalist reinforcements arrived, the garrison finally surrendered on 3rd December.

The newly Royalist garrison survived several attacks. In May 1645 the Royalists eventually surrendered the castle to a Parliamentary force under the command of Sir William Neale. Unusually, full honours were only partially granted to the defenders in the terms of surrender.

Hawarden Castle.

Headline: Prince Rupert’s soldiers failed to overcome a moat but still managed to loot and set Hawkesley Hall on fire.
Body Text: Hawkesley Hall, originally home to the strongly Royalist Middlemore family, was taken by Colonel Foz in 1644 and a Parliamentarian garrison was established. Royalist troops under the command of Prince Rupert and Prince Maurice arrived at the hall on 13th May 1645 to retake the manor. Guarded by a moat, Royalist soldiers were unable to get close and instead set about bombarding the garrison into submission. The defenders withstood for three days before the 120 defenders were forced to surrender. Rupert’s troops proceeded to sack the hall, before burning it to the ground.
Caption Image 1:
Prince Rupert.
“Prince Rupert, Count Palatinate” by Gerrit van Honthorst, licensed by National Portrait Gallery.

Headline: Sir Thomas Fairfax survived a gunshot wound at Helmsely Castle and lived to besiege another day.
Body Text:
Helmsley Castle was garrisoned for the King from 1642.  After the Battle of Marston Moor and the surrender of York, Parliament turned its attentions to the remaining Royalist garrisons in Yorkshire. In August 1644, Helmsley was besieged by a Parliamentarian force, led by Sir Thomas Fairfax.  The 200 strong Royalist garrison commanded by Sir Jordan Crosland, held out for a while but on 22nd November starvation eventually forced them to surrender.

During an attack by the Royalist garrison, Fairfax was dangerously wounded when a musket ball broke his shoulder. By the end of 1644, Fairfax had recovered enough to take part in the siege of Pontefract Castle.

Helmsley Castle.
