Tags: Starved out; After Marston Moor; Sir Thomas Fairfax

Headline: A Roundhead tax office became the scene a bloody siege.
Body Text:
At the start of the Civil War, Hemyock Castle was garrisoned and held for Parliament by the Popham family. The castle’s defences were outdated so they were repaired and strengthened. During the war, Hemyock Castle was used as a base for tax collection to fund Parliamentarian forces.

On 6th March 1644, Major Carne led a Royalist force against the castle but was soon forced to retreat. Major Carne and many of his troops were killed during the attack. Three days later, Lord Poulett led a larger force against the castle. A day later Poulett forced over 200 defenders to surrender. Three Parliamentarian officers were hanged on the spot. The rest were taken prisoner to Exeter.
Tags: Surrendered on terms; No quarter

Headline: Trickery and the horrendous abuse of animals characterized the siege of Hereford.
Body Text:
Hereford, with its circuit of medieval walls, changed hands several times during the Civil War.  It was close to Parliamentarian Gloucester and Royalist Worcester.  Although predominantly Royalist, on 30th September 1642 Hereford was taken for Parliament by the Earl of Stamford. The city was garrisoned until December, when the Roundhead garrison, largely unwanted by the people of the town, withdrew to Gloucester. Hereford was soon garrisoned for the King under the command of Colonel Lawdey.

The Royalists tried to improve the fortifications of the city but the citizens were not very supportive.  On 25th April 1643, Sir William Waller led a Parliamentarian force against the city.  A cannonball fired at one of the town gates cut a Royalist officer in half.  When the defenders saw how easily the gates were breached, they offered to negotiate surrender, but Waller and his men abandoned Hereford less than a fortnight later, possibly because of rumours that the King’s nephew Prince Maurice was approaching the city. Hereford fell into Royalist hands once again, and Sir William Vavasour was appointed governor.  The Royalists in Hereford had two years to strengthen their position. The defences were strengthened and the buildings outside the city walls dismantled to prevent them from being used by an attacking army. Colonel Barnabas Scudamore was appointed governor

In July 1645, a Covenanter force led by Alexander Leslie besieged the city. Cannon bombarded the walls and mines were dug. The breaches in Hereford’s walls were instantly repaired by courageous townspeople, working under enemy fire. The defenders employed unusual methods for keeping the besiegers at bay. It is thought they may have tied explosives to cats, dogs and old horses and let the unfortunate animals out of the city amongst the besiegers. One legend tells that a bull was covered in twigs, wood and pitch before being set on fire and let loose amongst the Roundheads. The Royalists also staged a foxhunt on the city walls in full view of the besieging Scots. On 30th August, the King's army marched from Oxford. As they approached Hereford on 4th September, the Covenanters withdrew.

The siege was renewed in November. In December 1645 the Parliamentarians, led by Colonel Birch, took Hereford by trickery. Soldiers dressed as labourers with shovels and picks approached the gates. When one of the town gates was opened, the soldiers seized control of the gate and let the Roundheads in.

Alexander Leslie.
“Alexander Leslie” by Sir Anthony van Dyck, licensed by University of Leicester Fairclough Collection.
Tags: Relieved; Mines and petards; Townspeople

Headline: Besieged three times in three years, the Hall finally fell to Parliament following bombardment.
Body Text:
At the time of the Civil War High Ercall Hall was owned by Richard Newport, 1st Baron Newport, a Royalist supporter.  He fortified the buildings as a Royalist stronghold and garrison, with large earthen ramparts thrown up against the curtain walling to protect the buildings from artillery fire. The garrison consisted of around 200 troops. Between 1644 and 1646 the Hall was besieged three times by Parliamentary forces. The first siege caused damage to the nearby church and resulted in the loss of the drawbridge, but ended with a Parliamentarian withdrawal. The second siege ended when the now reinforced garrison again beat off a Parliamentarian attack.

The third siege began in July 1645, with Parliamentary forces now able to conduct an artillery bombardment of the buildings.  Despite Lord Newport arriving with reinforcements, the Royalist commander, Sir Vincent Corbet, surrendered on 28th March 1646.  Under the terms of surrender the 212 surviving members of the garrison, were allowed to leave for the Royalist city of Worcester. 40 of the cavalry were allowed to keep their arms, but the rest of the garrison had to leave their weapons behind.
Caption Image 1:
High Ercall Hall.
“High Ercall Hall” by John McLinden is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Besieged again and again

Headline: A Parliamentarian pincer movement took the Royalists by surprise at Highnam.
Body Text:
Around the middle of February 1643, a Royalist force, commanded by Lord Herbert, advanced from south Wales towards the Parliamentarian stronghold of Gloucester. Finding Gloucester too strongly defended to attack, Lord Herbert set up his headquarters at Highnam, two miles from Gloucester, on the north bank of the River Severn. The Welsh Royalists remained at Highnam for five weeks waiting for reinforcements from Oxford to mount an attack on Gloucester.

Meanwhile, Sir William Waller had been appointed commander of Parliament's Western Association army. Waller's presence in the west threatened the routes between the Royalist capital at Oxford and south Wales, a vital recruiting-ground for the King. Waller intended advancing on Cirencester, but after learning that Prince Rupert had marched from Oxford to secure the garrison, Waller joined forces with Colonel Massey, the Parliamentarian governor of Gloucester. Waller and Massey planned a coordinated attack on the Welsh army encamped at Highnam. On 23rd March, Waller's forces crossed the River Severn several miles downstream from the Royalist camp unobserved and advanced up the western bank. The next day, Massey's forces from Gloucester advanced towards Highnam House. Just as the Royalists ventured out to meet the attack, Waller's army appeared at their rear. Taken completely by surprise, the Royalists defended their position until their ammunition ran out, then laid down their weapons and surrendered. Lord Somerset escaped with most of the cavalry, but around 1,500 Welsh infantry were taken prisoner. They were held under guard for ten days in Gloucester. Those who would not agree to join the Parliamentarian army were released on a promise never to fight against Parliament again.
Tags: Taken by surprise; Sir William Waller; Edward Massey

Headline: A church spire provided an excellent Royalist lookout until the town of Highworth was bombarded and stormed.
Body Text: In 1644, the town of Highworth declared its support for the King. Royalist soldiers soon established a garrison of 200 men there, under the governorship of Major Henry Henne. The soldiers set themselves up in the tower of St. Michael’s Church, which provided an excellent lookout point. A series of earthworks including ditches and bastions were added to the defences.  On 27th June the next year, Sir Thomas Fairfax bombarded the town before storming the garrison. Highworth remained under Parliamentary control until 14th August 1646 when it was ordered that the garrisons of Malmesbury and Highworth were to be slighted and dismantled to free up troops to be sent to Ireland. At the time the town was suffering from a severe and devastating outbreak of plague which killed hundreds of soldiers and civilians.

Church of St Michael and All Angels, Highworth.
“The Church of St Michael” by Robert Cutts is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Stormed; Slighted; After Naseby; Sir Thomas Fairfax; Churches at war; Townspeople

Headline: Fighting around the church at Hillesden left musket ball holes that can still be seen today.
Body Text:
The owner of the manor house at Hillesden was Sir Alexander Denton. He was a Member of Parliament for Buckingham but a Royalist. Hillesden occupied an important position between Royalist Oxford and the Parliamentary garrison of Newport Pagnell. Denton fortified the house for the King and Hillesden became part of the outer ring of defences around the Royalist capital at Oxford.

In January 1644, Parliamentary forces occupied Hillesden House, but they were quickly ejected. In early February Colonel William Smith was sent from Oxford to garrison Hillesden House with about 260 men. He began strengthening the defences with the help of the locals and built a ditch around the house and a gun platform.  However, before they were completed a force of over 2,000 men under Oliver Cromwell and Samuel Luke laid siege to the house on 4th March 1644. Colonel Smith tried to obtain terms, but was offered only unconditional surrender. The ditch surrounding Hillesden was not very deep in some places and was overrun, with the fighting moving to the church. As bodies lay across the grass, Colonel Smith surrendered the house before it was stormed, to stop the killing. After the surrender Smith and Denton were taken prisoner and moved to the Tower of London. Denton died a prisoner on New Year’s Day 1645. Hillesden House was destroyed but musket ball holes can still be seen in the church door.
Caption Image 1:
Oliver Cromwell.
“Oliver Cromwell” by Robert Walker, licensed by National Portrait Gallery.
Tags: Stormed; Oxford's ring; Oliver Cromwell; Family homes; Churches at war

Headline: Celebrations were cut short when a gunpowder explosion following the surrender at Hoghton Tower killed over 100 of the Parliamentarian victors.
Body Text:
The Hoghton family were one of thousands that found themselves on different sides during the Civil War. Sir Gilbert Hoghton fought for King Charles I and was an important Royalist figure.  His son Richard chose the Parliamentarian cause. Sir Gilbert remained at the family home of Hoghton Tower on the advice of Charles who wrote to him saying:

?Now that the Rebels seeme to ayme at a more forcible disturbance thereof, repaire unto and continue at your proper Mansion with your family and usuall retinue that others being encouraged and counterbalanced by your good example, you and they may be the better at hand to assist each other for the preservation and defence of the county.?

Shortly after in early February 1643, Hoghton Tower and its 40 strong garrison were besieged by Parliamentarian troops under the command of Captain Nicholas Starkie. The house did not withstand attack for long and surrendered on 14th February. As the Parliamentarians entered the house a nearby gunpowder store exploded, killing over 100 of the victorious soldiers including Captain Starkie.
Caption Image 1:
Hoghton Tower.
“Hoghton tower” by mjtmail (tiggy) is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Family homes

Headline: The bridge across the River Dee made Holt strategically important for both sides.
Body Text:
Holt was secured for the Royalist cause early in the First Civil War and was of key strategic value as one of only two bridges across the River Dee. Both the bridge and the town’s defences were fortified and the castle and church were garrisoned. In 1643, Sir William Brereton led a force of Parliamentarian soldiers to capture the bridge, but after a few months Royalists were able to recapture it and the Roundheads were forced to surrender. After they were captured, 13 of the Parliamentarian garrison were executed and their bodies thrown in the moat.

In 1646, the Parliamentarians tried to capture the town once more and besieged Holt. Nine months later, in January 1647, the Royalist governor Sir Richard Lloyd surrendered to the Parliamentarian commander Thomas Mytton, leaving the Royalists with only one stronghold left in Wales.
Caption Image 1:
Holt Castle.
“Heading to Holt Castle ” IMGP1189? by Bev Norton is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Surrendered on terms; No quarter; Churches at war

Headline: Were the defenders slaughtered following an agreement they would be allowed to live, or did their commander’s stubbornness lead to their deaths?
Body Text: Hopton Castle, owned by Robert Wallop, was one of the few castles held for Parliament in the west of England. In 1644 it was defended by a garrison of around 30 men, commanded by Samuel More.   In late February 1644, Sir Michael Woodhouse, with a force of about 500 Royalist soldiers, laid siege to the castle.  More wrote an account of what happened next - although it is muddled and contradicted by other accounts.  According to More terms for the surrender were agreed. However, once the garrison had surrendered on 13th March, Woodhouse had each of the defenders apart from More, bound, their throats were cut and their bodies dumped in the moat. Other accounts state that following a three week siege, More delayed surrendering until the bailey had been taken and the entrance to the keep was on fire, at which point the garrison surrendered.  Sir Michael Woodhouse decided not to grant the majority of his prisoners quarter and they were killed by their captors. This was his prerogative under the laws of war as they were practiced at that time. Not everyone believed Woodhouse’s version of events and as word spread ?Hopton Quarter' became a byword for treacherous treatment by your opponents.
Tags: Stormed; No quarter

Headline: A co-ordinated diversion at Hornby allowed the Parliamentarians to take the castle.
Body Text:
The owner of Hornby Castle at the start of the Civil War was Henry Parker, a fierce Royalist who declared for the King. The castle was a key target for the Parliamentarians and in June 1643 a force led by General Ralph Asherton the Commander of Parliamentary forces in Lancashire, attacked. Asherton split his force: sending a group of them to the front of the castle to attack and a larger group of troops attacked the east wall. The diversion worked and Asherton’s men entered the castle, forcing the Royalists to surrender.

The castle did not remain in Parliamentarian hands; it was recovered by the Royalists later in the war and eventually occupied by Scottish forces in July 1648.
Caption Image 1:
Hornby Castle.
“Hornby Castle” by C & N is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Stormed

Headline: Guarding a key river crossing, Hougham House became a target for Royalists.
Body Text:
The Parliamentarian garrison at Hougham House guarded a key crossing over the River Witham. It became a target for the nearby Royalist commander, Sir Richard Willis, Governor of Newark. Royalist troops left the stronghold of Newark under cover of night, arriving undetected on 10th June 1645. The forces overpowered the guards, silencing them before they could raise the alarm, and managed to capture the house without losing a single man.

The Royalists established a garrison of 60 men in the fortified manor house to fight off any reprisals from the Parliamentarians. Willis’ men did not have long to wait. The next day an attack was mounted by forces under the command of Colonel Rossiter. The Parliamentarian forces attacked the house from all sides, but in daylight the fortifications caused them problems. Having waded through the waist deep moat, Rossiter’s men were bombarded with stones and hit by musket butts as they tried to climb the ramparts. Despite this, the attack was over in 30 minutes with the Parliamentarians successfully retaking the house, though Rossiter lost 18 men in the process.
Tags: Stormed; Newark's ring

Headline: Owned by an uncommitted Royalist, Howley House was taken for Parliament.
Body Text:
At the start of the First Civil War, Howley House was owned by Sir Thomas Saville. Thomas was a Royalist, but frequently refused to show any support for the King. This caused many to distrust him. On one of the occasions when he was away visiting the King, the house was taken without force by Sir John Saville, a Parliamentarian commander.

This provided a problem for the Royalist commanders, who were planning to attack and besiege Bradford. Fearing that a Parliamentarian force, at nearby Howley, might launch a counter attack, orders were given to retake the house. On 22nd June 1643, the Earl of Newcastle and his troops bombarded the house with cannon fire. The defenders held out for three days, before Sir John Saville was forced to surrender.
Tags: Surrendered on terms

Headline: Flooding of the surrounding area hampered the Royalist besiegers at Hull.
Body Text:
In April 1642, King Charles I attempted to secure the town of Hull. Hull was a major port with trading links to Europe and the site of an arsenal of weapons stored after the recent wars against Scotland. Parliament had taken precautions to secure Hull for themselves. They appointed Sir John Hotham as Governor and issued instructions that the town and its arsenal were not to be surrendered without Parliamentary authority. When Charles arrived at Hull on 23rd April 1642, he found the town gates barred against him. After several hours of fruitless negotiation, the King rode away to York. The following day, he pronounced Sir John Hotham guilty of high treason.

With a force of 3,000 infantry and 1,000 cavalry, the King returned to Hull early in July 1642. He set up his court at Beverley and quartered his forces around the village of Anlaby. Parliament had ordered the removal of most of the weapons and ammunition from the northern arsenal to London, but enough was left in Hull for the town's defence.  The citizens of Hull had also strengthened their defences with new earthworks. On 6 July, the sluices were opened and the River Humber flooded the land for two miles around the town. On 10 July, a Royalist raiding party approached Hull to intimidate the defenders by burning down buildings outside the town walls. In the first military action of the Civil War, the Royalists were driven away by gunfire.

Following an appeal to Parliament, Sir John Meldrum arrived by sea, with 1,500 troops, to direct Hull's defence. The flooding of the surrounding land had made it difficult for the Royalists to set up artillery positions. Using the defenders' local knowledge, Meldrum directed attacks on the Royalist positions. The attacks culminated with a night raid on the Royalist headquarters at Anlaby, with the attackers approaching by raft across the flooded land. The Royalists were taken by surprise and beaten. The Parliamentarians captured several artillery pieces. Discouraged by the strength of the Parliamentarian defence, King Charles abandoned the siege of Hull at the end of July and withdrew to York.
Caption Image 1:
King Charles I.
“Charles I” by Sir Anthony van Dyck, licensed by Royal Collections Trust
Tags: Besiegers gave up; Ports and the sea; Besieged again and again; Townspeople

Headline: The Royalists’ failure to capture Hull ended any hope of securing London for the King.
Body Text:
Early in September 1643, the Earl of Newcastle's troops occupied the towns and villages around Hull. They began constructing earthworks and gun emplacements to besiege the town. The bombardment of Hull began on 2nd September, but was largely ineffective because the Royalist siege works were too far from the town walls. The main Royalist fort was captured and destroyed in a Parliamentarian raid during the first week of the siege. On 14th September, Lord Fairfax ordered the sluices to be opened so that the River Humber would flood as had happened during the first siege in 1642.

Parliamentarian warships patrolled the Humber estuary, allowing supplies to be shipped in. On 22nd September, Oliver Cromwell crossed from the Lincolnshire side with muskets and gunpowder for the defenders before returning to Lincolnshire. Four days later, Sir Thomas Fairfax moved his cavalry and dragoons across the Humber to join forces with the Eastern Association. He left the defence of the city in the hands of Lord Fairfax, who was reinforced with 500 soldiers commanded by Sir John Meldrum.

On 9th October, the Royalists attempted to storm the defences. Although outlying fortifications were captured, the Royalists were driven back. Two days later, Meldrum led an attack on the Royalist gun emplacements. The Parliamentarian force of about 1,500 men was composed of soldiers from the garrison, sailors from the warships and citizens from the town. Meldrum attacked in two divisions, one led by Colonel Lambert, the other by Thomas Rainsborough. The raiders overran the Royalist gun emplacements and succeeded in capturing several great siege cannon.

On 12th October, the Earl of Newcastle abandoned the siege of Hull and fell back to York. The failure of the siege, as well as the Parliamentarian victory at Winceby in Lincolnshire, ended Royalist hopes of an advance towards London by the Earl of Newcastle's northern army.

Sir Thomas Fairfax.
“Thomas Fairfax” by William Marshall, licensed by National Portrait Gallery.
Tags: Besiegers gave up; Ports and the sea; Besieged again and again; Sir Thomas Fairfax; Oliver Cromwell; Townspeople

Headline: Cockburn’s poetic response to a surrender demand could not save Hume Castle from bombardment.
Body Text:
During Oliver Cromwell’s invasion of Scotland during the Third Civil War, the Royalist held Hume Castle was targeted. Cromwell sent Colonels Fenwick and Slyer to take the castle. The two commanders approached the castle before ordering those inside to surrender. The Royalist Governor, Colonel John Cockburn, responded to the demands by stating that he had no idea who Cromwell was and sent a note to Fenwick reading:

"I, King of the Wastle,
Am now in my castle,
And a? the dogs in the toun
Shanna gar me gang doun."

Despite Cockburn’s confident response, when the Parliamentarian troops began bombarding the castle, it was clear that victory was impossible. The Royalists surrendered on the condition that all the soldiers in the garrison would be allowed to live.
Caption Image 1:
Hume Castle.
“Hume Castle April 2009” by Dave McLear is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Scotland and Ireland

Headline: Cromwell’s birthplace received a visit from the King when Royalists took the town.
Body Text: Famously the birthplace of Oliver Cromwell, Huntingdon had been held for the Parliamentarians from the beginning of the First Civil War. In 1644, fearing an attack, the defences and garrison were strengthened by the town’s governor. In August 1644, after their defeat at the Battle of Naseby, fleeing Royalists attacked Huntington. Led by King Charles I himself, the Royalists drove the Parliamentarian defenders back to two of the town’s churches, capturing the town later in the day.
Caption Image 1:
King Charles I.
“Charles I” by Sir Anthony van Dyck, licensed by Royal Collections Trust
Tags: Stormed; After Naseby

Headline: Treachery was to blame when the Parliamentarians took Huntley.
Body Text: The village of Huntley was an outpost of Parliamentarian Gloucester. It was taken by Royalist troops from nearby Newnham in 1643. The next year Huntley was betrayed and the Parliamentarians regained control of the town.
Tags: Turncoats and treachery

Headline: Irish defenders were hanged and officers beheaded following the surrender of Huntly Castle.
Body Text: The castle, which had been partially destroyed in 1594 by order of James VI, had largely been restored by 1602, but it was more of a palace than a fortress. Captured from the Covenanters in October 1644, the Huntley Castle was briefly held for the Royalists by James Graham, 1st Marquis of Montrose, against the Duke of Argyll. In 1647, it was gallantly defended against General David Leslie by Lord Charles Gordon.  Gordon was forced to surrender after its garrison was starved into submission. Savage treatment was meted out. The Irish troops were hanged and their officers beheaded. In December of the same year the Marquis of Huntly himself was captured. On his way to execution at Edinburgh he was held prisoner in his own mansion. His bodyguards were shot against the walls of the castle, before Huntly was sent on to be executed.
Caption Image 1:
Huntly Castle.
“DSC09584” by Bethany Weeks is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Starved out; No quarter; Scotland and Ireland

Headline: The last Royalist threat to Commonwealth shipping fell despite stubborn resistance.
Body Text:
By the end of May 1651, Sir George Carteret's privateers were the last Royalist threat to Commonwealth shipping in the Western Approaches. On 20th September 1651 an expedition against Jersey was ordered. Colonel James Heane was appointed military commander of a force of 2,200 men. The naval commander was Robert Blake. The Commonwealth expedition sailed from Weymouth on 17th October. After being forced back by storms, it finally arrived off St Ouen's Bay at noon on 20th October before attempting a landing at 11.00pm on 22nd October. Despite a strong start, the Royalists were driven back and Sir George Carteret escaped to Elizabeth Castle.

Blake secured safe anchorage for the fleet, while Colonel Heane advanced unopposed to St Helier. On 24th October, Heane summoned Carteret to surrender but was refused. Elizabeth Castle was regarded as an impregnable stronghold. Situated on a tidal island, it could only be approached across a causeway at low tide. Leaving a force in St Helier to blockade the castle, Heane marched north to Mount Orgueil which was held by Sir Philip Carteret, brother of Sir George. On 25th October, Heane summoned him to surrender. Although Sir Philip was defiant, the garrison was reluctant to fight and threatened to mutiny if he refused to negotiate. The terms offered were generous: Sir Philip was allowed to keep his estates on Jersey and the garrison was granted indemnity for any actions carried out during the war. 60 men who wanted to continue fighting for the Royalists were allowed to join Sir George Carteret in Elizabeth Castle, the rest were given free passage overseas.

During the last week of October artillery was set up on a low hill outside St Helier and the bombardment of Elizabeth Castle began. Six demi-cannon, firing 36-pound shot, had little effect on the castle and a further six guns and three mortars were added to the battery in early November. On 9th November a direct hit by a mortar shell blew up ammunition and gunpowder stored in the castle. The massive explosion killed six men and buried 40 others. Morale in the garrison declined quickly and a number of men deserted. Sir George Carteret remained defiant, even after Charles II had sent a message giving him permission to surrender. Carteret ordered the evacuation of the women in the garrison and hanged a man caught in the act of desertion. By early December provisions were almost exhausted. A blockade by Blake's fleet ensured that there was no possibility of relief.  On 8th December, Carteret finally agreed to open negotiations for surrender. Generous terms were offered. Carteret was allowed to go to France with his money and possessions. His men were also given free passage. The castle was delivered up to the victorious Commonwealth forces at noon on 12th December 1651. With the surrender of Jersey, all major Royalist resistance came to an end.
Caption Image 1:
Elizabeth Castle.
“Elizabeth Castle” by Xlibber is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Ports and the sea

Headline: Held by the Royalists through two Civil Wars, Kildrummy Castle finally fell to Parliament in 1654.
Body Text: During the First Civil War Kildrummy Castle had been a Royalist stronghold under the command of the Marquis of Montrose. A decade later, during Cromwell’s invasion of Scotland, the castle was still a Royalist garrison. On 13th February 1654, a Parliamentary force, under the command of Colonel Morgan, finally managed to capture the castle and a new garrison was installed.
Caption Image 1:
Kildrummy Castle.
“Kildrummy Castle” by Stu Smith is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Scotland and Ireland

Headline: Despite an outbreak of plague, the town’s people helped resist Cromwell’s assault.
Body Text:
Early in 1650, Oliver Cromwell planned a major offensive in Munster and Leinster. His goal was to capture the Royalist strongholds of Kilkenny and Clonmel. Once Gowran was captured on 21st March, Kilkenny was isolated and the Earl of Castlehaven was powerless to prevent Cromwell and the Parliamentarian army from approaching the following day.  For several months, Kilkenny had been ravaged by the plague. Fewer than 400 soldiers were left alive out of a garrison of 1,200. As there were so few soldiers, the citizens defended Irish Town and Sir Walter Butler and his reduced garrison guarded the castle and High Town. Cromwell hoped to take Kilkenny without a siege. An Irish officer, Captain Tickell, had been bribed to betray the city. However, when Cromwell arrived he found that the plot had been discovered and Tickell had been hanged.

Despite generous terms, allowing the citizens to remain unharmed or to depart with their goods and the garrison and its priests to march away, Butler rejected Cromwell's summons to surrender. The following morning, a Parliamentarian cavalry regiment stormed the gate of Irish Town. The citizens held firm and the attack was held off. At the same time the Parliamentarians seized St Patrick's Church, outside the south-western walls of High Town, where an artillery battery was established. The bombardment of the southern wall of High Town began on the morning of 25th March. By noon, the wall had been breached. Cromwell ordered a two-pronged assault: Colonel Hewson led the attack on the breach in the south wall of High Town and Colonel Ewer led an attack on the west side of Irish Town, hoping to burn or batter Dean’s Gate down.

When the attack began, the citizens fled from Dean's Gate. This allowed Ewer's regiment to force its way in and to seize the Cathedral of Saint Canice, which was situated on high ground overlooking Irish Town. However, the attack on the southern breach was pushed back. Butler had ordered earthwork defences to be constructed immediately behind the breach, which were lined with musketeers waiting for the Parliamentarian attack. Under heavy musket fire, Hewson's men were driven back. They suffered up to 40 casualties, including Hewson himself who was wounded. After this setback, Cromwell renewed his offer of terms. Butler asked for time to consider which Cromwell granted, though he continued preparations for taking the city by storm.

From the Parliamentarian foothold in Irish Town, Cromwell sent Colonel Giffard across the River Nore and into the eastern suburb of St John's. Giffard's men captured the suburb with minimal losses. They then prepared for an assault against High Town across St John's Bridge. Butler transferred enough men to counter the threat, but was dismayed to find that the Parliamentarians were building a second artillery battery on the eastern side of Kilkenny. By the morning of 27th March, a second breach had been opened near St John's Bridge and another attack was being prepared. Realising that his situation was hopeless, Butler surrendered on terms that same day.

Oliver Cromwell.
“Oliver Cromwell” by Robert Walker, licensed by National Portrait Gallery.
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Scotland and Ireland; Oliver Cromwell; Turncoats and treachery; Churches at war; Townspeople

Headline: Failure of the well forced the garrison at Kincardine to surrender prematurely.
Body Text: Kincardine Castle was garrisoned for the Royalist cause during the First Civil War. It was held by 50 men, commanded by Lord Napier and his cousin George Drummond of Balloch. On 5th March 1646, General Middleton commenced a siege of the castle with an army of 1,800 infantry and 1,000 cavalrymen. The defenders held out for 10 days against constant artillery bombardment. They would probably have held out for longer had the well in the castle not failed, but with no water supply, defeat was certain. Under cover of nightfall, Napier and Balloch escaped to a nearby Royalist stronghold. With no leader, the next morning the castle had no alternative but to surrender. 35 of the defenders were taken prisoner and a further 12 were shot on 16th March. The castle was burned and only a small portion of the wall remained.
Tags: Surrendered on terms; No quarter; Scotland and Ireland

Headline: A Royalist commander obtained good surrender terms for his own regiment, at the expense of the other defenders.
Body Text: Built at the mouth of Dartmouth harbour, Kingswear Castle was a key part of the town’s defences. It was held for the King by Sir Henry Cary, who repaired and added fortifications. Parliamentarian forces under the command of Sir Thomas Fairfax attacked the castle on 19th January 1646. They took both the castle and the town on the same day. Cary managed to get Fairfax to agree to generous terms for his own regiment, allowing them to walk free. In exchange the 1,000 other men in the garrison were taken prisoner, with the exception of the Cornishmen who were given money and sent home.
Caption Image 1:
Kingswear Castle.
“2003-D20 Devon” by Gerry Labrijn is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Ports and the sea; Sir Thomas Fairfax

Headline: As the only openly Royalist town in East Anglia, Kings Lynn was an early target for the Earl of Manchester.
Body Text:
Although the people of King’s Lynn supported Parliament, the local families of Dereham and L’Estrange were strong Royalists. In response to Royalist successes in the East Midlands and Lincolnshire, Lynn was ordered to strengthen its fortifications in July 1643. On 13th August, Sir Hamon L’Estrange of Hunstanton led a successful Royalist rising in King’s Lynn. He became the town’s governorr and refused to pay Parliament's tax assessment. King’s Lynn was now the only openly Royalist town in East Anglia and had a garrison of around 2,000 men and 40 guns.

Parliament appointed the Earl of Manchester as commander of the Eastern Association. He was given orders to prevent any further Royalist advances towards London. Manchester’s first goal was to secure East Anglia by taking King’s Lynn. The siege began on 23rd August with Parliamentarian forces securing the road and river bridges into the town.  Ships, under the command of the Earl of Warwick, blockaded Lynn from the sea. The town was bombarded across the Great Ouse River from the village of West Lynn. During one attack, on Sunday 3rd September, a cannonball went through the west window of St. Margaret’s Church and the congregation fled in terror. The Gaywood River was diverted and the piped water supply to the town was cut off by the Parliamentarians.

The town was asked to surrender several times, but the leaders hoped the Royalist army would arrive to aid them.  Plans were made by the Parliamentarian forces to take the town by storm on Saturday 16th September. Manchester warned the Royalists to remove the women and children of the town. On 15th September 1643, after three weeks under siege, King’s Lynn surrendered. At dawn the next day the Parliamentarian army entered the town.
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Ports and the sea; Townspeople

Headline: The people of Knaresborough attempted to sneak food to their families in the besieged castle.
Body Text:
The castle at Knaresborough was held for the King from 1642. After the Parliamentarian victory at Marston Moor in July 1644, nearby Parliamentarian troops began a siege of the castle. The stronghold was besieged for six months. Food in the castle became scarce. For family members living in the town, knowing their loved ones fighting in the castle were without food proved to be too much and they attempted to sneak food into the stronghold. In Knaresborough, there were reports of a woman, named Mrs. Whincup, successfully leading a group of locals to plead with the Parliamentarian commander for the life of a boy who had been discovered taking food to his besieged father.

The castle eventually surrendered on 21st December 1644 on honourable terms. The buildings had suffered little structural damage, but in a 1648 Act of Parliament, Knaresborough was mentioned as one of several Royalists castles that were to be slighted.

Knaresborough Castle.

Headline: Although well prepared for a siege, an isolated position led to the Royalist’s surrender at Lacock Abbey.
Body Text: Lacock Abbey was garrisoned for the Royalists at the start of the First Civil War. The abbey was surrounded by earthwork fortifications and presented a challenge to attackers. However, the garrison surrendered soon after it was besieged by Parliamentarian forces, under the command of Colonel Devereux, on 24th September 1645. Although the Royalists could have continued to fight, Oliver Cromwell’s capture of the nearby town of Devizes meant that the chances of reinforcements or relief were slim. Fighting on would have been futile.
Caption Image 1:
Lacock Abbey.
“Lacock Abbey” by George Redgrave is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Surrendered on terms; After Naseby

Headline: The castle at Lancaster withstood several Royalist attempts to take it.
Body Text:
Lancaster Castle was captured by a small Parliamentarian force in February 1643 The Parliamentarians then set about building fortifications and improving the town’s defences. In March of the same year, a Royalist force managed to break through the outer defences to besiege the castle. After just two days Parliamentarian reinforcements arrived. The attackers were forced to retreat and give up the town they had captured, but only after they had burnt 90 homes in the town.

Royalist forces tried repeatedly to take the castle, but failed each time. Parliamentarian commanders later ordered that: "all the walls about [Lancaster Castle] should be thrown down?, but the order was never carried out.

The castle found itself at the centre of fighting again in 1648, this time with the Parliamentarian garrison holding out against a Scottish army fighting for the King. In 1649, after King Charles’ execution, the castle was finally slighted, apart from several buildings that were used as a jail.
Caption Image 1:
Lancaster Castle.
“Lancaster Castle, John of Gaunt’s gatehouse” by Gidzy is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Besiegers gave up; Slighted; Townspeople

Headline: A daring night time assault took this Staffordshire manor house for the Royalists.
Body Text: Lapley House and church were garrisoned for Parliament by around 70 men, commanded by Colonel William Careless. The garrison was captured on 21st December 1643 by Royalist Colonel Heveningham. During a night attack Heveningham and his troops used ladders to scale the courtyard wall of the Elizabethan manor house.  Once inside they overpowered the guards in the gatehouse and opened the gate to the rest of the Royalist force.  Despite being fired on from the windows of the house, a determined attack got them inside. The defenders were forced to surrender.  A Parliamentarian detachment stationed in the adjacent church also surrendered.  Although a skirmish between both sides’ reinforcements followed, Colonel Leveson was able to hold the garrison for the Royalists.
Tags: Stormed; Churches at war

Headline: This house’s strategic location made it valuable to the Royalists and a target for the Parliamentarians.
Body Text: Lark Stoke House’s strategic value lay in its location on the road between Warwick and Gloucestershire. As a result, it was a valuable asset to the Royalist force in the area and a key target for the Parliamentarians. In February 1645, a Parliamentarian force, under the command of Colonel Bridges, seized the house and burnt it to the ground, ensuring that Royalist forces could never again capitalise on its strategic location.
Tags: Stormed

Headline: The formidable Countess of Derby and 300 supporters defended Lathom House until relieved by Prince Rupert.
Body Text:
James Stanley, 7th Earl of Derby, was the leading Royalist in the northwest of England when war broke out in 1642. The family seat was at Lathom House in Lancashire. When Derby was ordered to fortify the Isle of Man in 1643, his wife, Charlotte de la Tremoüille, was left in charge. Sir Thomas Fairfax saw Derby's absence as an opportunity to strengthen Parliament's position in Lancashire and set out to take Lathom House. Following the fall of Warrington, the Parliamentarians requested that the Countess acknowledge Parliament's authority and surrender her house. She refused on the grounds that doing so would dishonour her husband.

When Fairfax arrived at Lathom House in February 1644, he demanded that the Countess surrender the House to him. She asked for a week to consider his offer, and then insisted that it was only appropriate that he visit her at Lathom House for further negotiations. He was received as an honoured guest, but his terms for surrender were categorically dismissed. He gave her two more days to consider her situation, but the representative he sent to receive her reply was scornfully dismissed.

The siege began with 2,000 Parliamentary soldiers against a garrison of 300. Charlotte had assembled a militia of seasoned marksmen who were able to inflict significant losses on the Parliamentarians.  The fortifications sustained continuous cannon and mortar fire with little damage. The Royalists launched several successful attacks to disrupt Parliamentary efforts to set up gun batteries. As a result, the Parliamentarians were unable to establish any major artillery positions against the house. Morale among the Roundheads suffered greatly as the besieged marksmen continued to shoot their soldiers and engineers.  Fairfax persisted in demanding that Charlotte surrender, going so far as to obtain a letter from the Earl of Derby asking for safe passage for her. She refused to surrender under any terms.

Fairfax returned to Yorkshire in March and Colonel Alexander Rigby was left in charge. When Captain Hector Schofield, a messenger from Rigby, arrived to offer Charlotte an honourable surrender, she threatened to hang him from the tower gates.  A further demand to surrender was issued on 23rd May and was dismissed by Charlotte once again. The siege was lifted on the night of 27th May as Prince Rupert approached Lathom with thousands of cavalry and infantry. Charlotte and her household departed for the Isle of Man, leaving the care of Lathom House to Colonel Edward Rawstorne.

After the Parliamentary victory at Marston Moor the north of England was largely under Parliamentary control.  In July 1645, 4,000 Parliamentary troops under the command of Colonel Peter Egerton returned to begin a second siege. The garrison did not surrender quickly. When it became clear that no relief could be expected, and supplies were running short Rawstorne was forced to surrender Lathom House to Egerton on 2nd December 1645.

Prince Rupert.
“Prince Rupert, Count Palatinate” by Gerrit van Honthorst, licensed by National Portrait Gallery.
Tags: Relieved; Besieged again and again; Prince Rupert; Sir Thomas Fairfax; Family homes

Headline: Laugharne was the top priority for Parliamentarians taking back land in Wales
Body Text:
In February 1644, Colonel Rowland Laugharne united with a Parliamentarian naval force in a series of assaults on Royalist positions around Pembroke, seizing them one after another. By the end of March, Laugharne had captured the whole of Pembrokeshire. During April, he went on to take possession of Carmarthenshire and Cardiganshire with almost no resistance.

Following his successes in the West Country, Lieutenant-General Charles Gerard was appointed to lead the Royalist forces in Wales by Prince Rupert. Gerard drove the Parliamentarians out of Cardiff and then advanced westwards. By the end of June, he had re-captured the whole of Carmarthenshire and the castles of Cardigan and Newcastle Emlyn. Colonel Laugharne abandoned his territorial gains and withdrew his forces to the strongholds of Pembroke and Tenby. From here he could maintain contact with the Parliamentarian navy for reinforcements and supplies. By October 1644, Gerard was able to leave the region fully garrisoned while he marched with 3,000 troops from Wales to reinforce the King.

As soon as Gerard left Wales, Colonel Laugharne and the Pembrokeshire Parliamentarians emerged to retake the territory they had lost. Their first objective was Laugharne Castle on the estuary of the River Taff. Gerard had stationed a 200-strong Royalist garrison under the command of Lieutenant-Colonel Russell to protect the castle. Colonel Laugharne approached the castle in late October 1644 with a force of 2,000 men and several cannon. A summons to surrender was issued on 29th October, but was refused.

Laugharne set up artillery on high ground to the north east and north west. However, the Parliamentarian guns could not be used against the main gate of the castle from either of these positions. On the night of 30th October, the Parliamentarians stormed and captured one of the town gatehouses which was situated 100 yards from the outer gates of the castle, with a clear line of fire. Guns were brought up and a two day bombardment commenced, eventually breaching the castle gates. The Parliamentarians stormed the breach on the evening of 2nd November. The Royalists fell back to the inner ward. When the Parliamentarians began to mine the wall, Lieutenant-Colonel Russell asked for a parley. Negotiations continued throughout the night, and the Royalists surrendered early in the morning of 3rd November. They were allowed to march away, but left behind weapons, ammunition, supplies and 33 dead.

Laugharne Castle.

Headline: Parliamentarian soldiers ensured Lea Castle didn’t fall back into Royalist hands.
Body Text: Lea Castle was garrisoned for the King at the start of the Civil War in 1642, but fell in October 1645. A Parliamentarian force lead by John Middleton seized the garrison before destroying the buildings to ensure they were of no strategic value to Royalist forces.

Headline: Vastly outnumbered, the Royalists desperately tried to hold off the Parliamentarian army at Leeds.
Body Text:
Despite strong Parliamentarian leanings in the city, at the beginning of the First Civil War Leeds was garrisoned for the King, under the command of Sir William Saville. Saville fortified the town, building earthworks and digging trenches to build up the city’s defences.

On 23rd January 1643, those defences were put to the test by a Parliamentarian force led by Sir Thomas Fairfax. Saville declined the calls to surrender despite being outnumbered by Fairfax's 2,500 strong army. In response and making the most of his larger force, Fairfax attacked the city on two fronts: splitting the defence. The attack began at 2.00pm and it took just two hours for a Parliamentarian victory to be secured. The Parliamentarian forces took 500 of the defenders prisoner. They were released on the promise that they would never again take up arms on behalf of the King.

Sir Thomas Fairfax.
“Thomas Fairfax” by William Marshall, licensed by National Portrait Gallery.
Tags: Stormed; Sir Thomas Fairfax

Headline: The first siege of Leicester was followed with ruthless looting by Prince Rupert’s soldiers.
Body Text:
Leicester had been the headquarters of Lord Grey of Groby since the beginning of the war, but he left the region late in 1644 after a quarrel with Sir Arthur Hesilrige. Leicester was left vulnerable. Realising this, Prince Rupert and around 10,000 men set out to attack the city.  Sir Robert Pye arrived with cavalry to reinforce the Leicester garrison immediately before the Royalist attack.

Sir Marmaduke Langdale's Royalist forces surrounded Leicester on 29th May, cutting off all approaches to the town. Prince Rupert issued a summons to surrender around noon on 30th May. Three hours later, a messenger was sent out from the town to request a delay of one day before replying to the summons. The defenders hoped to gain time in order to complete the construction of earthworks to strengthen Leicester's Roman and Medieval walls. Their request breached the terms of the summons and Rupert ordered the bombardment to begin immediately.  The Royalist artillery concentrated on a section of the town wall next to Leicester Castle and by 6.00pm a breach had been made. That night, Rupert launched an assault from three directions at once. George Lisle led the main force which stormed the breach on the south side. Sir Henry Bard and Sir Bernard Astley led two smaller storming parties with scaling ladders against the north and east gates. The three assaults were held off with heavy losses, but the resistance faltered when Bard and Astley forced their way into the town. The gates were thrown open and the Royalist cavalry charged in. The defenders continued to resist, fighting street by street and making a last stand in the market square before finally throwing down their weapons. Exasperated by the town's resistance even after the walls were breached, Rupert and his officers made no attempt to restrain the Royalist troops from sacking Leicester. Nine pieces of ordnance, 1,000 muskets, 50 barrels of gunpowder and 400 horses were captured.  Although the sacking was severe, the comparisons made in London news books to the terrible sack of Magdeburg during the Thirty Years War were greatly exaggerated. Up to 25,000 people were massacred at Magdeburg, whereas in Leicester 300 defenders were killed. The Royalists lost around 400 men.  It is recorded that 140 cartloads of goods were confiscated from Leicester.

Prince Rupert.
“Prince Rupert, Count Palatinate” by Gerrit van Honthorst, licensed by National Portrait Gallery.
Tags: Stormed; No quarter; Besieged again and again; Prince Rupert; Townspeople

Headline: Within three days of their victory Naseby, the Parliamentarians set their sights on retaking Leicester.
Body Text: On Sunday 15th June 1645, the day after the Royalist defeat at the Battle of Naseby, Sir Thomas Fairfax and his men marched towards Leicester to retake the strategic town. The following day the Parliamentarians surrounded Leicester. Fairfax sent a summons to surrender the town. It was refused. On 17th June, Fairfax raised a battery of cannon on the Raw Dykes, just as Prince Rupert had done the previous month.  Fairfax began to bombard the wall at exactly the same spot the Royalists broke through 18 days previously. Before the morning was out, a large breach was made. The Royalist commander Lord Loughborough had to decide whether to resist or surrender. Without hesitation Loughborough surrendered, unwilling to sacrifice himself and any more men for the King. He proposed conditions for the surrender of the town. Fairfax agreed to the terms, but discussions continued for the rest of the day between Lord Loughborough and the Parliamentary colonels Pickering and Rainsborough.  Fairfax was unsure what the outcome would be, and didn’t know whether the Royalists were simply playing for time, so he continued with preparations for a siege.  At 2.00am on 18th June, the surrender was formally agreed. The Royalists were guaranteed safe passage to Lichfield and Ashby, and the officers were allowed to take their horses and private arms with them. At 10.00am that same day, the Royalists marched out of Leicester for Lichfield. They left behind 14 cannons, 2,000 weapons, 50 barrels of gunpowder, ammunition, 500 horses, many carriages, baggage and 30 stands of colours.

Sir Thomas Fairfax.

Tags: Surrendered on terms; After Naseby; Besieged again and again; Sir Thomas Fairfax

Headline: Not even “divine judgement” was able to save the Royalist stronghold at Lichfield.
Body Text:
The commander of Parliament's forces in Staffordshire and Warwickshire was the Puritan magnate Lord Brooke. On 25th February, Brooke defeated Colonel Wagstaffe's Royalists at Stratford-upon-Avon. He then advanced on Lichfield which commanded the main north-south road through Staffordshire. The Royalist Earl of Chesterfield had occupied Lichfield early in 1643. The town had no castle or walls so the garrison was established in the Cathedral Close, which was encircled by a high wall. Ammunition was stored in the cathedral itself and cannon were mounted at strategic points around the building.

On 2nd March, Lord Brooke and his 1,200 troops arrived and besieged the Cathedral, badly damaging the towers and spires during their bombardment.  On 4th March, Lord Brooke was shot through the eye and killed while observing the Royalist position. The sniper who shot him from the central spire of the cathedral was "Dumb Dyott", the deaf younger son of local gentry. The death of the radical Puritan peer on the festival day of St Chad, the patron saint of Lichfield, was regarded as a divine judgment by the Royalists. Brooke’s deputy Sir John Gell took over the siege. On 3rd March, Parliamentarian attacks on the south and west gates were resisted.  At one stage the attackers used human shields, including some of the defenders families, to aid their attack.  Further reinforcements for the attackers, under Sir William Brereton, arrived soon after. On 4th March a mortar arrived from Coventry and began to create havoc.  As a result, the Royalist garrison negotiated terms for surrender to Gell. The Earl of Chesterfield was sent to London and imprisoned in the Tower and his troops were disarmed and allowed to head for the Royalist garrison at Stafford.

Lichfield Cathedral.

Tags: Surrendered on terms; Besieged again and again; Sir William Brereton; Churches at war

Headline: Lichfield’s second siege saw a landmark moment in English warfare.
Body Text: After taking Birmingham, on 3rd April 1643, Rupert besieged Lichfield in an attempt to retake it for the King.  Lichfield was without proper fortifications, but the cathedral had been transformed into a temporary fortress, with windows and statues having been destroyed by the Parliamentarians. By 8th April, the cathedral was surrounded. The Royalist artillery was set up on the highest ground to the north, known as Prince Rupert’s Mount, but the walls surrounding the cathedral were strong and well-built. Several attempts were made to storm the walls during the 13 day siege, but they were lacking heavy siege guns and the lighter guns had little effect.  Rupert called up 50 miners from Cannock Chase to drain the moat around the cathedral and then to tunnel up to the walls. The tunnels were packed with gunpowder. On 20th April Rupert's engineers detonated the first explosive mine to be used in an English siege. The explosion opened a massive breach in the defences. Fighting was fierce and Royalist losses were high in hand to hand fighting. However, the defenders had little food or ammunition left. The surrender was signed and on 21st April. Colonel Russel and his surviving men were allowed to march out, drums beating and colours flying. A Royalist garrison was established under Colonel Richard Bagot.

Prince Rupert.

Headline: A Royalist last stand was cut short by orders from the King.
Body Text: By 1646, the King was losing the war and individual strongholds were left to fend for themselves in the absence of any specific instructions of what to do. On 9th March, the Parliamentary army, commanded by Sir William Brereton, entered Lichfield seeking to take the cathedral. The Royalists were now led by Sir Thomas Tyldesley and preparations had been made for a potential siege. Stocks of food and ammunition were high and defences had been strengthened. Brereton decided not to attempt to storm the cathedral immediately, but surrounded it and cut it off from re-supply. Timber-framed houses on Beacon Street were burned by the defenders to prevent them providing cover for attack. Brereton’s summons to surrender on 13th April was rejected by Tyldesley.  Heavy guns were brought up and a bombardment began on 7th May, aimed principally at the cathedral itself. The central spire fell on 12th May, but still the garrison refused to surrender. In June, a letter was received from the King, telling loyal garrison governors to seek the best terms they could to lay down their arms honourably. On 10th July, terms were agreed. On 16th July, Tyldesley’s men marched out, drums beating and colours flying, before laying down their weapons. In all, 700 soldiers and 80 officers of various ranks were counted.

Lichfield Cathedral.

Headline: The historic buildings of Lilleshall Abbey did not escape destruction, thanks to a Parliamentarian bombardment.
Body Text: Owned by Sir Richard Leveson, Lilleshall Abbey was fortified and garrisoned with 160 men for the King in 1643. Throughout much of the war, the building sheltered a Royalist garrison. In August 1645, Parliamentarian troops under the command of Colonel Braine approached the abbey. The attacking force bombarded the buildings with cannon fire. They caused huge damage and destroyed the abbey’s towers. The building was stormed soon after and Leveson’s men finally surrendered on 23rd August.
Caption Image 1:
Lilleshall Abbey.

Tags: Stormed

Headline: Cromwell held back a Royalist relief force whilst Parliamentarian troops scaled the walls of the castle at Lincoln.
Body Text:
Despite his successful relief of the second siege of Newark, Prince Rupert decided he could not hold the territory he had gained. After garrisoning Lincoln and placing it under the command of Sir Francis Fane, he retreated into the West Midlands. With the Royalists gone, the Earl of Manchester, the Parliamentarian commander, ordered his cavalry to advance. Under the command of Oliver Cromwell, they cleared Lincolnshire of raiding parties of Royalists from Newark and drove them across the Trent. Manchester then marched to Lincoln, arriving on 3rd May 1644.

Manchester's army consisted of around 6,000 infantry and cavalry. The Royalist garrison was about 2,000 strong. On 3rd May the Parliamentarians managed to capture parts of the lower town. The Royalists retreated to the defences surrounding t castle and cathedral. The next day, the Parliamentarians were unable to press home their advantage, because it rained heavily making the steep mound under the castle very slippery. At 3.00am on Monday 6th May the castle was stormed using scaling ladders.  The Parliamentarians took about 15 minutes to reach the walls of the castle. Despite the scaling ladders being too short and defenders throwing boulders down upon them, the Parliamentarians managed to scale the walls and enter the castle. The Royalists fled from the parapet and begged for quarter, which was granted. Parliamentarian casualties amounted to eight deaths and about 40 wounded. 50 Royalists were killed and 100 officers and between 650 and 800 soldiers were taken prisoner.

Prince Rupert.

Headline: Long-time supporters of King Charles at Lindisfarne were finally overcome by Parliamentarians in 1645.
Body Text: In June 1639, King Charles I visited the Holy Islands to gain their support during the Bishop’s Wars in nearby Scotland. The King received a warm and hospitable welcome from the castle’s governor Captain Rugge. From that moment the island’s Royalist allegiance was assured. Throughout much of the First Civil War, the Tudor fort continued to support the King. In 1645 Lindisfarne was besieged and captured by the Parliamentarians who installed Captain Batton as the new governor.
Caption Image 1:
Lindisfarne Castle.
“Lindisfarne Castle” by Neil Roger is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0

Headline: A sniper’s bullet caused chaos at Littledean Hall’s surrender negotiations.
Body Text: In 1643, Prince Maurice fought through the spring to control the town of Littledean and garrisoned Littledean Hall for the King soon after. A year later, on 7th May 1644, Colonel Edward Massey led a group of Parliamentarian soldiers to retake the town and besiege the hall. With the town lost and realising victory was unlikely; the Royalist commander began negotiations with the Massey. During the talks, a Royalist sniper killed one of the Parliamentarian soldiers. Furious, Massey immediately halted the talks and stormed the hall, killing many of the Royalist soldiers in the process.
Tags: Stormed; Edward Massey

Headline: Despite preparations, Liverpool failed to repel Prince Rupert’s Royalist army.
Body Text:
On 5th June 1644, Prince Rupert advanced to Wigan, where the Royalist townspeople scattered flowers on the ground to welcome him. Most of Lancashire was now under Rupert's control, except Manchester and Liverpool. An attack on the well defended town of Manchester was likely to prove costly and time-consuming, but the garrison at Liverpool was weaker. Liverpool’s port was also strategically important as a potential landing place for troops returning from Ireland. Rupert sent an advance guard under Colonel Washington to inspect the defences. He then followed with his main army on 7th June.

Liverpool was protected by a Medieval wall and ditch running in an arc around the landward side of the town, with a 13th century castle dominating the southern defences. The Parliamentarian engineer, Johan Rosworm had strengthened the fortifications in May. On 8th June, the Parliamentarian Governor, Colonel Moore, rejected Rupert's summons to surrender.  He underlined his defiance by shooting the Royalist messenger’s horse. Rupert promptly ordered siege artillery to begin bombarding the town walls. At noon on 10th June, Rupert ordered an assault, but the Royalists were driven back after an hour's fighting.  Colonel Moore realised that he could not continue the defence and, under cover of darkness, began to evacuate the garrison and its stores by sea. Next morning, while the evacuation was still in progress, Colonel Tillier's regiment spearheaded a second Royalist assault. They drove the defenders back towards the Town Hall, where they surrendered.  Although they were granted quarter, nearly 400 men, including some who were unarmed were slaughtered as Rupert’s troops entered the town.

Prince Rupert.
“Prince Rupert, Count Palatinate” by Gerrit van Honthorst, licensed by National Portrait Gallery.
Tags: Stormed; No quarter; Ports and the sea; Besieged again and again; Prince Rupert

Headline: Fearing for their lives, Irish defenders overruled their officers and agreed terms for surrender.
Body Text:
During the Royalist occupation of Liverpool, the Royalist engineer Sir Bernard de Gomme made plans to strengthen the defences. It is likely that they were not completed before the Parliamentarians attempted to retake the town.  Following the Royalist defeat at Marston Moor the Parliamentarians attempted to take control of the north and on 20th August a Parliamentarian force, under Sir William Brereton, began a siege of Liverpool.  The Royalist Earl of Derby gathered a force to relieve the siege. They were no match for Brereton’s troops losing around 500 men, either killed or captured.  Birkenhead fell to Brereton on 22nd September, increasing the Parliamentarian stranglehold on Liverpool.  However, Brereton was ordered to go to the aid of Montgomery Castle, which was besieged by the Royalists, and was forced to withdraw some of his troops. The Parliamentarians successfully raised the siege of Montgomery Castle and then defeated the Royalists in battle.

Following this victory Brereton marched to blockade Chester. Sir John Meldrum took over the siege of Liverpool.  Johan Rosworm, who had done much to strengthen the defences, was now put in charge of directing the siege for the Parliamentarians.  Some of the English soldiers in the garrison now began to desert and the Irish troops left to defend the town feared for their lives if their commanders rejected a demand to surrender.  Desperate to avoid this, they seized their officers and offered to surrender on terms.  Meldrum offered generous terms, despite the Parliamentary order of 24th October directing that Irish prisoners should be put to death.  He allowed them to take a ship back to Ireland, as long as they promised never to serve in England again.  The remaining English soldiers were also released, with many choosing to enlist in Parliament’s army. On 1st November the city surrendered to Meldrum.
