Sir Thomas Fairfax.
“Thomas Fairfax” by William Marshall, licensed by National Portrait Gallery.
Tags: Surrendered on terms; After Marston Moor; Ports and the sea; Besieged again and again; Sir William Brereton

Headline: The Marquis of Montrose resorted to underhand tactics to take this Covenanter stronghold.
Body Text: During the First Civil War, Loch Dochart was one of the castles under the control of Clan Campbell. Committed to the Covenanter cause, the clan sided with Parliament to fight against King Charles I. This action placed them squarely in the path of James Graham, the Marquis of Montrose and a key Royalist commander in Scotland. In December 1644, Graham’s Royalist army came across the castle as they were travelling west. Instead of mounting an attack, Graham ordered a small party of soldiers to infiltrate the castle by pretending to be messengers from the Marquis of Argyll, a key Covenanter figure. The unsuspecting Parliamentarian defenders let the “messengers” into the castle, at which point they threw off their disguises and overcame the garrison, securing it for the King.
Tags: Taken by surprise; Scotland and Ireland

Headline: Events in November 1642 showed the need to fortify London, although it was never besieged.
Body Text:
Although London was never besieged during the Civil Wars, events during 1642 highlighted the danger of leaving London undefended.  At the beginning of the First Civil War, the city immediately and unsurprisingly declared for Parliament. Following the Battle of Edgehill the Royalists advanced on London. On 12th November 1642, Prince Rupert’s troops captured and looted nearby Brentford.  The following day, the Royalists were confronted by the Earl of Essex’s army and London’s Trained Bands at Turnham Green. The outnumbered Royalists decided to withdraw, rather than engage in battle.

In 1642 some basic fortifications were built, in the form of street barricades and small earthworks. On 7th March 1643, Parliament passed an order for “entrenching and fortifying the City of London”.  As a result a major construction effort was made, providing a comprehensive ring of fortifications around the city, which became known as the Lines of Communication. Most of the work was done by volunteer labour. With up to 20,000 people involved, the works were completed in less than two months. It is believed that Sergeant-Major-General Phillip Skippon designed the defences as he had experience of siege warfare during the Thirty Years War.  The defences consisted of a strong earthen rampart reinforced with a series of 23 fortifications of differing types surrounding the whole city, at a distance of one and a half to two miles from the city centre. The fortifications failed their only test when the New Model Army entered London in 1647 and they were levelled by Parliament the same year.

Headline: Longford Castle fell to the Parliamentarians after a near miss for Oliver Cromwell.
Body Text: Longford Castle was held by a Royalist garrison under the command of Sir Bartholomew Pell in October 1644. A year later, the garrison was put to the test when Cromwell arrived with a Parliamentarian army on 16th October 1645. Taking the high ground, Cromwell issued a demand for surrender and prepared to bombard the Castle if his demand was refused. While they waited for a response, a small number of shots were exchanged. One of these shots, fired by a defending Royalist, barely missed Cromwell, killing an officer with whom he had been deciding how best to take the castle. Two days later on 18th October, the castle and garrison were surrendered without any further violence. Though the castle was not damaged, the inhabitants of a local village were required to level the earthworks and other defences around the castle.
Caption Image 1:
Oliver Cromwell.
“Oliver Cromwell” by Robert Walker, licensed by National Portrait Gallery.
Tags: Surrendered on terms; After Naseby; Oliver Cromwell

Headline: A 400 year old building didn’t escape the destruction of the Civil Wars.
Body Text: At the start of the First Civil War, the 400 year old Longford Hall was owned by the Earl of Shrewsbury. Shrewsbury declared for Parliament and established a garrison soon after. On 2nd April 1644, the hall was captured by a Royalist force and subsequently demolished to prevent it being recaptured and garrisoned by Parliament.
Tags: Slighted

Headline: Within days of taking the town, the Earl of Essex was surrounded by a Royalist force commanded by the King.
Body Text:
The Parliamentarian Earl of Essex marched into Lostwithiel on 2nd August 1644. Most of the town garrison fled as the Parliamentarians approached, but a small band took refuge in the tower of St Bartholomew's Church. The Parliamentarians exploded a barrel of gunpowder at the base of the tower to drive them out, destroying part of the church roof. Royalists later alleged that Essex's soldiers held blasphemous mock services in the half-ruined church, christening a horse "Charles" in a ceremony around the font. Essex deployed his forces in a defensive arc with strong concentrations at Beacon Hill to the east of Lostwithiel and Restmorel Castle to the north.

Keen to retake the town, the Royalist army, commanded by King Charles, moved to contain the Parliamentarians and seal off all avenues of escape. On 6th August, the King called upon Essex to surrender his forces but he refused. On 21st August, the Royalists made a carefully coordinated advance. The ruins of Restmorel Castle were stormed and Beacon Hill was taken. The Royalists continued their containment of the Parliamentarian army, which was now trapped in a narrow tract of land five miles long and two miles wide.

The Earl of Essex decided to abandon Lostwithiel and withdraw to Fowey in the hope that the infantry could be evacuated by sea. The Royalists immediately occupied the town and set off in pursuit of the Parliamentarian army. A running battle developed with the Royalists contesting every hedge and field.  King Charles spent the night under a hedge amongst his frontline troops in anticipation of the defeat of the enemy the next day. The Earl of Essex, accompanied by Lord Robartes, commandeered a fishing boat and escaped to Plymouth, abandoning the Parliamentarian infantry and artillery. Major-General Philip Skippon was left in command. He wanted to fight his way out, but the officers and men were so dejected that Skippon was obliged to surrender on 2nd September.

The defeated army was allowed to march away after surrendering all its weapons, artillery and stores, on condition that they not take up arms until reaching the Parliamentarian garrisons of Portsmouth or Southampton. The disarmed Roundheads were set upon and robbed by local Cornishmen, who claimed to be recovering their own plundered property. Many of the exhausted, half-starved soldiers died of exposure and disease on the terrible march from Lostwithiel. Hundreds of others deserted. Little more than 3,000 of Essex's infantry eventually arrived at Southampton.
Caption Image 1:
St. Bartholomews Church, Lostwithiel.
“P1210340 St. Bartholomews Parish Church Lostwithiel” by Tadie88 is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Ports and the sea; Churches at war; Townspeople

Headline: A local group took initiative but were foiled by Cromwell’s army.
Body Text: Lowestoft did not immediately declare an allegiance at the start of the First Civil War. This left it as a target for both Royalists and Parliamentarians. In March 1643, a group of local Royalists decided to make a move to seize and fortify the town. Unfortunately for them, Oliver Cromwell was marching to nearby Norwich and received intelligence of the gathering of Royalists. The next day on 14th March, Cromwell and his men seized the port and arrested all involved, ensuring the town’s support for Parliament.
Caption Image 1:
Oliver Cromwell.
“Oliver Cromwell” by Robert Walker, licensed by National Portrait Gallery.
Tags: Taken by surprise; Ports and the sea; Oliver Cromwell

Headline: The massacre at Hopton Castle came back to haunt a Royalist commander at Ludlow when he was called to surrender.
Body Text: When war broke out, Ludlow and the surrounding region declared for the King.  A Royalist garrison was established in the town under the command of Sir Michael Woodhouse. The defences were strengthened, with artillery being brought from nearby Bringwood Forge for the castle. As the war turned against the King in 1644, the men from the garrison were sent to provide reinforcements for a Royalist army nearby. In April 1646, Sir William Brereton and Colonel John Birch led a Parliamentary army to take Ludlow.  The town was taken on 24th April but the castle held out for a further five weeks. Woodhouse knew surrender was inevitable, but was cautious. As the commanding officer of the victorious Royalist attack at Hopton Castle, Woodhouse had killed a dozen of the surrendering garrison. Fearing a reprisal, Woodhouse made it clear that he would only surrender the keys to Colonel Birch in person, as he believed that he would be treated honourably by him.  He surrendered the castle on good terms on 26th May.
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Sir William Brereton

Headline: The Royalist garrison at Lundy was forced to wait for King Charles’ permission before surrendering,
Body Text: Lundy declared for King Charles I and was held by Thomas Bushell. Unsatisfied with the island’s defences, Bushell rebuilt, refortified and garrisoned Marisco Castle at his own expense at a cost of £5570 (equivalent to around £500,000 today). In 1647, Bushell was attacked by Parliamentarian forces and requested permission to surrender from King Charles I. He received permission on 24th February and surrendered to Richard Fiennes, the Parliamentarian commander.
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Ports and the sea

Headline: Royalists burnt down their garrison at Lydney rather than let it fall into enemy hands
Body Text:
During the First Civil War, Lydney was garrisoned for the King by Sir John Wintour. With its proximity to Parliamentarian Gloucester, the garrison was vulnerable to frequent attacks from Roundhead soldiers. In April 1645, these attacks, carried out by Colonel Edward Massey, culminated in a blockade of Lydney. On 2nd April, Prince Rupert and Prince Maurice arrived in the Forest of Dean with the aim of plundering the nearby countryside and clearing the blockades. On 6th April, the County Committee reported:

?a great oppression, cruel plunders and continual marches and inroads of the enemy lying near and heavy upon us on every side; our County was so extremely exhausted and miserably destroyed that it was even ready to give up the ghost.'

Massey was heavily outnumbered by the 2,000 strong Royalist army. He withdrew his forces from the attack on Lydney’s garrison soon after. By the 9th April 1645, having stripped the area and destroyed many homes, Rupert’s forces moved on to Herefordshire. Taking advantage of his absence, Massey turned around and returned to Lydney. Realising that without Rupert’s firepower they stood little chance of victory, Wintour decided to burn his property rather than let it fall into enemy hands. He then withdrew to Chepstow Castle. Massey was able to rescue some spoils from the flames at Lydney. He captured eight large guns from the earthworks defending the mansion, as well as some beef, corn and horses.
Caption Image 1:
Prince Rupert.
“Prince Rupert, Count Palatinate” by Gerrit van Honthorst, licensed by National Portrait Gallery.
Tags: Defenders withdrew; Prince Rupert; Edward Massey

Headline: A two month siege at Lyme cost the Royalist besiegers hundreds of lives, before they were forced to abandon the attempt.
Body Text:
On 20th April 1644, Prince Maurice appeared before the port of Lyme in Dorset with a force of 6,000 men. Although it was a relatively minor port, Lyme was a staunchly Parliamentarian outpost in the mainly Royalist held West Country. Its garrison, commanded by Colonel Were and Lieutenant-Colonel Robert Blake, mounted regular raids and its harbour, the Cobb, was a safe haven for Parliament's warships. By capturing Lyme, the Royalists hoped to complete a chain of strongholds linking Bristol with the English Channel.

The town was overlooked by high hills. It had no walls but was defended by a ring of earthwork banks and ditches. The Parliamentarians defiantly rejected Maurice's call to surrender and the Royalists deployed in an arc around the town. Maurice systematically took outlying Parliamentarian outposts and began setting up guns to bombard the town's defences. On 24th April, a raiding party from the garrison drove the startled Royalists from their guns and chased them up the hill until forced back by Maurice's main force. This was the first of several raids mounted by the defenders throughout the siege. After a major Royalist assault was thrown back with heavy casualties on 28th April, the besiegers kept up an intense artillery bombardment, interspersed with attempts to take the town by storm.

Parliamentarian control of the sea meant that the Royalists could do nothing to prevent the Earl of Warwick's fleet from shipping supplies and reinforcements into Lyme. Around 14th May, Prince Maurice ordered the re-positioning of several heavy guns to target shipping. A determined attack was made on 21st May resulting in the destruction of most of the supply boats in the harbour. Gradually, the relentless Royalist assaults wore the defenders down. Around 28th May, the defences were breached. The Parliamentarians wavered and were almost overrun but finally rallied to a soldier, Ensign Moizier, who stood firm with the colours. The Royalists tried to set the town ablaze by shooting flaming arrows onto the thatched roofs. Although several houses caught fire, the wind direction didn’t allow a large blaze.

Unable to re-supply the town indefinitely, Warwick reported that Lyme's plight was growing desperate and that it must be relieved by land. Sir William Waller was ordered to march to the relief of Lyme, but his superior, the Earl of Essex, took it upon himself. On 6th June, Essex abandoned the Oxford campaign and set out for the south-west, ignoring the Committee's orders calling him back. On 15th June, with Essex's army at Blandford, Prince Maurice lifted the siege of Lyme and withdrew with his army to Exeter. The two-month siege had cost the Royalists around 2,000 casualties and large supplies of ammunition. The defenders admitted to only 120 dead.
Tags: Relieved; Ports and the sea

Headline: Established as a Parliamentarian outpost of Gloucester, Lypiatt Park faced a Royalist attack on New Year’s Day.
Body Text: In February 1643, the Parliamentary forces at nearby Gloucester established an outpost at Lypiatt Park. By the end of 1644, Lypiatt housed a garrison and served as a base for raiding parties. On New Year's Day 1645 Royalist troops, commanded by Sir Jacob Astley, captured and burned Lypiatt Park House. Two years later the owner, John Stephens, was temporarily granted part of Astley's estates in compensation for the damage.

Headline: This moated manor house’s proximity to Worcester bound it to the city’s uncertain fate.
Body Text: At the beginning of the war Madresfield was owned by Colonel William Lygon, a halfhearted Parliamentarian.  The house was close to Royalist Worcester and was occupied by both sides throughout the city’s three sieges. When Colonel Lygon’s forces were defeated by the Royalists at Worcester in 1646, Madresfield was garrisoned for the King, by a force commanded by Captain Aston.  Soon after, Royalist fortunes took a turn for the worse. When Worcester surrendered to Parliamentarian forces on 22nd July 1646, Madresfield was surrendered to Parliament at the same time and under the same terms.
Tags: Surrendered on terms

Headline: Parliamentarian Manchester relied on preparation and good fortune to help it resist a Royalist attack in one of the earliest clashes of the First Civil War.
Body Text:
Despite Manchester’s pro-Parliament stance, the County of Lancashire was dominated by the staunchly Royalist James Stanley, Lord Strange. Having quickly taken command of the supplies of other northern towns, such as Preston and Lancaster, Strange turned his attention to Manchester.  Strange’s efforts were resisted by the town’s inhabitants who declared their support for Parliament and refused to hand over the munitions.

The German engineer Johan Rosworm had just completed the defences of Manchester when Lord Strange gathered his forces in Warrington on Saturday 24th September. They approached on both sides of the River Irwell, but by the time they arrived at around midnight, his men were exhausted.  Most were poorly armed, with few Pikemen having breastplates or helmets. Lord Strange summoned the defenders to surrender, but was not surprised when this was refused.

At about 4.00pm on Sunday 25th September the Royalists prepared for battle. The defenders awaited them armed mainly with only scythes and hoes. Weapons were scarce for both sides at this early stage of the war.  Despite their lack of weapons, the natural and engineered defences of Manchester assisted the defenders as did the weather.  The first day of the siege saw further calls for surrender, which were again rejected.  That night Lord Strange received the news that his father had died and he was now the 7th Earl of Derby. He was keener than ever to bring Manchester under control quickly so he could go home and mourn for his father. On Monday 26th September, when the defenders rejected further demands to surrender, the Royalist cannon opened fire. After capturing a house close to the Salford side of Salford Bridge, Stanley ordered his men to hurl burning bundles of wood onto the rooftops of Manchester’s houses, but the wet weather meant that this had little effect.  Attacks continued over the next few days. A Royalist officer was killed by a musketeer firing from the steeple of what is now Manchester Cathedral. Attacks were costing the Royalists dearly. One attack cost them 100 men and only four Parliamentarians were killed. This, along with ammunition and food shortages, helped to demoralise the Royalist besiegers. The Earl of Derby’s men began to desert him and he realised that he had little real chance of taking Manchester for the King. By Friday 30th September, Derby had made the decision to start a tactical withdrawal, digging a new trench to cover the start of his retreat.  On 1st October there was an exchange of prisoners and the Royalists abandoned the siege.
Tags: Besiegers gave up; Churches at war; Townspeople

Headline: Although never taken by Royalists, the town of Melton Mowbray was victim to their attacks.
Body Text: Melton Mowbray was a Parliamentarian garrison commanded by Colonel Rossiter. In November 1643, Royalists raiders from Newark caught the garrison unaware and looted the town, carrying away prisoners and valuables. On 25th February 1645, Sir Marmaduke Langdale, commanding a Royalist force of 1,500 men and aided by Newark Royalists, inflicted severe losses on Rossiter’s forces. Around 300 men were said to have been killed.
Tags: Besiegers gave up; Newark's ring; Townspeople

Headline: Royalist defenders hid in a church to escape the Parliamentarian onslaught.
Body Text:
In January 1643, Sir Thomas Aston was appointed Major-General of Royalist forces in Cheshire and Lancashire, in an effort by the King to maintain Cheshire for the Royalists. Parliament had also realised Cheshire’s importance and sent Sir William Brereton to raise support for their cause there.  In his account of the Battle of Middlewich, Aston did not say why he came to Middlewich, but explained that he had no wish to linger in an undefended town with Parliamentarian forces nearby. Sir William Brereton thought the Royalist stay at Middlewich resulted from overconfidence in their fighting ability. On Sunday 12th March, Brereton, wanting to "annoy" the enemy, set out with two or three companies of dragoons to harass the Royalists at Middlewich. He arranged to meet other Parliamentarian forces from Nantwich at 6.00am on 13th March to make a joint attack on Middlewich.

On the morning of Monday 13th March, the Nantwich forces had not arrived at the appointed time so Brereton decided to attack with his cavalry and about 200 musketeers.  Following skirmishes in the fields outside the town, and the eventual arrival of the Nantwich Parliamentarians, the Royalists were forced back into the town. The Parliamentarians were then able to bring up their cannons. They advanced towards St Michael and All Angels church from three directions, so Aston ordered a party of dragoons to defend the churchyard. The Parliamentarians charged the Royalist infantry which promptly disappeared. This left Aston's cavalry exposed and unable to charge because of a large ditch. Aston found all the infantry in the church and they could not be persuaded to come out to face the attackers. After trying to rally his cavalry he became separated from them and found himself alone. The rest of his forces were either scattered or sheltering in the church. The Parliamentarians soon took the church and with it over 400 soldiers and two cannon. Brereton had secured a complete victory.
Caption Image 1:
St Michael & All Angels Church, Middlewich.
“St Michael & All Angels” by SteHLiverpool is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Stormed; Sir William Brereton; Churches at war

Headline: In the path of the Royalist’s plan to retake Scotland, the defenders at Mingary Castle were forced to endure a seven week siege.
Body Text:
Following the Covenanter invasion of England in 1644, the Royalists immediately began to retaliate. They planned to distract the Covenanter army by inciting uprisings in Scotland, and then sending an invading army from Ireland under the command of the Earl of Antrim to take them by surprise.

The Earl of Antrim had succeeded in raising an invasion force of 1,600 men led by Alasdair MacColla. The army landed at Ardnamurcham in the western Highlands on 8th July 1644. They captured Mingary Castle after a two day siege on 14th July.  The capture was a coup for the Royalist forces who intended to use the castle as a secure base for further attacks in Scotland. Realising this, the Covenanter commander Sir Duncan Campbell decided to retake the castle and laid siege to it in late August. The siege lasted seven weeks.  The defenders were forced to drink the rainwater that gathered on parts of the wall. A Royalist force, led by Alasdair MacDonald, set out to relieve the siege. Fearing that they would be overwhelmed, Sir Duncan Campbell abandoned his siege on the night of 5th October 1644.
Caption Image 1:
Mingary Castle.
 “Mingary Castle” by Tom Parnell is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Relieved; Scotland and Ireland

Headline: The Royalist defenders  at Monmouth surrendered before the besiegers could fire their mines under the castle walls.
Body Text: A month after it was captured by the Parliamentarians, Monmouth Castle was back in Royalist hands.  Keen to retake the castle, Colonel Sir Thomas Morgan besieged the stronghold in October 1645 with a Parliamentarian force of around 3,000 men. Morgan ordered miners to be brought in from the Forest of Dean and oversaw the construction of six mines underneath the castle wall. Morgan’s plan was to fill them with explosives and light the fuse, but before he got the chance, the defenders surrendered. When they marched out on 25th October they left behind seven cannon, 300 muskets, 600 pikes, ammunition and food.  In March 1647, the castle was slighted by Colonel Kyrle, while the townsfolk were at church.
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Mines and petards; Slighted

Headline: The Royalists suffered a major defeat after trying to retake Montgomery, permanently weakening their position in Wales.
Body Text:
Early in September 1644, Sir Thomas Myddelton and Colonel Thomas Mytton intended to secure Parliamentarian control of the Upper Severn Valley. On 3rd September, they surprised and overwhelmed Newtown in Montgomeryshire and seized a powder convoy. Laden with their captured gunpowder, Myddelton and Mytton advanced to attack Montgomery.

Although the town of Montgomery was poorly defended by a ruinous Medieval wall, its castle was one of the most formidable fortresses in the region. It was held by the elderly Lord Herbert, who lived in a mansion within the castle. Myddelton's forces occupied the town on 4th September and called upon Herbert to surrender the castle. Terms were agreed on 5th September, with Myddelton promising that no harm would come to Herbert or to his possessions, in particular his valuable library. A Parliamentarian garrison then occupied the castle.

Within days, the Royalist commanders Major-General Sir Michael Erneley and Sir William Vaughan marched to counter-attack. They approached on 8th September when most of the Parliamentarians were on a foraging expedition. Surprised and outnumbered, the remaining Parliamentarian infantry fell back to the castle. Myddelton rode away with most of the cavalry to seek reinforcements. The Royalists surrounded Montgomery, digging trenches and building earthworks in preparation for a long siege. Myddelton gathered all available Parliamentarian forces to mount a relief attempt. Sir John Meldrum withdrew a large body of his forces from the siege of Liverpool. Sir William Fairfax brought troops from Yorkshire and Sir William Brereton mustered the Cheshire infantry. The combined army of around 2,000 infantry and 1,500 cavalry approached Montgomery on 17th September.

Meanwhile, the Royalists had also been reinforced. Lord Byron had marched from Chester and Sir Michael Woodhouse from Ludlow. Their combined army consisted of around 2,800 infantry, 1,400 cavalry and 300 dragoons. Leaving enough troops to guard the trenches and siege works, Byron deployed the bulk of his forces on a steep sided hill. The Parliamentarians drew up on flat ground two miles north of the town. The two armies remained in position overnight. The following day, with no sign of an engagement, the Parliamentarians sent out nearly a third of their cavalry to gather provisions for the garrison in the castle. Byron took this opportunity to order a general attack.

The initial attack seems to have gone the way of the Royalists. The outnumbered Parliamentarian cavalry were driven back and the Royalist infantry gained ground. Major-General Lothian succeeded in rallying the Cheshire infantry to halt the Royalist advance. The tide of the battle then turned dramatically against the Royalists. It is possible that the Parliamentarian foraging party returned to tip the balance. The Parliamentarians regrouped and counter-attacked. Myddelton’s horse charged and defeated the Royalist cavalry, while Brereton's infantry broke through the Royalist infantry. Colonel Mytton's forces rushed out of Montgomery Castle to overwhelm the Royalists guarding the trenches. After an hour's fighting, the battle ended with a Parliamentarian victory. Around 500 Royalist soldiers were killed and 1,500 were taken prisoner. The Parliamentarians in comparison lost forty men, including Sir William Fairfax, commander of the Yorkshire contingent.

Montgomery Castle.

Tags: Relieved; Sir William Brereton

Headline: The strategic value of the Royalist garrison at Montford Bridge made them a target for nearby Parliamentarians.
Body Text: During the First Civil War, Royalist forces were quick to establish a garrison at Montford Bridge, due to its key strategic position over the River Severn. The bridge was held for the King for over a year until June 1644, when an attack from Parliamentarian troops under the command of the Earl of Denbigh forced them to surrender.
Tags: Stormed

Headline: A crack team of a dozen Parliamentarian soldiers managed to overwhelm a much larger Royalist garrison.
Body Text:
Like most of the Shropshire Gentry, Sir Vincent Corbet was a staunch Royalist and at the outbreak of the First Civil War in 1642, he garrisoned his home for the King. The castle formed part of the county’s Royalist defences and was attacked several times throughout the war. Most significant of these was an attack in September 1644 when the castle was captured for the Parliamentarians with only a dozen men.

Under cover of darkness, a team of crack Roundhead soldiers made their way towards the castle. Despite their small numbers, the troops imitated a larger force by banging drums to simulate the sound of marching and shouting orders to imaginary reinforcements. Upon reaching the castle, two attackers distracted a sentry while others scaled the walls with ladders. The Royalists, fearing that they would be overwhelmed, retreated into the main house. They were followed by Parliamentarian soldiers throwing hand grenadoes. When the attackers entered the house through a smashed window, the Royalists were so fearful that they surrendered immediately. It was only later that it dawned on them that their garrison of six officers, 80 soldiers, 30 horses and six barrels of gunpowder had been captured by just a dozen Parliamentarian soldiers.
Caption Image 1:
Moreton Corbet Castle.
 “Castle” by James is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Taken by surprise; Family homes

Headline: 300 years after it was built, Morpeth saw its first major action during the First Civil War
Body Text:
Despite being built in the 1340’s, Morpeth Castle had to wait until the First Civil War to see major military action. It was garrisoned by the Scots for Parliament, but its strategic location on the border made it a target for nearby Royalist troops under the command of the Marquis of Montrose, James Graham. In March 1644, Montrose led his army of 2,700 men to bombard the castle for 20 days. This caused serious damage to the building, until the Scottish commander Somerville surrendered to Montrose.

The Cavalier’s victory was not an enduring one as the castle reverted to a Parliamentarian garrison after the Royalist defeat at the Battle of Marston Moor.
Caption Image 1:
Morpeth Castle.
 “Morpeth Castle 2013 (46)” by Steve Brown is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Surrendered on terms

Headline: A thorn in the side of Parliament, the garrison at Mount Edgecumbe finally surrendered in April 1646.
Body Text:
Colonel Piers Edgecumbe commanded a Royalist regiment at Plymouth. Like many members of the Cornish gentry, he supported the King.  His home at Mount Edgecumbe, overlooking Plymouth Sound, became a Royalist garrison. Guns were set up there to help prevent Parliamentarian ships entering the harbour during daylight.

The garrison was raided by Parliamentarians on 3rd March 1644 and several cannon were taken.  Although there were several attempts to take the garrison over the next few months, it was not until 21st April 1646 that it finally surrendered to Colonel Hammond, following a short siege. This left Salcombe standing alone for the Royalist cause in Devon.
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Ports and the sea; Family homes

Headline: Despite preparations, Mulgrave Castle still struggled to fight off Parliamentarian troops.
Body Text: During the Civil War, the owner of Mulgrave Castle was an ardent Royalist, Edmund Sheffield. Recognising the castles’ strategic importance, Sheffield refortified and garrisoned it for the King. Unfortunately for Sheffield, Parliamentarian troops attacked the castle in 1645 and after a short siege, it was surrendered. On the orders of Parliament in 1647, it was slighted to prevent any future use as a military site.
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Slighted

Headline: A collapsed bridge split the Royalist forces, allowing Fairfax to take advantage and relieve the siege of Nantwich.
Body Text:
Having cleared most of Cheshire of the King's enemies, in early 1664 Lord Byron advanced towards Nantwich, the last Parliamentarian stronghold in the county. Nantwich had been a Parliamentarian garrison since January 1643. Fearing an attack, the commanders Sir George Booth and Colonel Croxton made preparations for a possible siege and the garrison of nearly 2,000 men was well-supplied.

Byron set up his headquarters at the nearby village of Acton and summoned Nantwich to surrender on 10th January 1644. The following day, after the summons was rejected, Royalist artillery opened fire on the town. The bombardment continued for several days and was accompanied by frequent skirmishing between the besiegers and troops from the garrison. On 18th January, after Byron's second summons had been refused, the Royalists attempted to take the town by storm. The defences were attacked at five points simultaneously. The assault was fiercely resisted and the Royalists were driven back with heavy losses of around 500 killed and wounded. Things got even worse for the Royalists as Byron's army declined in strength as a result of sickness, desertion and the bitter weather.

On 21st January, Sir Thomas Fairfax marched from Manchester with a combined force of around 3,000 infantry and 1,800 cavalry. He had intended to reinforce the garrison at Nantwich rather than engage Byron's army in battle. As the Parliamentarians approached, there was a change in the weather.  A thaw set in and heavy rain began to fall. On 25th January, the River Weaver became so swollen that Lord Byron transferred his artillery and most of his infantry to the western bank.  Byron and most of his cavalry were still on the eastern side. The flood swept away a bridge, splitting the Royalist army in two. Byron was forced to march to the next bridge to try to reunite his forces.

The Royalist troops on the western side of the river were commanded by Colonel Gibson who drew up his forces around Acton church. The Parliamentarians approached Gibson's position at around 2.00pm.  At the same time, news reached Fairfax that Byron's cavalry was approaching the rear of the Parliamentarian column. Fairfax sent two regiments to hold the Royalist cavalry at bay and continued his advance towards Acton. He planned to defeat Gibson’s Royalist infantry at Acton before Byron arrived to reinforce them. Despite the lack of cavalry support, the Royalist wings held firm and inflicted heavy casualties. In the centre, however, the Royalists gave ground. At this critical point, a force of musketeers from the Nantwich garrison marched out and swept aside the Royalist reserve regiment guarding the road into the town. The Royalist centre collapsed completely. Fairfax's Parliamentarians swept through the gap and quickly overwhelmed the regiments holding out on the flanks. The Royalists fell back to Acton church where Colonel Gibson surrendered to Fairfax under terms. The artillery and baggage train were captured and about 1,500 officers and men taken prisoner.
Caption Image 1:
Sir Thomas Fairfax.
“Thomas Fairfax” by William Marshall, licensed by National Portrait Gallery.
Tags: Relieved; Sir Thomas Fairfax; Churches at war

Headline: The Hays family switched allegiance in 1650 and found themselves repelling attacks from the Parliamentarians that they supported in First Civil War.
Body Text:
During the First Civil War, the Hays family who owned Neidpath Castle established a Parliamentarian garrison. They frequently repelled attacks from Royalist troops under James Graham, the Marquis of Montrose.

By the Third Civil War, following Cromwell’s invasion of Scotland John Hay had changed his allegiance. Now opposing the Parliamentarian forces, Neidpath Castle was attacked multiple times in 1650 and besieged late in the year. The castle held out until February 1651, only surrendering when Cromwell’s cannons started destroying the walls.
Caption Image 1:
Neidpath Castle.
 “Neidpath Castle” by John Denham is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Scotland and Ireland; Oliver Cromwell; Turncoats and treachery

Headline: Royalists led a counter attack that foiled the Parliamentarians at this key strategic battleground.
Body Text:
Newark had been a Royalist stronghold since the start of the war and was a key strategic location.  Newark Castle dominated the crossroads of the Fosse Way and Great North Road and guarded the last crossing place of the River Trent before it becomes tidal.

In late February 1643, Governor Sir John Henderson received intelligence that a Parliamentarian force under Major-General Thomas Ballard intended to take the town.  In order to prevent the attack, Henderson planned an ambush on Ballard’s forces at Beckingham in Lincolnshire. His plan was discovered and he was forced to call off the attack. On 27th February 1643, Ballard approached the town with 6,000 men and ten pieces of artillery.  Although Henderson attempted to intercept Ballard’s forces on Beacon Hill he lacked artillery and was forced to withdraw behind the earthworks.  Henderson was summoned to surrender, but he refused.  Ballard then divided his men into three brigades, with the artillery sent to bombard the town.  A second brigade was sent to capture Exeter House. The third attacked Henderson’s troops and engaged them in close combat.  Ballard’s forces fought their way towards the town, but Henderson had hidden some of his troops in barns on the route and although outnumbered, they successfully pushed the Parliamentarians back.

As evening approached and believing Ballard’s men to be tiring, Henderson gambled on a counter attack.  This scattered the Parliamentarians and 60 prisoners and three cannon were captured.  These were the first cannon for the Newark garrison.  The Royalists had inflicted a humiliating defeat on the Parliamentarians, but the attack highlighted how fragile Newark’s earthwork defences were. They were described as “Most pitiful works...very low and thin, and with a dry ditch which most men might easily leap...”  The defences were later strengthened at strategic points with the addition of pitfalls.
Caption Image 1:
Newark Castle.
“Newark Castle” by Peter Sharman, licensed by Newark Photographic Society.
Tags: Besiegers gave up; Newark's ring; Besieged again and again

Headline: Prince Rupert relieved Newark’s second siege in what was probably his finest military victory.
Body Text:
Following the Royalist defeat at Winceby on 11th October 1643 and the loss of Gainsborough to the Parliamentarians, Royalist Newark became isolated.  Sir John Henderson was replaced as Governor by Sir Richard Byron. He had little time to organise his forces before the town was besieged for a second time.  On 29th February 1644, Sir John Meldrum surrounded the town with 7,000 Parliamentarian troops, 11 cannon and two mortars.  The bombardment raged day and night, with one cannonball causing a hole in the church spire.  During this siege, Alderman Hercules Clay dreamt three times that his house had been destroyed by a grenadoe shell.  After the third dream he moved his family to safety and on 11th March his home was destroyed, just as he had dreamt.  Clay left bequests of £100 each for an annual sermon to be held on the anniversary of his “deliverance” and for the benefit of the poor.  However, the £100 he had left to the poor was immediately used to strengthen the town’s defences.

Meldrum’s forces strengthened their stranglehold on the town by taking outlying Royalist outposts.  Lord Loughborough, the Royalist Commander in the region, appealed to Prince Rupert for assistance.  On 21st March, following a march from Bridgnorth, Shropshire, Rupert’s force of about 6,400 men approached Newark via Balderton.  At dawn his forces were on nearby Beacon Hill.  From here he could see Meldrum’s forces below him.  His men charged downhill and after a fierce fight drove the Parliamentarian cavalry off before turning their attention to the foot soldiers.  Some of the Newark garrison then mounted an attack on the Island and Muskham Bridge on the River Trent. Rupert then moved some of his troops across the river, trapping the Parliamentarian forces.  Realising he was trapped Meldrum agreed to a truce. His troops were allowed to march off with their colours, drums and horses, although their weapons were seized by the garrison.  The haul consisted of 11 cannon, two mortars and around 3,000 muskets and ammunition.  One of the guns was a 32 pounder, known as “Sweet Lips”; supposedly named after a Hull prostitute. The taking of the town was a significant military victory for Rupert, with added prestige from the skill and speed with which it had been carried out.

Following Rupert’s departure Byron ordered the defences to be strengthened further.  Earthwork defences were extended south beyond the corn and gunpowder mills on Millgate. It is probable that the earthwork known as the Queen’s Sconce was built around this time to defend the southern approaches to the town.  The Queen’s Sconce can still be seen today and is probably the best preserved 17th Century earthwork in the country.
Caption Image 1:
Prince Rupert.
“Prince Rupert, Count Palatinate” by Gerrit van Honthorst, licensed by National Portrait Gallery.
Tags: Relieved; Newark's ring; Besieged again and again; Prince Rupert; Townspeople

Headline: Weakened by malnutrition and plague, Newark refused to surrender until ordered by the King.
Body Text:
Lord John Belasyse became governor of Newark in October 1645. He quickly prepared for Newark’s final siege. On 26th November a Scots army, commanded by General Alexander Leslie, appeared to the north of Newark. Within a few days Leslie had secured key outposts including Muskham Bridge and the Island. Major General Sydnam Poyntz’s Parliamentarian forces occupied the villages to the east and south of the town. Despite the harsh winter the garrison continued to launch attacks against Parliamentarian forces. The attacks encouraged the besieging Parliamentarians to tighten their hold around the town.  The Scots established their headquarters at an enormous fortified camp known as “Edinburgh”.  A continuous chain of small earthwork camps about 200 – 250 yards apart were built.  Upstream from Newark Castle, Poyntz dammed the River Devon and the Trent to stop the watermills grinding corn for bread and the gunpowder mills producing powder.  Food became scarce with defenders forced to eat their horses.  Malnutrition weakened the people of Newark and their resistance to disease was lowered. By March 1646, plague was rife in the town. One contemporary account stated that Newark had become “a miserable stinking infected town”. On 28th March, Poyntz called upon Newark to surrender but he was refused. The noose around Newark continued to tighten.  The Parliamentarians thought that it was only a matter of time before the starving and sick Royalists trapped inside Newark would be forced to give in.

What neither side knew was that events elsewhere would bring the siege to a sudden end.  King Charles arrived in Southwell on the morning of 5th May and entered into negotiations with the Scots.  The King was taken to Kelham House for talks with General David Leslie. He was treated as a prisoner and forced to write to Belasyse ordering him to surrender.  Belasyse was bitterly disappointed with the King’s command, believing the town could hold out for much longer. Newark’s Mayor urged Belasyse to ignore the order and “Trust in God and sally forth” but the terms of the town’s surrender were agreed.  On 8th May, Lord John Belasyse and between 1,500 – 1,800 men marched out of Newark, leaving behind 12 cannon, two mortars and a large amount of gunpowder and muskets.  Parliamentarians ordered the townsfolk and people from neighbouring villages to “come in with spades, shovels, pickaxes and other necessaries” and “assist in the demolishing of the workes”.  The Parliamentarians soon left Newark, probably fearful of the plague.  Weakened by the effects of malnutrition and disease, those tasked with bringing down Newark’s castle and its siege defences had little energy or enthusiasm to go about their task. Their lack of industry has ensured that the castle and the most complete Civil War earthworks in the country, survive today.
Caption Image 1:
Newark Castle.
“Newark Castle” by Peter Sharman, licensed by Newark Photographic Society.
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Slighted; Newark's ring; Besieged again and again; Townspeople

Headline: The castle changed hands several times before finally being taken and slighted by the Parliamentarians.
Body Text:
Newcastle Emlyn castle was initially a Royalist stronghold.  An earthwork was constructed in front of the Gatehouse to strengthen the defences.  During the war the castle changed hands several times. Taken by the Parliamentarians in 1644 the castle was quickly re-captured by a Royalist force under Sir Charles Gerard, during his conquest of Wales. When Gerard left Wales for England to support the King, the castle was besieged by the Parliamentarian Major-General, Rowland Laugharne. By March 1645, Gerard and his army had returned to Wales.  Gerard advanced rapidly across the Cambrian Mountains and on 23rd April he attacked Laugharne's Parliamentarians at Newcastle Emlyn. The Roundheads were taken by surprise and routed. Over 500 Roundhead soldiers were killed or captured.

Following the Battle of Naseby the Royalist cause was in decline. A short final siege saw the castle taken by Parliament for the final time.  Its fortifications were slighted to prevent any further military use.

Newcastle Emlyn Castle.

Tags: Slighted

Headline: Fleeing from the Scots at the Battle of Newburn, the English added to their disgrace by abandoning Newcastle without a fight.
Body Text:
In 1640, during the Second Bishop’s War an army of Scottish Covenanters led by Alexander Leslie invaded England and advanced on Newcastle. Rather than attack the strongly fortified northern approach to Newcastle, Leslie marched west along the River Tyne to Newburn Ford. Newburn Ford was the first crossing point over the Tyne and a few miles upstream from Newcastle. Leslie wanted to secure control of the northern and southern banks of the Tyne and encircle Newcastle.  To defend against the Scots, Viscount Conway sent 1,500 cavalry and 3,000 infantry to reinforce the troops guarding the ford. Leslie sent a messenger to Conway saying that the Scots did not wish to fight but only wanted free passage in order to petition the King. Conway had no option but to refuse. In the early afternoon of 28th August 1640, the English were beaten back by the Scots, at what became known as the Battle of Newburn.

Most of the English ran away from the Scots in panic, fleeing towards Newcastle. To avoid causing ill feeling by inflicting unnecessary casualties, General Leslie ordered his troops not to pursue the fleeing English. To the amazement of the Scots, Viscount Conway decided that Newcastle could not be defended and withdrew his soldiers to Durham. On 30th August, Leslie’s men marched unopposed into Newcastle. The Scots occupied Newcastle for nearly a year.  Under the terms of the Treaty of Ripon, signed on 14th October, the English agreed to pay the Scots £850 per day.  Charles’ need to raise money to pay the Scots was the primary reason he recalled Parliament. It was an act that would ultimately lead to the Civil Wars.

Alexander Leslie.
“Alexander Leslie” by Sir Anthony van Dyck, licensed by University of Leicester Fairclough Collection.
Tags: Defenders withdrew; Besieged again and again

Headline: Initially passed by, due to the strength of its defences, Newcastle later fell to Parliament following a two month siege.
Body Text:
Following the signing of the Solemn League and Covenant the Scottish army, led by Alexander Leslie, Earl of Leven crossed the border to support Parliament. Leven advanced cautiously southwards through Northumberland but encountered no opposition. Sir Thomas Glemham, the Royalist governor of Newcastle, not having enough men to properly challenge the Covenanters, abandoned the garrison at Alnwick and retreated back to Newcastle. On 28th January William Cavendish, Marquis of Newcastle marched from York with the main body of the Royalist northern army to stop the Scottish invasion. Leven stayed at Morpeth for several days in order to gather all of his forces before advancing. This delay proved critical, allowing the Royalists time to occupy Newcastle having arrived just a few hours before the Scottish army appeared to the north of the city. On 3rd February Lord Leven's summons for the surrender of Newcastle was rejected.
The Scots stormed and captured the outer defences to the north-east of the city but were unable to mount a full assault. Sir Thomas Glemham had improved Newcastle's defences and it soon became clear that the city could withstand a long siege. Rather than commit his forces to a long and difficult siege, Leven decided to bypass Newcastle and advance further into England. Leaving six regiments to blockade Newcastle, Leven's forces moved south. For a time, the Scottish army based itself at Sunderland which had declared for Parliament. At the end of March 1644, Leven led his army south and attacked York.
In June preparations for the capture of Newcastle began in earnest. A smaller Scottish army, under the command of the Earl of Callender, crossed the border. After securing several other north-east towns, Callender marched on Newcastle, taking possession of the Gateshead side of the Tyne Bridge. On 27th July, the Scots began a blockade of Newcastle. Reinforcements were needed before a full scale siege could be mounted. After the fall of York, Leven's army marched back north arriving at Gateshead on 12th August. Within a few days siege operations were fully under way. The Royalist garrison rejected commands to surrender. At 5.00pm on 19th October 1644, after a day of artillery bombardment and mine explosions, huge gaps appeared in the town walls and the town was finally stormed. There was desperate hand to hand fighting and a last stand in the Cloth Market-Bigg Market area. Some of the garrison retreated to the castle keep and resisted for a few more days before surrendering to the Scots.
Tags: Stormed; Mines and petards; After Marston Moor; Besieged again and again

Headline: During the storming of the church at Newnham, an exploding gunpowder keg caused chaos on both sides.
Body Text:
Newnham is on the River Severn, near Gloucester and hosted a small port which traded with Ireland.  Newnham was garrisoned several times by the Royalists seeking to protect their lines of communication between Gloucester and Wales. It also provided an easy crossing of the Severn. In April 1643, the Royalists positioned themselves in the parish church and built earthwork defences. On 8th May 1644, a Parliamentarian force, led by Colonel Edward Massey, stormed the church and castle. During the commotion, the Royalists exploded a powder keg in the church causing a great deal of damage.

Royalist casualties included 20 dead and 100 prisoners were taken.
Tags: Stormed; Edward Massey; Churches at war

Headline: A mistaken order led to a town changing hands without a shot having been fired.
Body Text:
Commanding one of the major routes to the Midlands, Newport Pagnell was recognised by Royalists as a key strategic town. By the end of summer 1643, the Cavaliers had taken Newport Pagnell and ?forced the inhabitants to come in and entrench it and draw the river about it the better to strengthen and fortifie it ?? On 6th October 1643, a Royalist garrison was established by Sir Lewis Dyve. The garrison was short lived. On the 26th October, reportedly due to a mistaken order sent from Oxford, Dyve oversaw a night time evacuation of the town. Unfortunately for Dyve, a Parliamentary force under the command of General Philip Skippon was advancing towards the town at the time. Finding the town deserted, Skippon moved in. By the morning of the 27th October Newport Pagnell was in Parliamentarian hands. Not one shot had been fired by either side.

Sir Samuel Luke was quick to establish a Parliamentarian headquarters in Newport Pagnell. He refortified the town in January 1644, after heavy rain had caused the earthworks to give way.
Tags: Defenders withdrew; Townspeople

Headline: A largely derelict castle was restored only to be left derelict once more following a bombardment by the Parliamentarians.
Body Text: Originally established as a Norman stronghold to control Wales, the military purpose of New Radnor Castle became largely redundant under the pro-Welsh Tudor dynasty.  By 1535 what remained of the castle was in ruins. During the Civil War the castle defences were repaired and garrisoned for the Royalists. The castle even hosted a visit by King Charles I in 1642.  During the war, once the Welsh Royalists’ cause had begun to weaken, the castle was besieged by the Parliamentarians. Following heavy damage from Parliamentary artillery, the castle fell. Its fortifications were destroyed to prevent further use by the Royalists.
Tags: Slighted

Headline: This Royalist outpost survived a three week siege, only to fall to the Scots later in the year.
Body Text: From February 1645, following several attacks by Colonel Rossiter’s Lincolnshire Parliamentarians, Royalists in nearby Newark decided to garrison the moated manor house at Norwell.  Overhall Manor was commanded by Lieutenant-Colonel Kirby and defended by 60 men. Within days a Parliamentarian force from Retford besieged Overhall Manor. The siege lasted three weeks until the attackers departed when Colonel Rossiter was called away to fight Royalists at Melton Mowbray.  Having survived a Parliamentarian siege the manor house fell to the Scots besieging Newark in November 1645.  Although the house is long gone the moat can still be seen to the south of the church.
Tags: Besiegers gave up; Newark's ring

Headline: Men dressed in women’s clothes attempted to take Nottingham for the King.
Body Text:
Despite King Charles raising his standard at Nottingham, the town soon became a Parliamentarian stronghold. In July 1643, John Hutchinson was appointed Governor and would hold Nottingham for Parliament throughout the war.

On 3rd July 1643, when Queen Henrietta Maria departed from Newark, she left behind 2,000 infantry and 20 companies of cavalry. This increase in strength allowed the Newark garrison to launch three attacks on Nottingham between June and September.  One of the attacks was led by Baron Dohna, a German commander, who was reportedly cut in half by a cannon ball whilst directing an assault from a boat on the River Trent. The most serious attack occurred on 18th September, when a force of 600 Royalists led by Sir Richard Byron was let into the town by Alderman Toplady. The Royalists nearly succeeded in taking Nottingham Castle, surprising a number of defenders who had stayed in the town overnight. The Royalists took possession of St Nicholas’ Church and used the position to pour musket fire into the castle.  Hutchinson managed to hold out for five days until a relief force of 500 cavalry from Leicester and Derby forced the Royalists to withdraw.   Hutchinson had St Nicholas’ Church demolished.  The Royalists established a fort at Trent Bridge. The fort was garrisoned by 80 men, under the command of Captain Rowland Hacker. The Royalists held the fort for a month. Hacker and his men withdrew when it looked like the fort was about to be taken in a counter attack.  The Royalists demolished two spans of the bridge before withdrawing back to Newark.

On 15th January 1644, around 1,500 Royalists, led by Sir Charles Lucas, attempted a night time attack through knee deep snow.  With all the defending Parliamentarians inside the castle this time, the Royalists were able to take the town with ease until they were chased out by Colonel Thornhaugh’s cavalry and troops from the castle. The retreating Royalists attempted to set fire to Nottingham by firing their pistols into the thatch roofs of the buildings around them.  As the Royalists made their escape it is said that there was a trail of blood in the snow left by injured men that stretched part of the way back to Newark.

On 17th February 1644 the Royalists attempted to enter the town in disguise.  Hutchinson had been warned about a plot to attack Trent Bridge by Rowland Hacker’s troops. It was a market day and around 30 Royalists approached, disguised as women or market traders, with knives, daggers and hatchets hidden under their cloaks or in carts. The Parliamentarians were expecting them and chased them back across the bridge. Ten of Royalists were forced to jump into the river. Five drowned. Four were captured. Their Captain swam to freedom.  The rest were taken prisoner.  Having been captured in disguise, Hutchinson regarded the prisoners as spies and therefore could be executed.  Hutchinson threatened to torture them, but instead the captive Royalists were exchanged for Parliamentarian prisoners.
Tags: Besiegers gave up; Newark's ring; Churches at war

Headline: Colonel Prater refused to surrender to Parliament. A 36 pounder changed his mind.
Body Text: Nunney Castle was owned by the Catholic Prater family. When war broke out, like many Catholics Colonel Richard Prater supported the Royalist cause.  After the Battle of Naseby, the Royalist situation deteriorated with the south-west becoming one of the few remaining Royalist strongholds. Nunney Castle was garrisoned in anticipation of a Parliamentary attack. The castle took in a number of refugees, many of whom were Catholics.  In September 1645, a Parliamentary army under the command of Thomas Fairfax and Oliver Cromwell advanced into Somerset. They took Sherborne, Cary and Shepton Mallet before turning their attention to Nunney.  On 6th September, Fairfax, supported by Colonel Rainsborough and Colonel Hammond’s Regiments, arrived at Nunney. Prater refused to surrender. By 8th September a 36 pounder cannon had been brought from Shepton. The cannon smashed a breach in the walls. Colonel Prater’s position was impossible. He surrendered.
Caption Image 1:
Nunney Castle.

Tags: Surrendered on terms; After Naseby; Sir Thomas Fairfax; Oliver Cromwell

Headline: Damage inflicted during a Civil War siege can still be seen on this Yorkshire church.
Body Text: In December 1642, Sir Hugh Cholmley held Scarborough Castle for Parliament, while the Earl of Newport held Old Malton for the Royalists. Cholmley decided to attack Old Malton early in January 1643 and took the town. Cholmley left a garrison and marched north to fight and defeat the Royalists at Guisborough. There are cannon ball marks on the west front of Malton Priory Church, which probably result from the attack.
Tags: Churches at war

Headline: Concerned woman talked Royalist defenders into surrendering to a much smaller force.
Body Text:
Oswestry had been garrisoned for the Royalists by Lord Capel in 1643. The town was protected by a castle under the command of Colonel Edward Lloyd. On 22nd June 1644, Lord Denbigh and Colonel Mytton approached Oswestry. They sent cavalry to stop any attempt by Royalists to relieve Oswestry.  Denbigh and Mytton sent a small force of 200 infantry to attack the Royalists defending St. Oswald's Church, situated outside the town walls. The church was captured after 30 minutes fighting and a number of prisoners were taken. The Parliamentarians brought a small cannon which quickly blew in the town gate. An intrepid volunteer climbed the gatehouse and cut the chains, letting down the drawbridge. As the Royalist defenders withdrew to the castle, Lord Denbigh led his troops in to occupy the town.

The Parliamentarian field gun had little effect on the walls of Oswestry Castle. That night, Denbigh and his officers agreed to burn down the castle gate with pitch. Next day, before the fire had been lit, the women of the town begged Denbigh to let them try and persuade the garrison to surrender. Reluctantly the garrison marched out, surrendering their weapons and ammunition even though the 400 Royalists defenders actually outnumbered Denbigh’s attacking force. The townspeople paid £500 to the Parliamentarians to stop the Roundheads plundering the town. Colonel Mytton was left to garrison Oswestry while Lord Denbigh withdrew to Cheshire

In late June, the Royalist commander Sir Fulke Huncke approached the town with 2,000 infantry, 600 cavalry and two pieces of artillery. News of the Royalist advance had reached Lord Denbigh, who sent Sir Thomas Myddelton, with all the forces that could be spared from Cheshire, to reinforce Mytton. As Myddelton approached Oswestry, Huncke ordered Colonel Marrow to send out scouts to discover the strength of the Parliamentarian army. Colonel Marrow, apparently acting against Huncke's orders, took all of the cavalry and attacked Myddelton at Whittington, three miles east of Oswestry.  The Royalist cavalry were defeated and Huncke was obliged to lift the siege and retreat with his guns to Shrewsbury.
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Churches at war; Townspeople

Headline: The siege of Oxford was lifted after a decoy allowed the King to escape.
Body Text:
From November 1642, Oxford was occupied by the Royalists and became their headquarters throughout the war.

Late in May 1644, Parliamentarian forces commanded by Edmund Ludlow joined Sir William Waller to blockade Oxford. On 27th May, Waller attempted to cross the Thames but was defeated by Royalist dragoons. The following day the Earl of Essex’s Parliamentarian army forded the river. The King stood on top of Magdalen College Tower to watch the Parliamentarian army conduct its manoeuvres. On 2nd June, Waller crossed the Thames and by the evening, at nearby Woodstock, the King heard that Waller’s forces were three miles away. The Royalists retreated to Oxford, arriving there in the early morning, on the 3rd June. It was discovered that there were few supplies. If the army stayed and the city was besieged, all would be lost in a matter of days. It was decided that the King should leave Oxford that night. The King ordered a large part of the army to march through Oxford towards Abingdon to act as a diversion. After a few hours this force returned from Abingdon, having successfully diverted Waller’s troops. At about 9.00pm on 3rd June, the King and Prince Charles, accompanied by various Lords, and a party of 2,500 musketeers, joined some of the cavalry and left Oxford heading for Burford. They reached Burford at about 4.00pm the next day. Once the King’s escape was discovered, Waller hurried off in pursuit. The King and his forces continued to march on to Worcester.

King Charles I.
“Charles I” by Sir Anthony van Dyck, licensed by Royal Collections Trust
Tags: Besiegers gave up; Oxford's ring; Besieged again and again; Sir William Waller

Headline: Fairfax abandoned the second siege at Oxford for a chance to recapture Leicester.
Body Text: In the New Year of 1645, one of the first objectives of the New Model Army was the blockade and siege of Oxford. From 30th April 1645, Thomas Fairfax moved from Reading and began the siege of Oxford on 22nd May.  Assisted by Colonel Thomas Rainsborough, Fairfax tightened the siege. On 2nd June, Royalist troops from Oxford attacked the Parliamentarians, killing 50 and taking 96 prisoners.  On 3rd June, prisoners were exchanged. The following day Parliament withdrew their forces on news that the King, Prince Rupert and Prince Maurice, had left Oxford on 7th May.  On 5th June, Fairfax abandoned the siege, having received orders to recapture Leicester instead.
Caption Image 1:
Sir Thomas Fairfax.
“Thomas Fairfax” by William Marshall, licensed by National Portrait Gallery.
Tags: Besiegers gave up; Oxford's ring; Besieged again and again; Sir Thomas Fairfax

Headline: Following the King’s capture by the Scots, the Governor of Oxford was ordered to surrender.
Body Text:
King Charles I returned to Oxford for the winter on 5th November 1645. The Royalists planned to resume fighting in the spring but instead suffered a number of setbacks. As spring approached Parliament sent forces to take Oxford. 2,000 Roundhead troops under the command of Colonel Thomas Rainsborough entered nearby Woodstock in March. In April, Rainsborough was joined by Colonel Henry Ireton and his troops. On 15th April, the sound of cannons firing at Woodstock Manor House could be heard in Oxford. Rainsborough's troops attacked Woodstock House but were beaten back, losing 100 men. On 26th April, Woodstock Manor House surrendered. The defending soldiers, having given up their weapons, were allowed to go to Oxford.

The King left Oxford early in the morning on 27th April, without disclosing his destination.  The Parliamentarians presumed he was on his way to London.  The King instead went to Southwell, where he surrendered to the Scots on 5th May 1646.

On 1st May, Fairfax returned to Oxford and placed the city under siege. 10 days later on 11th May, Fairfax demanded that Sir Thomas Glemham, the Governor of Oxford, surrender the city. Glemham sent a letter to Fairfax offering to meet. Although Glemham didn’t actually want to meet with Fairfax, in the King’s absence the Privy Council acted as the authority for the Royalists and Glemham was obliged to obey. Fairfax and Glemham met on Monday 18th May and the Royalists’ terms of surrender were submitted to Parliament. Parliament dismissed the terms and gave Fairfax the freedom to do what he thought best in order to take Oxford. At the same time, on 18th May, the King sent a letter to Glemham ordering him to obtain honourable conditions for the surrender of Oxford preventing any further bloodshed.  On 15th June, the Commons read the King's letter. Parliament also received a similar letter from the King, dated 10th June. The second letter included an order from the King "directed to the Governors of Oxford, Lichfield, Worcester, Wallingford, and all other Commanders of any his Towns, Castles, and Forts within England and Wales". In the Commons it was ordered that the second letter be sent to all Governors "for Preventing of the further Effusion of Christian Blood?.  While negotiations with Oxford continued there were still minor outbreaks of fighting as cannon exchanged fire.  A cease fire was agreed and on 17th June the fighting stopped. The two armies met and mingled on friendly terms. On 20th June the Articles of Surrender were agreed.

The Articles included provisions for academics and citizens. On 24th June, the Royalist evacuation of Oxford began. Prince Rupert and Prince Maurice had gone already, having been ordered to leave the city and go overseas. On 25th June, the keys to the city were formally handed over to Fairfax.

King Charles I.
“Charles I” by Sir Anthony van Dyck, licensed by Royal Collections Trust
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Oxford's ring; Besieged again and again; Sir Thomas Fairfax

Headline: A Royalist Catholic family’s home changed hands several times throughout the civil war.
Body Text:
Pembridge Castle acted as an outer defence to Royalist Monmouth for most of the war.  The castle was really a fortified house owned by the Catholic Kemble family, but by 1644 it had fallen into Parliamentarian hands.  Following a two week siege, Pembridge Castle was recaptured by the Royalists in November and a Royalist garrison was installed in the castle.  In 1646, the castle was retaken by the Parliamentarians. Once it had been decided that it was no longer necessary to
maintain a garrison there, the castle’s fortifications were destroyed.

Headline: It was Colonel Rowland Laugharne vs. Charles Gerard in the fight for south west Wales.
Body Text:
Pembroke had survived two sieges in 1644 and one in 1645.  At the start of 1644, the Parliamentarian captain of the town militia John Poyer overthrew the Royalist mayor of Pembroke. Poyer seized Pembroke Castle for Parliament, supported by Colonel Rowland Laugharne, Parliament's military commander in Pembrokeshire and a force of only 100 soldiers.  Soon south-west Wales was firmly under Parliamentarian control so there was now no chance Wales’ seaports being used to land the Royalist troops wanting to return from Ireland.

The defeated Royalist commander was replaced by one of Prince Rupert’s most trusted officers – Charles Gerard.  Gerard left Oxford for Wales on 8th May 1644 with an army of 1,000 infantry, 700 cavalry and 200 dragoons. Although relatively small, Gerard's force was enough to overwhelm the Parliamentarians. By the end of June, he had captured the whole of Carmarthenshire. Laugharne abandoned the countryside and withdrew his forces to the fortresses of Pembroke and Tenby where he could keep in touch with the Parliamentarian navy who would provide him with reinforcements and supplies. The Royalists laid waste to large areas of countryside around Pembroke and Tenby with crops, supplies and buildings destroyed. This denied support to Laugharne's forces, which remained blockaded in Pembroke.

By October 1644, Gerard was able to leave the area well garrisoned with Royalist soldiers while he marched with 3,000 troops from Wales to reinforce the King. As soon as Gerard’s Royalist army left Wales, Colonel Laugharne’s Pembrokeshire Parliamentarians emerged to reconquer the territory that they had lost. By April 1645 though, Gerard had returned and recaptured most of the territory lost since his departure with Laugharne being once again confined to Pemboke and Tenby.
Caption Image 1:
Pembroke Castle
 “Pembroke Castle” by Mario Sanchez Prada is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Besieged again and again

Headline: After a long siege at Pembroke, a traitor was executed in Covent Garden.
Body Text:
In 1648, a series of revolts against Parliament broke out around the country. In South Wales, Parliamentarian soldiers, angry over unpaid wages, mutinied against orders to disband and return to their homes. This escalated into a general uprising when army officers and Royalist gentry from Pembrokeshire joined the troops. In early March 1648, Colonel Poyer, the governor of Pembroke Castle, refused to hand the castle over to his appointed successor. On 23rd March, Poyer declared for the King. Major-General Laugharne, who had been Parliament's commander in south Wales during the First Civil War, took charge of the rebel army.

Keen to retake Pembroke from the rebels, Cromwell arrived to supervise the siege on 24th May. He found that the artillery he had brought with him weren’t powerful enough to break down the town or castle walls. On 4th June, an attempt to storm the town failed because Parliament’s siege ladders were too short to scale the walls. On 24th June, a second attack was driven back. The defenders raided the Parliamentarian siege works, killing 30 of Cromwell's soldiers. Attempts were made to bring heavy siege artillery by sea from Bristol but the transport vessels were driven back by storms. It wasn’t until 1st July that the heavy guns were brought up to Pembroke.  After a heavy bombardment, breaches opened in the town and castle walls. The defenders, running short of food and ammunition were becoming mutinous. On 10th July, Cromwell issued a final summons to surrender. Poyer and Laugharne surrendered the next day.

Laugharne, Poyer and Powell were sent to London. On April 1649, they were court-martialed and all condemned to be executed by firing squad. It was later ruled that only one of them would receive the sentence of death. Who lived and who died would be decided by drawing lots. Colonel Poyer lost. He was executed at Covent Garden on 25th April.

Oliver Cromwell.
“Oliver Cromwell” by Robert Walker, licensed by National Portrait Gallery.
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Ports and the sea; Besieged again and again; Oliver Cromwell; Turncoats and treachery

Headline: Sir John Arundell swore he would die rather than surrender, and then surrendered.
Body Text:
In autumn 1642, Cornish Royalists secured the fortresses at Pendennis and St Mawes. Both fortresses guarded the approaches to Falmouth.  Sir Nicholas Slanning, a Royalist soldier, organised a fleet of Falmouth privateers to raid merchant shipping in the Channel.

In March 1646, Thomas Fairfax entered Cornwall with a substantial army. Almost all the other Royalist fortresses had fallen.  On 17th March, the siege of Pendennis Castle began. Pendennis was defended by around 1,000 soldiers under the command of the 80 year old Sir John Arundell, who announced that he would die rather than surrender.  Colonels Fortescue and Hammond directed the Parliamentarian bombardment of the castle from the land. Captain Batten, with ten ships, blockaded the castle by sea, preventing fresh supplies from arriving.   The garrison's defences were supported by cannon fire from a Royalist warship that had been deliberately run aground.  By July, food had begun to run short and some of the garrison tried unsuccessfully to break out by sea to acquire supplies.  On 15th August, Arundell agreed to an honourable surrender with around 900 defenders left inside the fortress.

Pendennis

Tags: Starved out; Ports and the sea; Sir Thomas Fairfax

Headline: Picton Castle stood in the way of the Royalist’s plan to retake Wales for the King.
Body Text: After their victory at the battle of Montgomery in 1644, Parliament had established a strong presence in Wales. King Charles I ordered Charles Gerard to take back Wales for the Royalist cause. To do this, Gerard needed to take Picton Castle. The Royalist army moved quickly through Pembrokeshire and arrived at Picton in April 1645. On the 25thApril Gerard stormed the garrison in a midnight attack and captured the castle for the King.
Caption Image 1:
Picton Castle.
“Picton Castle” by James Stringer is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Stormed

Headline: The Parliamentarian port at Plymouth held out under siege for nearly four years.
Body Text:
The important port at Plymouth was controlled by Parliament during the First Civil War. It was well-fortified against attack and the defences were further strengthened by the addition of an outer line of earthworks and forts. The Parliamentarians ensured the townsfolk helped fortify the town; Men, women and children were forced to dig trenches, build earthworks, and supply the soldiers with ammunition, food and drink. Every man in Plymouth signed an oath to die defending the town rather than see it taken by the King.

In early December 1642, the Royalist commander Sir Ralph Hopton took the Cornish side of the bay at Plymouth, known as Plymouth Sound.  The Royalists attempted to blockade Plymouth from this position but their plans were ruined by the Parliamentarian’s determined defence.  Hopton soon realised that a siege could not be maintained. On 6th December, 500 Parliamentarian cavalry from Plymouth launched a surprise attack and dispersed the Royalist militia. Hopton and his officers narrowly escaped.

In September 1643, Prince Maurice, the King’s nephew, took command of the Royalist forces in the region.  He captured Exeter and Dartmouth and advanced to besiege Plymouth, but was met with strong resistance. Despite the blockade, Parliamentarians from across the South West trickled into Plymouth. The population grew and there were outbreaks of plague and typhus.  Despite their many hardships, the people of Plymouth were defiant. In mid-November Maurice fell ill with camp fever and withdrew from the siege to recover. By December 1643, the siege of Plymouth was abandoned.

In April 1644 the siege of Plymouth began again under the command of Sir Richard Grenville. Grenville treated his enemies harshly. He was accused of committing atrocities against prisoners and of using his authority to settle personal scores against old enemies. The Royalist commander abandoned the siege on 23rd July after he learned that the Earl of Essex’s Parliamentarian army was advancing westwards. When Essex was defeated at the Battle of Lostwithiel though, the Royalists returned. King Charles marched on to Plymouth and on 11th September, called for the town to surrender.  He was refused.  The King left Grenville with a small force to blockade Plymouth and departed with the main Royalist army to Exeter.

The blockade was kept in place throughout 1645 but by early 1646 the Royalist cause was collapsing. On 12th January 1646, as Sir Thomas Fairfax advanced to relieve Plymouth, the Royalists abandoned the siege for the final time.  Plymouth had held out for nearly four years.

Sir Thomas Fairfax.
“Thomas Fairfax” by William Marshall, licensed by National Portrait Gallery.
Tags: Relieved; Ports and the sea; Sir Thomas Fairfax; Sir Ralph Hopton; Townspeople

Headline: The defenders of Pontefract castle received a nasty Christmas present.
Body Text: As the main Royalist castle in the north of England, Pontefract was a vitally important fortress for the King’s cause. In 1644, after the fall of York and Parliament’s victory at the Battle of Marston Moor, Sir Thomas Fairfax and Colonel Lambert moved to besiege Pontefract. The siege began on Christmas Day.  The Parliamentarians mined under the castle walls and bombarded the stronghold with cannon fire, but were unable to breach the defenses. The siege ended on 1st March 1645 when Royalist forces won a victory at nearby Wentbridge, forcing the Parliamentarian attackers to retreat.

Pontefract Castle.

Headline: Pontefract’s defenders were starved into submission during the town’s second siege.
Body Text: The Royalist’s success in the first siege of Pontefract was short lived, as they lacked the soldiers to maintain their advantage. The second siege began on 21st March 1645 when Parliamentarian troops arrived under the command of Colonel General Sydnam Poyntz. The siege dragged on for four months, as the Parliamentarians starved the Royalists out. The castle finally surrendered on 21st July 1645.
Caption Image 1:
Pontefract Castle.

Tags: Starved out; Besieged again and again

Headline: By 1649, Royalist Pontefract was the last castle standing.
Body Text:
Having lost Pontefract castle to Parliament, the Royalists were keen to retake it. On 6th June 1648, Royalist supporters under Captain W Paulden and Colonel John Morris entered the castle in disguise. The Roundhead soldiers were taken completely by surprise and the castle was quickly overwhelmed.

In October 1648 Parliament retaliated and besieged the castle under the command of Oliver Cromwell. The task was a daunting one, as Cromwell wrote;

"The castle is very well known as one of the strongest inland Garrisons in the Kingdom; well-watered; situated on rock in every part of it; and therefore difficult to mine.  The walls are very thick and high, with strong towers; and if battered, very difficult of access".

Cromwell didn’t remain at Pontefract for long. He returned to London to take part in the trial of Charles I. Once Charles had been executed, Pontefract immediately proclaimed his son, Charles II, King, and minted coins with his likeness. These were the first coins to be struck in Charles II's name. Pontefract's official motto comes from this event; 'Post Mortem Patris pro Filio', or 'After the Death of the Father, we support the Son'. By March 1649, after five months of siege, Pontefract was the last Royalist stronghold in the country. The hopelessness of the Royalist’s situation was obvious and the garrison surrendered for the final time on 24th March. The castle was slighted by Parliament to prevent it from ever being used again for military purposes.
