Pontefract Castle.
“Pontefract Castle” by William is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Slighted; Besieged again and again; Oliver Cromwell

Headline: The townsfolk of Portishead were no match for Parliament’s professional soldiers.
Body Text: The fort at Portishead was garrisoned by local people loyal to the King. Unfortunately for them, they only had six guns between them. In 1645, Sir Thomas Fairfax ordered his soldiers to take Portishead. On 28th August, as Fairfax’s men approached, the locals realised that they were outnumbered and outclassed. They promptly surrendered. Parliament made the locals promise not to take up arms in the name of the King ever again.
Caption Image 1:
Sir Thomas Fairfax.
“Thomas Fairfax” by William Marshall, licensed by National Portrait Gallery.
Tags: Surrendered on terms; After Naseby; Sir Thomas Fairfax

Headline: Royalist attackers resorted to underhand tactics to take the fortress at Portland.
Body Text:
When King Charles raised his standard in 1642, Portland immediately sided with Parliament and garrisoned the town’s Tudor fort.  In 1643, the castle was targeted by Royalist troops. Not wanting to risk an assault, the Cavaliers opted for more underhand tactics to take the fortress. A group of cavalry troops carrying Parliamentarian standards were seen galloping towards the castle, being chased by Royalist troops. The garrison opened its gates to the fleeing Parliamentarians, not realising until it was too late that they were Cavalier soldiers in disguise. The disguised soldiers quickly overtook the surprised defenders and the castle fell to the Royalists.

Portland was secured for the King for the rest of the war, but had to endure several further sieges, including one that lasted for four months in 1644. In April 1646, with a Royalist defeat almost certain, the garrison commander Colonel Thomas Gollop secured a bloodless and generous surrender. The troops marched out with their weapons, flags flying and drums beating.

Portland Castle.
“Portland Castle” by James Stringer is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Taken by surprise; Ports and the sea

Headline: George Goring conned £5,000 out of Parliament and used it to fortify Portsmouth for the King.
Body Text:
Portsmouth was the most important and heavily-defended port on the south coast of England. Since 1639, Portsmouth had been governed by Colonel George Goring. In preparation for the now inevitable Civil War, the House of Commons granted Goring £5,000 to fortify Portsmouth against the King. What they didn’t know was that Goring was also in secret correspondence with Queen Henrietta Maria, who gave Goring a further £3,000 to fortify Portsmouth against Parliament. On 2nd August 1642, with the outbreak of Civil War imminent, Goring declared openly for the King. He had provided the Royalists with a major port, where it was hoped that aid for the Royalist cause from France and the Netherlands could be received.

Unfortunately for the Royalists, Goring's declaration was premature and poorly-timed. The King was busy gathering forces in the north of England and was unable to support him with troops or supplies. Goring's 400 man garrison seemed secure behind a circuit of Medieval walls and earth ramparts, but Parliament, furious at Goring’s trickery, were determined to take it. On 8th August, the Earl of Warwick's squadron of five warships arrived off Portsmouth and seized Goring's only ship, the Henrietta Maria, ensuring that no help could arrive by sea. Sir William Waller, assisted by Sir John Meldrum, marched to besiege Portsmouth from the land, and arrived on 12th August. They seized key outposts around the town, preventing the Royalists bringing in reinforcements or supplies by land.

With the town cut off by land and sea, morale in Portsmouth sunk to a new low. There was only food and provisions for a few days. Many townsmen and soldiers fled. Towards the end of August, Waller ordered the construction of gun platforms at Gosport to bombard the garrison. On 28th August Waller's commissioners came into Portsmouth to negotiate a peaceful surrender but Goring was unwilling to accept the terms offered. On 2nd September, the Parliamentarian guns opened fire, badly damaging the tower of St Thomas's Church.  The next day, Roundhead troops under Colonel Richard Norton led a surprise night attack on Southsea Castle. The castle was defended by only 12 soldiers and was easily captured. With the guns of Southsea Castle now turned towards the town, only a handful of dedicated Royalists were prepared to continue fighting. Goring surrendered to Waller on 7th September and left England for the Netherlands.

Southsea Castle, Portsmouth.
“Southsea Castle in all seasons” by Matty Ring is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Ports and the sea; Sir William Waller

Headline: Taking the castle at Powderham was a key part of the Parliamentarian plan to capture Exeter.
Body Text: Powderham Castle was an important Royalist outpost for the city of Exeter. It was garrisoned by 300 soldiers under the command of Sir Hugh Meredith. Powderham’s importance to Exeter made it a viable target for Parliamentarians, and in December 1645, they launched an offensive. The attack failed, but just six weeks later, a reinforced army led by Colonel Robert Hammond attacked and the castle fell on 25th January 1646. Soon after, Sir Thomas Fairfax captured Exeter, in a huge blow for Royalist hopes and morale.

St Clement’s Church, Powderham.

Headline: A petard gave Royalist soldiers a rude awakening at Powis Castle.
Body Text: During the Civil War, Powis Castle was home to the Herberts, a staunchly Royalist family. In 1644, a Parliamentarian force under Sir Thomas Myddelton arrived to take the castle. They launched a night attack on 2nd October. A petard, or small bomb, was used to blast away the outer gate and the surprised Royalists surrendered immediately. A Parliamentarian garrison was established soon after and was held for the rest of the war. When the Herbert family finally got their home back after the restoration, the castle had to be extensively rebuilt.
Caption Image 1:
Powis Castle.
“Powis Castle” by sion_a is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0

Headline: The most important bridge in the British Civil Wars?
Body Text: Radcot Bridge was 20 miles downstream from Oxford; the Royalist capital during the Civil War. The River Thames was a key supply route to the city and a result, the crossing at Radcot Bridge became an incredibly important Royalist garrison.  The bridge stayed in Royalist hands for four years, but by early May 1646, Parliament had all but won the war.  The bridge was successfully taken by Sir Thomas Fairfax and a month later, Oxford surrendered.
Caption Image 1:
Radcot Bridge.
“Radcot Bridge” by Mike Freedman is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0

Headline: The Marquess of Worcester went to great lengths to protect his valuables but couldn’t stop the locals from stealing his fish.
Body Text:
Raglan Castle was the family home of Henry Somerset, 5th Earl of Worcester. When the King’s son, Prince Charles, was sent on a fund-raising tour to raise money for the war, his first port of call was Raglan Castle. Following the Prince’s visit, Henry Somerset was promoted to the first Marquess of Worcester and the defences of Raglan were improved. Earthwork bastions were built around the castle and a garrison of around 300 men was established at a cost of £40,000. King Charles I visited Raglan twice, first in June 1645 after the battle of Naseby and again in 1646, where he played bowls on the castle's green.

By 1646 the Royalist cause was close to collapse. Realising that an attack on Raglan was imminent, the garrison was increased to around 800 soldiers. The avenue of trees outside the castle gates were cut down and neighbouring buildings were destroyed to avoid them being used by Parliamentary forces. Supplies of food were brought in to support the growing castle community, which included members of the wider Herbert family and other regional Royalist leaders. The Marquess sent some of his valuables, including oak panelling and many paintings to his brother at nearby Troy House, for safe keeping.

A Parliamentary army commanded by Colonel Thomas Morgan and Sir Trevor Williams, arrived at Raglan Castle in early June 1646. After several calls for the castle to surrender, the siege began in earnest and lasted through the summer months. The castle was subjected to a daily bombardment of 60lb cannonballs. The bombardment made little impression on the great tower but damaged other parts of the castle. General Thomas Fairfax arrived in August with Parliamentarian reinforcements. Fairfax's men dug trenches and used them to move mortars forward, bringing them within range of the castle interior. On 19th August, after an 11 week siege, the Marquess surrendered the castle, receiving relatively generous terms for the garrison. The Marquess himself however, was not so lucky. He was arrested and sent to Windsor Castle, where he died shortly afterwards. Fairfax ordered the castle to be totally demolished, but the fortifications proved too strong and in the end only a few of the walls were destroyed. After the siege, local people dredged the castle moat in search of treasure and emptied the fishponds of valuable carp.

Raglan Castle.

Headline: Colonel Fielding was sentenced to death for surrendering Reading, but help came from an unexpected ally.
Body Text:
At the beginning of the First Civil War, as the King's army was forced out of London, Reading was occupied by the Royalists. A 2,000 strong garrison was established, under the command of Sir Arthur Aston. The town's defences were reinforced by a system of ditches, earthworks and forts and the existing walls were strengthened with stone taken from Reading Abbey.

On 14th April 1643, the Earl of Essex arrived at Reading with a huge army of 16,000 foot, 3,000 horse and train of artillery, and demanded the town’s surrender.  Aston responded, declaring that he would rather die or starve than lay down his arms. The defenders were reinforced by 600 musketeers and a supply of ammunition that had arrived by boat from Sonning. To guard against the possibility of more reinforcements arriving from Oxford, Roundhead troops swept around the southern outskirts of the town and seized Caversham Bridge. Gun batteries were set up and opened fire on the town on the morning of Sunday 16th April.  King Charles sent urgent orders recalling Prince Rupert from the siege of Lichfield to go to and relieve Reading. On 19th April, Sir Arthur Aston was seriously injured when struck on the head by a falling brick. Aston’s deputy, Colonel Richard Fielding, took command.
Fielding called a truce and began negotiations for the surrender of Reading.  The same day, Prince Rupert arrived and attacked Caversham Bridge in a last ditch effort to keep the town. Fielding refused to support Rupert on the grounds that he did not want to break the truce.  Without reinforcements, Rupert’s soldiers were driven back and on 26th April terms for surrender were agreed. The next day, the defeated Royalist garrison marched away to Oxford and Essex's soldiers occupied Reading and spent the next two days plundering the town before order was restored. When he arrived at Oxford, Colonel Fielding was court-martialed for surrendering the town and sentenced to death.  At the last minute his life was saved when Prince Rupert, the very man he had defied, spoke up for him.

King Charles I.
“Charles I” by Sir Anthony van Dyck, licensed by Royal Collections Trust
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Oxford's ring; Prince Rupert; Townspeople

Headline: The impressive defences at Restormel were not enough to fight off a Parliamentarian attack, but the tables were soon turned.
Body Text:
At the outbreak of the Civil War, Restormel Castle declared for the King. The castle boasted an excellent defensive position, sat high on steep artificial slopes and surrounded by a 17 metre wide moat. The defences acted as an excellent deterrent, as the castle did not see military action for much of the war. That all changed on 21st August 1644 when Sir Richard Grenville, a local MP, stormed the castle and established a garrison under Colonel John Weare.

Parliamentarian celebrations were cut short, however, when Weare’s men surrendered without a fight as Royalist troops advanced later that same month.

Restormel Castle.
“Restormel Castle” by Caroline Ingram is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Stormed

Headline: Starvation forced the Royalists at Rhuddlan Castle to surrender following a three month siege by Parliamentarians.
Body Text: During the Civil War, Rhuddlan Castle was garrisoned for the Royalists, and even hosted King Charles I following his defeat at the Battle of Naseby.  In 1645, the Governor was Colonel Robert Byron, one of seven brothers who all fought for the King.  Between April and July 1646, the castle was subjected to a three month siege by a Parliamentarian force led by General Thomas Mytton.  When supplies ran out and his men began to starve, Byron was forced to surrender the castle. Two years later the castle was slighted on the orders of Parliament.
Caption Image 1:
Rhuddlan Castle.

Headline: A single cannon shot was all it took to destroy the garrison Rose Castle, but not in the way you might expect.
Body Text: The Medieval castle in Cumbria was a Royalist stronghold and home to the Bishop of Carlisle.  Although not directly targeted by Parliament, in 1645, Oliver Cromwell was marching in the nearby countryside. One member of the garrison rashly decided to fire a cannon at Cromwell’s troops. Much the dismay of the Royalist soldiers, Cromwell changed course and led his army straight towards them. The Parliamentarian soldiers attacked and set fire to the castle.
Caption Image 1:
Rose Castle.
“Rose Castle Cumbria” by phillip evans is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0

Headline: Parliament shot the messenger who attempted to bribe the commander of Rushall Hall into surrender.
Body Text:
At the start of the Civil War in 1642, Edward Leigh, an MP and an opponent of the King, fortified his family home and joined the army. His wife was left in command of Rushall Hall.  During Prince Rupert’s attack on nearby Birmingham in early April 1643, the house was defended by Mrs Leigh and a handful of servants and maids. Unfortunately for them, they were no match for the professional soldiers and were soon defeated. They were allowed to surrender on honourable terms.  The Hall was then occupied for the Royalists by Colonel Lane. It was used as a storage depot for plunder taken from Parliamentarian convoys passing between London and Lancashire.

In May 1644, the Royalists were removed from Rushall Hall after a short siege and bombardment led by the Earl of Denbigh. In September, an attempt was made by members of the King’s forces to bribe Captain Tuthill, the Parliamentarian commander who was in charge at the Hall. £2,000 was offered if he would surrender to the King. He refused. The chief go-between in the affair, Francis Pitt, was executed in October 1644 for his role in trying to betray the garrison at Rushall Hall.

Prince Rupert.

Headline: Despite being owned by a Parliamentarian commander, Ruthin Castle was garrisoned for the Royalists throughout the First Civil War.
Body Text:
Ruthin Castle was owned by the Parliamentarian Sir Thomas Myddelton, but at the beginning of the Civil War, Royalists seized the estate.  Following the Battle of Montgomery in September 1644, the Parliamentarians established a base in central Wales from which Myddelton could launch attacks on Royalist garrisons. On 19th October, a Parliamentarian attack managed to retake Ruthin, but was unable to capture the castle. Myddelton lacked the men and supplies to advance further into North Wales.

Following the virtual collapse of the Royalist cause in 1645, Parliamentarian forces under the command of Major-General Mytton were tasked with the capture of the castles of north Wales. Their first target was Ruthin. Between May and July 1646 the castle withstood an 11 week siege, during which the walls were bombarded. The defenders surrendered only when the attacking forces announced their intention to mine the walls. Honourable terms were given for the surrender and the defenders marched away, flags flying.

Ruthin Castle.

Headline: Is a siege still a siege if the defender surrendered without a fight?
Body Text: Built in Falmouth by Henry VIII, St Mawes Castle was an important part of England’s supply route to Europe. In 1642, St Mawes declared for the King. In March 1646, as the war was drawing to a close, Sir Thomas Fairfax’s army arrived in Cornwall. Major Hannibal Bonithon, the captain of the castle’s garrison was invited to retreat to the nearby Royalist stronghold at Pendennis. Instead, Bonithon surrendered immediately. The garrison’s 160 small arms and 13 artillery pieces were captured. The castle’s guns were removed and used against Pendennis.

St Mawes Castle.

Headline: With the causeway guarded by cannon, the castle at St Michael’s Mount was virtually impregnable, until the Royalist cause collapsed in the south west.
Body Text:
St Michael’s Mount had been bought from the Earl of Salisbury by Sir Francis Bassett in 1640.  At the outbreak of the Civil War, Bassett garrisoned it for the King.  Guns were mounted to command the causeway, which was the only way of reaching the island at low tide. This made it virtually impregnable. During much of the Civil War, the castle was used as a prison, and in 1645 housed the Duke of Hamilton, who had fled Oxford having failed to keep Scotland loyal to the King.

Following the collapse of the Royalist cause in the south west, Parliamentarian forces led by Colonel Hammond, closed in. They besieged the Mount between March and April 1646. Sir Arthur Basset, brother of Francis, commanded the Royalist garrison and, after agreeing terms that allowed him and his men to depart by sea to the Scilly Isles, he surrendered on 23rd April 1646.

St Michaels Mount.

Headline: Salcombe became the last Royalist outpost in Devon to surrender, in May 1646.
Body Text: Salcombe Castle, later known as Fort Charles, was constructed in the 1540s by order of King Henry VIII. It was positioned on a natural rock island near the mouth of the Kingsbridge Estuary. Held for the King, the fort was reconstructed and strengthened in 1643 on the orders of Prince Maurice. Sir Edmund Fortescue was given the task of holding it when nearby Plymouth rose against the King. It was Fortescue who decided to rename the stronghold Fort Charles. The castle was besieged by Parliamentary forces under the command of Sir Thomas Fairfax, from 15th January until 7th May 1646, when its Royalist garrison finally surrendered. Fortescue only gave in when it became clear that almost all other Royalist strongholds in the area had been overrun. The defenders were allowed to march out with their colours flying.  Following the Civil War, the castle was slighted on the orders of Parliament.

Salcombe Castle.

Headline: A Roundhead prayer meeting ended in bloodshed at Sandal Castle.
Body Text:
Despite the capture of nearby Wakefield in 1643, the Royalists at Sandal Castle didn’t see any fighting until the latter years of the First Civil War. In early 1645, the Parliamentary commander, Sir John Savile besieged Sandal, but a Royalist counterattack broke the siege. In June, Parliament tried to besiege the castle for a second time. A second counterattack ended the siege. On one occasion the Parliamentarians were praying when the defending Royalists launched a surprise attack. 42 Parliamentarians were killed in the attack. 50 were taken prisoner.

After the Battle of Naseby, Royalist fortunes were in decline. Nearby Pontefract Castle had fallen to Parliament. Soldiers and guns that had been used against Pontefract were redirected against Sandal Castle. On 22nd July 1645, Sandal rejected the call to surrender and the castle was besieged for the third time. General Poyntz’s ordered extensive siege works to be used against Sandal and the castle was bombarded with heavy artillery. Cannon capable of firing 60 pound shot were brought from Hull.  From early September Parliament were able to bombard the castle keep from 500 yards away. The bombardment caused further damage to an already ruined building.  By the end of September Parliament was ready to storm the castle. On 1st October the defenders surrendered.  The 10 officers and 90 men defending the garrison were assured safe passage to Welbeck House in Nottinghamshire. The following year Parliament ordered that Sandal Castle be slighted.

Sandal Castle.

Headline: Sir John Meldrum survived a nasty fall at Scarborough Castle, only to be killed in hand to hand fighting.
Body Text:
At the beginning of the Civil War, Scarborough was held for Parliament by Sir Hugh Cholmley. In March 1643 Cholmley change sides and mounted attacks against Parliamentarian positions in Yorkshire. Piracy raids were launched from Scarborough’s harbour, which allowed Royalists to attack ships transporting coal to London.  Weapons from the continent were also imported to Scarborough, so the capture of the port became a priority for Parliament. After the surrender of York, Scarborough became the most important Royalist garrison in Yorkshire.  Despite this, many of Cholmley's soldiers deserted and the castle fell into disrepair.

In August 1644, a Parliamentarian force commanded by Lord Ferdinando Fairfax reached the edge of the town. Cholmley negotiated terms of surrender, but secretly, he had no intention of surrendering. He was buying time to improve Scarborough’s defences.  Thanks to Cholmley’s delaying tactics Scarborough was able to hold out against Parliament for another year.

On 18th February 1645, Sir John Meldrum finally took the town of Scarborough with 1700 men, suffering almost no casualties.  Meldrum took the port, cutting off all escape by land and sea.  Cholmley retreated into the castle.  Parliament prepared for a long siege. The garrison had access to water from local springs and stockpiled food, ensuring that the castle would be able to defend itself for months. In Spring, the siege was postponed for six weeks while Meldrum recovered from an astonishing accident. On the 24th March Meldrum fell off a cliff, trying to trying retrieve his hat which had blown away in the wind. Meldrum’s cloak saved his life, acting as a parachute.  In May, once Meldrum resumed command he set up a Cannon Royal which fired huge 56’65 pound cannonballs, pounding the castle's defences.  The bombardment partially destroyed the castle keep but the outer walls were not breached. Parliament was unable to take the castle. The large pile of rubble was now used by the defenders who hid behind it and returned fire. On the 10th May, the Royalists destroyed the artillery battery. The Parliamentarians retreated, taking heavy casualties. The next day saw a period of bloody hand to hand fighting around the barbican gateway. Meldrum was killed during the fighting.

By July 1645, Sir Matthew Boynton had replaced Meldrum.  Rather than use his infantry, Boynton preferred to bombard the castle from land and sea. Eventually, a combination of Scurvy, lack of water, the threat of starvation and the heavy bombardment forced the castle to surrender on 25th July. Cholmley received good terms of surrender and soon after left for exile in Holland. At the time of the surrender there were only 25 Royalists left fit to fight. Fewer than half of the original 500 defenders had survived the siege.

Scarborough Castle.

Headline: Poor pay led to mutiny and side changing in Scarborough.
Body Text: After Scarborough Castle’s surrender in July 1645 the fortress was repaired and rearmed for Parliament. The castle was garrisoned with 160 men, but when Parliament were unable to pay them, they rebelled. On 27th July 1648, Matthew Boynton, the castle’s new governor declared for the King. The fortress was besieged soon after and held out until 19th December. A combination of the strength of the Parliamentary forces and the onset of winter forced the castle’s surrender.

Headline: The Commonwealth joined forces with Dutch sailors to put a stop to Royalist privateers on the Isles of Scilly.
Body Text:
To begin with, the nominally Royalist Isles of Scilly took little part in the Civil War. From September 1646 though, after the Royalist defeat in the First Civil War, a Parliamentarian garrison was established. Royalist support resurfaced two years later in 1648, when the soldiers mutinied and declared for the King. In 1649, Sir John Grenville was appointed Royalist governor of Scilly by Charles II. Grenville strengthened the fortifications on St Mary's and the neighbouring island of Tresco.

The Scillies became a notorious base for attacks on English and Dutch ships. By 1651, the problem had become so serious that both the Commonwealth of England and the United Provinces of the Netherlands prepared to take direct action. On 30th March 1651, the Dutch admiral Maarten Tromp arrived off Scilly with a squadron of 13 warships. He demanded the release of captured Dutch ships, crews and cargoes. Grenville released a number of prisoners to Tromp but was unable to return the captured ships and cargoes to the Dutch because they had already been sold.

Parliament had ordered Sir George Ayscue and Robert Blake to both attack the Royalists and to ensure the Dutch did not take the islands. Admiral Tromp offered to co-operate with Parliament in capturing the Isles of Scilly. Blake agreed to a joint show of strength by the Dutch and English ships, but insisted that English troops alone should assault the islands.

Grenville had around 1,000 men under his command, most of whom were stationed on the main island of St Mary's. To give the Commonwealth force a safe place for their ships to anchor, Blake decided to secure Tresco and Bryher first. On the morning of 17th April, Blake invaded Tresco from the eastern side.  The daytime attack was unsuccessful so Blake changed tactics and launched a night assault. Between 11.00pm and 12.00am, the Parliamentarians set off.  The boats were spotted half-way between Tresco and St Mary’s. The alarm was raised but it didn’t make any difference. The Royalists couldn’t prevent the soldiers from coming ashore. The defenders counter attacked but were gradually overwhelmed. Grenville evacuated as many troops as he could to his stronghold on St Mary's.

On 25th April Blake summoned Grenville to surrender, and on 2nd May commissioners from both sides met to negotiate a treaty but they couldn’t reach an agreement. Dutch and Commonwealth warships pounded the Royalist positions.  With no hope of relief, morale among the Royalists plummeted. Blake offered lenient terms for surrender, which, on 23rd May, Grenville accepted. The garrison’s English soldiers were allowed either to go home, or were given safe passage to join Charles II in Scotland. Although Irish troops were liable for the death penalty, they were permitted to return to Ireland and allowed to go free. On 3rd June 1651 Commonwealth troops garrisoned the Scillies.
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Ports and the sea

Headline: Roundhead cannon fire induced labour pains in Lady Saville.
Body Text:
On 11th October 1642, Sheffield and its castle were seized by Sir John Gell for Parliament. In April 1643, Royalist forces led by the Earl of Newcastle entered Yorkshire and captured Leeds, Wakefield, and Rotherham before turning their attention to Sheffield. The castle’s defenders fled into Derbyshire, allowing the Royalists to take the fortress without a fight.  The Earl of Newcastle left a garrison at the castle under the command of Sir William Savile, who in turn left Sheffield in the hands of his deputy, Major Thomas Beaumont.

Following Parliament’s victory at Marston Moor, the Roundhead’s turned their attention to the surviving Royalist strongholds. On 1st August the Earl of Manchester sent a force of 1200 soldiers, under the command of Major-General Crawford and Colonel Pickering, to recapture Sheffield for Parliament. Realising that their artillery wasn’t powerful enough to breach the castle walls, Crawford sent a letter to Lord Fairfax for more powerful weapons including a demi-cannon called “the Queen's pocket-pistol”. These larger cannons were able to damage the fortifications, after which generous terms for the surrender were agreed.  On 11th August 1644, with their drums and colours flying, Beaumont, his officers and men were allowed to march to Pontefract Castle, or else go home. Lady Savile, who was pregnant at the time of the siege, went into labour the night after the castle was surrendered. Under the terms of the surrender she was allowed free passage to Wentworth Woodhouse. On 30th April 1646, Parliament passed a resolution that Sheffield Castle should be slighted. Today no sign that the castle ever existed survives.
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Slighted; After Marston Moor; Family homes

Headline: Royalists were smoked out and defenders massacred in the short but controversial siege at Shelford.
Body Text:
Described as "a fortified house surrounded by a very strong 'bulwark' and a great ditch on the outside of it partly filled with water," Shelford Manor was garrisoned under the command of Philip Stanhope. It formed one of Newark’s Royalist outposts.
On 1st November 1645, Shelford was surrounded by forces led by Colonel General Sydenham Poyntz and Colonel John Hutchinson the Governor of Nottingham. Stanhope rejected the summons to surrender and the Parliamentarians attacked.  During the fighting, some of the defenders took over the church tower, drawing up the ladder and bell ropes after them. Hutchinson sent for straw, set light to it and smoked the defenders out.  Of those who came out, Hutchinson recognised a boy, who had once been part of his own company. Hutchinson told the boy he wouldn’t kill him for changing sides if he told him the weaknesses in Shelford’s defences. Using the boy’s information, Shelford was stormed on Monday 3rd November. The attack began at 4.00pm and lasted just half an hour. Fearing the arrival of Royalists reinforcements from Newark, Poyntz ordered that no mercy be shown. Many defenders were massacred.  40 were killed on the staircase of the house, where the fighting was brutal. Around 160 were killed in total and another 40 were taken prisoner.  Philip Stanhope had been shot and badly wounded during the fight. According to John Hutchinson’s wife Lucy, Stanhope was stripped naked, flung on a dung heap and died the following day.  Shelford House was plundered for valuables and burnt to the ground, although some believed that the fire was started by local people.
Caption Image 1:
Sydnam Poyntz.
“Major General Poyntz”, licensed by National Civil War Centre - Newark Museum.
Tags: Stormed; No quarter; Newark's ring; Churches at war

Headline: A deadly combination of bombardment and undermining proved too much for the “impregnable” Sherborne Castle.
Body Text:
Owned by the Digby family, the castle at Sherborne became a Royalist stronghold. It contained a garrison of 400 men commanded by Sir Lewis Dyve. The garrison successfully resisted a short siege by Parliamentarian forces in September 1642.

The castle enjoyed relative peace for a few years, but as the Royalist cause in the south west began to collapse in 1645, Thomas Fairfax attempted to consolidate his control of the region by marching on Sherborne Castle. The siege began on 2nd August 1645. Although the castle had been described as impregnable, the Parliamentarians were able to dig into the soft stone and plant mines.  Fairfax continued to undermine and bombard the defences, although defending sharpshooters did manage to pick off several Parliamentarian officers.  After two weeks the castle walls had been shattered by the heavy bombardment and mining. Dyve agreed to surrender on 15th August and the Royalists were given quarter, although their possessions were looted.  The castle was destroyed and later a new castle was built, with the surviving ruins now known as Sherborne Old Castle.
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Mines and petards; After Naseby; Sir Thomas Fairfax

Headline: Sitting on the fence allowed the Chamberlain family to keep their castle at Shirburn.
Body Text: During the First Civil War, Shirburn Castle was held for the Royalists by the Chamberlain family. Although the Chamberlain’s declared for the King, they weren’t really that committed to the cause. The family’s status would be more accurately described as neutral. Being neutral was very effective for the Chamberlains, who lived through most of the war in peace. In June 1646, General Fairfax demanded the surrender of Shirborn. The family agreed immediately; keen that their home should avoid the sort of destruction that had been inflicted on so many castles during the war.
Caption Image 1:
Sir Thomas Fairfax.
“Thomas Fairfax” by William Marshall, licensed by National Portrait Gallery.
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Oxford's ring; Sir Thomas Fairfax; Family homes

Headline: The efforts of “The Devil of Shrawardine” were cut short by a Parliamentarian attack.
Body Text:
In 1644, the Royalist commander Sir William Vaughan took the castle at Shrawardine. Vaughan used the stronghold as a base to launch raids against Parliamentarians in the area, earning Vaughan the nickname “the Devil of Shrawardine”.

In June 1645, Shrawardine was captured by Parliamentarian soldiers who destroyed the wall of the keep. They took away much of the stone rubble so that the locals couldn’t use it to rebuild the defences.
Caption Image 1:
Shrawardine Castle.
“Shrawardine Castle” by John Clift is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0

Headline: A surprise attack and a daring raid at Shrewsbury meant victory for Parliament. Or, was a traitor really responsible?
Body Text:
Shrewsbury had been a Royalist stronghold since the beginning of the First Civil War and was protected by a large garrison in the castle. At 4.00am, on the morning of Saturday 22nd February 1645, the Parliamentarians launched a surprise attack. The infantry cut across the fields to the River Severn, where 30 of them embarked in a boat specially enlarged for the purpose. The boat rowed up the river and landed the men below the castle, before returning for more. The Royalists had strengthened the defences along the river with wooden palisades, but the Parliamentarians had brought carpenters and tools to cut them down. A sentry in the castle heard the noise and questioned who the men were. When the Parliamentarians called out “Friends!”, the sentry seemed unclear what to do, first arguing with them and then going off to fetch his corporal for advice.  By the time the sentry eventually decided to sound the alarm, 15 minutes had elapsed and the palisades had been breached. Lieutenant Benbow led the Parliamentarian troops round the bottom of the castle walls, all the while under fire from the defenders. They managed to break down the castle gates, which allowed the Parliamentary cavalry in. After a brief, but fierce, battle the Royalists were overcome. Later that day, realising that their position was hopeless, the garrison surrendered. The Governor, Sir Michael Erneley, 27 gentlemen and around 200 soldiers were taken prisoner. Most of the prisoners were allowed to march off to Ludlow, but 13 Irishmen were summarily hanged.

After the capture, rumours began to circulate that a traitor had opened one of the town gates which was why so many Parliamentary soldiers entered the town so quickly. It may be true, or else a tall tale circulated to explain why the town was taken so easily.

Shrewsbury Castle.
“Shrewsbury Castle” by Reading Tom is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Taken by surprise; No quarter; Turncoats and treachery

Headline: Sir John Pole lost his home at Shute Barton.
Body Text: At the outbreak of the Civil War, Sir John Pole, the owner of Shute Barton, declared for the King. Unfortunately for Pole, Shute Barton was taken for Parliament in early 1643. It remained a Roundhead garrison until May 1644, when Royalists retook the garrison.
Caption Image 1:
Shute Barton.
“Shute Barton” by James Stringer is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Family homes

Headline: Loosely blockaded for three years, Skipton was the last Royalist stronghold in the north of England to surrender.
Body Text: During the First Civil War, Skipton Castle was garrisoned for the Royalists, under the command of Sir John Mallory, and was used as a base for raiding nearby Parliamentarian strongholds. The castle was loosely besieged for three years, but after the Battle of Marston Moor in 1644, Skipton Castle was the only Royalist stronghold left in the north. The Parliamentarian grip tightened, cutting off supply routes.  With no hope of relief, the governor of the castle, Sir John Mallory, finally negotiated honourable terms for surrender. On 21st December 1645, the garrison marched out with colours flying and trumpets sounding. In 1648, after the Royalists temporarily re-occupied the castle, Oliver Cromwell ordered the removal of the roofs and the slighting of the walls and towers so that it could not be used as a defensive fortress again.
Caption Image 1:
Skipton Castle.
“Skipton Castle” by Tim Green is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Slighted; After Marston Moor

Headline: South Kelsey Hall was targeted by the Royalists shortly before the Parliamentarians took control of Lincolnshire.
Body Text: South Kelsey Hall, a moated manor house, served as one of the principal residences of the Ayscough family until the end of the 17th century. The owner, Sir Edward Ayscough was a Parliamentarian, so the house was attacked and taken by Royalists in 1642. Because of the strong Parliamentarian presence in Lincolnshire, rather than garrisoning the Hall, the Royalists just looted it and moved on.

Headline: The fight for Stafford leads to a bloodbath at the Battle of Hopton Heath
Body Text:
Alarmed at the loss of Lichfield in 1643, Charles I sent the Earl of Northampton to retake the city. When he reached Royalist controlled Stafford en route, Northampton joined forces with Colonel General Henry Hastings. The combined Royalist army numbered about 1,200 men, mostly cavalry.  At the same time, about three miles north-east of Stafford, a Parliamentarian army under the command of Sir John Gell and Sir William Brereton arrived, with the intention of taking Stafford for Parliament.
On 19th March, Northampton and Hastings marched out to confront Brereton and Gell at Hopton Heath. During the fighting Northampton was knocked from his horse and separated from his men. Surrounded by enemies, he managed to kill several Roundheads before he was killed himself by a vicious blow to the head. Come evening Parliament withdrew, abandoning their attempts to capture Stafford. Before he left, Sir John Gell stole the Earl of Northampton's body from the battlefield. When Northampton’s son refused to return a cannon the Royalists had captured during the battle, Gell paraded Northampton’s dead body through the streets of Derby.
Led by Brereton, the Roundheads returned to Stafford later that year and, following a brief siege, captured the town on 15th May 1643. Part of the defending garrison escaped to Stafford Castle which was under the command of Lady Isobel Stafford. Colonel Brereton rode up to the castle and called upon Lady Stafford to surrender. She refused. The ensuing siege ended on 5th June when Colonel General Hastings arrived with a relief force. A small Royalist garrison remained but in late June, on hearing the news that a large Parliamentarian army was approaching with powerful siege cannons, the garrison fled and the castle fell to Parliament.

Stafford Castle.
[Untitled] by steve p2008 is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Relieved; Sir William Brereton; Family homes

Headline: Ralph Hopton didn’t stick around long enough to see the house he saved fall to the Roundheads.
Body Text: In November 1643, Stansted House was taken for the Royalists by Ralph Hopton. Hopton didn’t stay for very long but left a garrison to defend the house against Parliament. Sir William Waller attacked soon after, and bombarded the house until those inside surrendered.
Caption Image 1:
Stansted House.
“Stansted House” by Natalie Bowers is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Sir William Waller; Sir Ralph Hopton

Headline: John Frecheville and his men changed sides twice in the hope of saving his home at Staveley.
Body Text: John Frecheville, the owner of Staveley Hall, supported King Charles I during the Civil War and garrisoned his home with a regiment of infantry and cavalry soldiers.  The regiment fought at the battle of Marston Moor. The Royalists suffered a crushing defeat and Frecheville and his regiment returned home from the battle pursued by 1,200 Parliamentarians under the command of Major General Crawford. Realising he was hopelessly outnumbered with no hope of support, Frecheville surrendered without a shot being fired. Frecheville and his men changed sides and fought for Parliament. A few months later they had had changed sides again and fought for the King.
Caption Image 1:
Staveley Hall.
“Staveley Hall nr. Chesterfield” by Fotorus is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Surrendered on terms; After Marston Moor; Turncoats and treachery; Family homes

Headline: Too strong to take until 1651, the garrison at Stirling was eventually overcome by Parliamentarian bombardment.
Body Text:
When Oliver Cromwell and the New Model Army left Scotland in pursuit of Charles II and the Scots Covenanter army in May 1651, General George Monck was appointed as commander in chief in Scotland. Left with around 5000 troops, Monck made his way through the country, taking strongholds loyal to the King and trying to prevent the rebels uniting against the Commonwealth army.

On 6th August, the Parliamentarians arrived at Stirling Castle and commanded the rebels to surrender, but they refused.  The stronghold presented a huge challenge to attack, but Monck brought up heavy guns and mortars to bombard the castle walls.  The garrison of around 300 men, commanded by Colonel Cunningham, became demoralised by the constant mortar fire and forced their commander to ask for surrender terms.  The stronghold surrendered to Monck on honourable terms on 14th August 1651.
Caption Image 1:
Stirling Castle.
“Stirling Castle” by dun_deagh is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Scotland and Ireland

Headline: Stokesay Castle got off lightly when it came to slighting time.
Body Text: William Craven, the owner of Stokesay Castle, was an ardent Royalist, and donated large sums of money to help fund the King’s armies. In February 1645, nearby Shrewsbury fell to Parliament and four months later in June 1645, 800 Parliamentarian soldiers approached the garrison at Stokesay Castle. Realising they were heavily outnumbered, the Royalists surrendered and the Parliamentarians took the garrison without any bloodshed. A few days later a Royalist force under the command of Sir Michael Woodhouse tried to retake the castle. He failed, and the Parliamentarian garrison was secured. In 1647, the castle was ordered to be slighted but only one wall was pulled down.
Caption Image 1:
Stokesay Castle.
“Stokesay Castle” by Les Dunford is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Slighted

Headline: Sitting on the fence didn’t stop John Whorwood from losing his castle.
Body Text: John Whorwood, the owner of Stourton Castle, didn’t choose a side during the Civil War. Unfortunately for him, Whorwood’s neutrality didn’t prevent the Colonel Fox from attacking the castle and taking it for Parliament in 1644. On 24th March that year, a Royalist force under Sir Gilbert Gerard arrived and besieged the castle. Three days later, the Parliamentarians were defeated and the Royalists established a garrison.

Headline: Lost and retaken by the Royalists, Sudeley Castle became the King’s nephew’s headquarters.
Body Text:
At the beginning of the Civil War, Sudeley Castle was owned by the Royalist Lord Chandos. In January 1643, Chandos was absent from the castle when, after a three day siege, it was surrendered to the Parliamentarians. Two days later King Charles’s nephew, Prince Rupert, arrived near Sudeley with 4000 men. Rupert attacked and captured the nearby town of Cirencester, which forced the Parliamentarians to abandon Sudeley but not before they had desecrated the Chapel of St Mary. In April, Lord Chandos re-garrisoned the castle for the Royalists. In September, after the defeat at Gloucester, Prince Rupert made Sudeley his headquarters and even hosted the King there.

On 9th June 1644, Sudeley Castle was attacked by Parliamentarians, under the command of Sir William Waller. After suffering a severe bombardment, Sudeley Castle surrendered. The castle’s Octagon Tower still displays the marks of cannon balls used in the assault.
Caption Image 1:
Sudeley Castle.
“Sudeley Castle” by Kathryn Yengal is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Surrendered on terms

Headline: A joint sea and land operation forced the Royalist garrison to evacuate Swansea.
Body Text: Swansea had been garrisoned for the King from the beginning of the Civil War, and was a key target for Parliament. On 15th May 1644, Captain Robert Moulton of the Parliamentarian fleet summoned the people of Swansea to surrender, but was refused.  A few months later, the town was besieged by Parliamentarians commanded by Major General Rowland Laugharne.  Following a heavy bombardment from land and sea, the Royalist garrison evacuated the town in August 1644.
Tags: Defenders withdrew; Ports and the sea

Headline: After changing hands several times, Parliament eventually managed to take the bridge at Swarkestone.
Body Text: Swarkeston was an important garrison because of its bridge over the River Trent. Parliament secured the bridge in autumn 1642 but soon after, the bridge was taken by Colonel Hastings’ Royalists. Keen to retake the garrison, Parliament tasked Sir John Gell with assaulting the bridge. Arriving on 5th January 1643, the attackers outnumbered the defenders and quickly took the bridge. A dozen soldiers from each side died in the fighting.
Caption Image 1:
Swarkestone Bridge.
“58/365 - ” Swarkestone Bridge? by Darren is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Stormed

Headline: Despite family support, Lord Fairfax was unable to hold the bridge over the River Wharfe.
Body Text: At the end of November 1642, Lord Ferdinando Fairfax occupied Tadcaster with 900 men. His son, Sir Thomas Fairfax occupied nearby Wetherby. Although the Parliamentarians controlled important crossings over the River Wharfe and seemed in a strong position to threaten York, they were greatly outnumbered by the Earl of Newcastle's Royalist army. On 6th December, Newcastle attacked Tadcaster. At 11.00am on Tuesday 7th December 1642, what became known as the Battle of Tadcaster took place on and around Tadcaster Bridge. Short of ammunition and outnumbered, Fairfax was unable to hold the town and fell back to Selby.
Caption Image 1:
Bridge at River Wharf, Tadcaster.
“Viaduct over the Wharfe” by vagueonthehow is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Defenders withdrew

Headline: Surrounded by the ocean on three sides, it took a combined land and sea assault to force the castle at Tantallon to surrender.
Body Text:
Tantallon Castle sat on top of a high point of rock looking out onto the Firth of Forth. The castle had a single wall blocking off the headland with the other three sides naturally protected by sea cliffs. It was an incredibly strong defensive position.
In February 1651, Oliver Cromwell’s lines of communication were under attack from a small group of Royalists based at Tantallon. Led by Captain Alexander Seton, the group comprised just 91 men. Cromwell sent around 3,000 troops commanded by General Monck, together with much of the artillery he had in Scotland to lay siege to Tantallon, with extra support from the Commonwealth Navy. After 12 days of heavy bombardment from land and sea, a breach was made in the Douglas Tower. The defenders were able to negotiate quarter before they were compelled to surrender on 23rd February 1651. Following the siege, Tantallon was left in ruins.
Caption Image 1:
Tantallon Castle.
“Tantallon Castle” by Magnus Hagdorn is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Ports and the sea; Scotland and Ireland

Headline: After taking Taunton, Robert Blake’s besieged forces were relieved and reinforced.
Body Text:
At the beginning of the Civil War, Taunton was held by a small Parliamentarian force but in June 1643, was forced to surrender to Sir Ralph Hopton and a Royalist army.  The Royalist established a garrison of 800 men, commanded by Colonel John Stawell.  As the Earl of Essex's army approached Taunton in summer 1644, the town was abandoned leaving only 80 men to defend the castle. On 8th July 1644, a Parliamentarian force, led by Colonel Sir Robert Pye and Lieutenant Colonel Robert Blake, surrounded the castle, taking Taunton back for Parliament without a fight. Robert Blake was tasked with improving the town’s defences. Taunton didn’t have any town walls, so Blake built earthworks to strengthen the defences.
The King had ordered a Royalist force numbering 3,000 troops, and command by Colonel Edmund Wyndham, to besiege Taunton. The siege began on 23rd September 1644, with a bombardment of the castle. After some early fighting, the Royalists’ broke through Taunton’s eastern defences, forcing Blake's troops back into the castle. Wyndham offered generous terms for surrender, but Blake rejected the offer. Food and ammunition were running out for the defending troops. Blake issued a call for help. Sir William Waller sent a force of 3,000 Parliamentarians, commanded by his deputy, Major General James Holborne. Wyndham had planned to attack Holborne's forces at Chard.  Instead, on 14th December 1644, he retreated back to his garrison at Bridgwater.  On 15th December, a supply caravan containing food, 2,000 muskets and 40 barrels of gunpowder restocked the town. Holborne left 1,000 of his own men to reinforce the town against further Royalist attacks.
Caption Image 1:
Taunton Castle.
“Taunton: Taunton Castle” by Michael Day is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Relieved; Besieged again and again; Sir William Waller

Headline: Colonel Robert Blake swore to eat his boots rather than surrender Taunton during the town’s second siege. He kept his word.
Body Text:
In early 1645, Colonel Robert Blake sent Parliamentarian raiding parties out from Taunton to disrupt Royalist activities.  The Royalist commander, Lord Goring, was sent to the south west of England to capture Taunton. The King also sent Sir Richard Grenville and John Berkeley to support Goring who arrived outside Taunton on 11th March 1645. Before the attack could happen, Goring was required to travel north to support the King. Following continued disagreements between Grenville and Berkeley, Sir Ralph Hopton was put in charge of besieging the town.
Supplies began to run out for the trapped defenders. On 28th April, Thomas Fairfax was ordered to relieve Taunton and marched out with his entire army toward the town. The Royalists considered sending their own army to meet Essex but the King’s nephew, Prince Rupert, convinced the Royalists to concentrate on securing the north of England instead. Fairfax split his army in two, sending a force of between 6,000 and 7,000 commanded by Colonel Ralph Weldon, to Taunton. Fairfax took the rest of his army and headed north. Aware that Parliamentarian soldiers were on their way, Hopton increased his attacks on Taunton. On 8th May the Royalists launched an all-out assault against the town and fought their way inside the outer perimeter. Roundhead musketeers stopped the Royalist advance. The attack began again the next day. Over the space of seven hours, Hopton's army fought their way through Taunton, securing the town one building at a time. The Parliamentarians were left with only the castle and a small area of surrounding land in the middle of Taunton to defend. Blake was commanded to surrender. Blake responded by saying that he "had four pairs of boots left and would eat three of them before he yielded.?
Colonel Weldon’s Parliamentarian army was moving ever closer to relieve Taunton. They fought with small parties of Royalists around the nearby town of Chard.  Under the mistaken belief that they were facing the whole of Fairfax's army, Hopton ordered his forces to retreat to Bridgwater. Weldon arrived in Taunton on 11th May. He relieved and restocked the town, before continuing eastward the following day.
Caption Image 1:
Taunton Castle.
“Taunton: Taunton Castle” by Michael Day is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Relieved; Besieged again and again; Sir Thomas Fairfax; Sir Ralph Hopton

Headline: A drunken commander failed to take Taunton in its third siege in under a year.
Body Text:
On 10th May 1645, Lord Goring replaced Sir Ralph Hopton as Commander of the Royalist Army in the West Country. Commanding around 10,000 men, Goring began the third siege that the Somerset town had suffered in under a year. Ignoring orders from the King to support Royalist efforts in the Midlands, Goring claimed that "Taunton would be taken in a few days.? Goring soon discovered that his army was too small to take the town quickly. Morale was low, and during the siege of Taunton Lord Goring was said to be often drunk. Many of his soldiers deserted him.
In June, Colonel Edward Massey, the regional commander of the Parliamentarian forces, was ordered to relieve Taunton but could only raise 3,000 men. After his victory against the Royalists at the Battle of Naseby, Sir Thomas Fairfax led his army towards Taunton.  Aware that Fairfax was approaching, Lord Goring mounted a final assault on Taunton on 9th July. Hoping to catch Robert Blake, Taunton’s commander, by surprise, Goring launched a cavalry to attack the town but was stopped in Ilminster by soldiers from Fairfax's army. On 10th July 1645, Goring left Taunton to fight Fairfax at the Battle of Langport. Goring was defeated.  The third and final siege of Taunton ended, giving Parliament control of the south west.
Caption Image 1:
Taunton Castle.
“Taunton: Taunton Castle” by Michael Day is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Relieved; After Naseby; Besieged again and again; Sir Thomas Fairfax; Edward Massey

Headline: A peace loving Royalist’s plans for a war free haven at Tenby were soon shattered.
Body Text:
With the exception of town of Pembroke, at the beginning of the Civil War much of south-west Wales was broadly Royalist, or else neutral. The Cavalier Lord Carbery had little interest in fighting Parliamentarians in the region. He was content to allow an informal truce to stand. Because of this, for most of 1643, the area was unaffected by the Civil War.
From September 1643, the cease fire in Ireland allowed government troops posted there to return to England and fight for the Royalist cause. Pembrokeshire’s seaports suddenly became important as potential landing places for the returning troops. All of a sudden Lord Carbery was required to enforce the King's authority in south-west Wales. On 18th August, Carbery summoned the leading Pembrokeshire gentry to Carmarthen. He persuaded them to sign a declaration promising to obey him and support his efforts to secure Tenby and Pembroke for the King.  By the end of 1643, Carbery's bloodless campaign of diplomacy appeared to have secured all the strongholds of Pembrokeshire.
At the start of 1644, the Parliamentarian leader, John Poyer overthrew the Royalist mayor of Pembroke. He seized Pembroke Castle and declared for Parliament. Poyer was supported by Colonel Rowland Laugharne and a small force of about 100 soldiers. Carbery responded to the threat by establishing garrisons in Tenby, Haverfordwest and every castle and mansion around the town. On 6th March 1644, three Parliamentarian ships began to bombard Tenby. The next day General Laugharne's Parliamentarian forces arrived and set up their artillery above the town. For three days, Tenby was bombarded from land and sea. When the main gate was blown in, Laugharne ordered an assault. The Royalists resisted fiercely but were driven back from the gate. The defending garrison engaged in street fighting until Commissary Gwynne, the military governor, was mortally wounded. The discouraged Royalists surrendered. Three hundred prisoners were taken.  Tenby was plundered. By mid-April, south-west Wales was firmly under Parliamentarian control. There was no possibility of its seaports being used to land Royalist troops returning from Ireland.
Caption Image 1:
Tenby Castle.
“Tenby 030” by Pete O’Shea is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Stormed; Ports and the sea; Besieged again and again; Townspeople

Headline: An argument over pay at Tenby got out of hand and snowballed into a full blown rebellion.
Body Text:
In 1648, a series of revolts against Parliament broke out around the country.  Parliamentarian soldiers in South Wales, who hadn’t been paid for some time, refused to fight. The disagreement escalated into a rebellion when officers and Royalist members of the Pembrokeshire gentry joined the troops in protest. In March 1648, Colonel Poyer, governor of Pembroke Castle, refused to hand the castle over to his appointed successor Colonel Fleming. On 23rd March, Poyer and his men declared for the King. Colonel Powell and Sir Nicholas Kemoys did likewise. The most serious defection was Major-General Laugharne, Parliament's commander in South Wales during the First Civil War, who changed sides and took command of the rebel army.
Tenby became a Royalist stronghold in the rebellion, and a furious Oliver Cromwell set about taking it back for Parliament. Cromwell marched to join 3,000 troops commanded by Colonel Horton at Tenby, arriving on 23rd March. Tenby was defended by 500 troops under the command of the newly Royalist Colonel Powell. The town was besieged for 10 weeks and eventually starved into submission. Powell finally surrendered on 31st May.
Caption Image 1:
Tenby Castle.
“Tenby 030” by Pete O’Shea is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Starved out; Besieged again and again; Oliver Cromwell; Turncoats and treachery

Headline: When Captain Heywood was shot dead the Parliamentarians seized their chance to take Thurgarton.
Body Text:
In Nottinghamshire most of the landowning gentry were staunch Royalists, including Sir Roger Cooper. Cooper lived at Thurgarton Priory, a Tudor house built by his great grandfather on the remains of a partially demolished Augustinian Priory. Sir Roger fortified his house and stables at Thurgarton for the King. Similar garrisons were established at Wiverton, Newstead, Shelford, Belvoir Castle and Staunton, providing a screen of outposts around Royalist Newark.

In December 1644, Nottingham Parliamentarians, led by Colonel Thornhaugh, mounted an attack on the small Royalist garrison of around 40 men, at Thurgarton. This account is taken from the memoirs of Lucy Hutchinson, wife of Colonel Hutchinson the parliamentary Governor of Nottingham.

?[Parliament ordered] all the horse of Nottingham and Derbyshire to join with three regiments of Yorkshire and quarter about Newark to straighten the enemy there; and accordingly they rendezvoused at Mansfield and from thence to Thurgarton where Sir Roger Cooper had fortified his house and lined the hedges with musketeers who, as the troops passed by, shot and killed one Captain Heywood, whereupon Colonel Thornhagh sent to the Governor and desired to borrow some foot to take the house. The Governor accordingly lent him three companies of foot who took the house and Sir Roger Cooper and his brother and forty men in it who were sent prisoners to Nottingham; where, although Sir Roger Cooper was in great dread of being put into the Governor’s hands, yet he received such a civil treatment from him that he seemed to be much moved and melted at it.?

After the house had been taken, it was ransacked and looted by the Parliamentarian soldiers.
Tags: Stormed; Newark's ring; Family homes

Headline: Colonel Rugby and his men soon reduced Thurland Castle to rubble.
Body Text: At the beginning of the First Civil War, Thurland Castle was held for the King by the Royalist Major-General Sir John Girlington. In late 1643, the castle was besieged by a Parliamentarian force under Colonel Rugby. Rugby used heavy artillery to bombard the garrison into surrender, destroying the castle in the process and leaving it in ruins.
Tags: Surrendered on terms

Headline: Despite being armed to the teeth, the defenders of Tickhill Castle surrendered without a fight.
Body Text:
The Hansby family of Tickhill Castle were Roman Catholics who declared for the King at the outbreak of the war in 1642. The castle was repaired, refortified and garrisoned with Royalist soldiers.

When the King was defeated at the Battle of Marston Moor, Parliamentarians in the North of England tried to rid the area of Royalists once and for all. On 26th July 1644, soldiers under the command of John Lilburne and the Earl of Manchester laid siege to Tickhill Castle. Two days later the Royalists surrendered. The Earl of Manchester took the castle without “the loss of one drop of blood”.  Once inside, the Roundheads realised that the Royalists had actually been well prepared for a siege. The garrison had a cannon, about 100 muskets and 60 horses.

In 1647, Parliament ordered that all northern castles which had served as Royalist strongholds were to be demolished. Tickhill’s fortifications were pulled down in 1649.
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Slighted; After Marston Moor

Headline: A quick victory netted a large hall of prisoners at Tissington.
Body Text: Tissington Hall was home to the Fitzherbert family, who declared for King Charles I at the outbreak of the First Civil War. The hall was garrisoned in January 1644.  A month later, a Parliamentarian force under Major Saunders, attacked the Hall. The Roundheads were victorious and 200 Royalist soldiers from the garrison were taken prisoner.
Caption Image 1:
Tissington Hall.
“The Tissington trail” by Martyn Wright is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0

Headline: A lucky shot proved disastrous for the garrison at Tiverton, and fatal for one Parliamentarian deserter.
Body Text:
During the First Civil War, the castle at Tiverton was held for the Royalists. It was garrisoned with 200 troops under Colonel Sir Gilbert Talbot. Parliamentarian troops, under Major General Massey, who were keen to move further into Devon with the ultimate aim of retaking Plymouth, entered Tiverton on 15th October 1645. The townspeople fled immediately, leaving only the garrison at the castle and a small group of soldiers at a nearby church.

Two day later, on the 17th, Thomas Fairfax arrived with his army to take the castle. The Parliamentarians bombarded the stronghold for two days, stopped on the Sunday, before continuing the next day. One of the Royalist commanders, Major George Sadler, withdrew his troops from the castle to the nearby church, leaving the garrison vulnerable. On the 20th October, a lucky shot from the Parliamentarian artillery broke one of the drawbridge chains and the bridge crashed down. Fairfax’s men immediately rushed into the castle, taking the Royalists completely by surprise. Realising he had no real hope, Talbot hung a white flag from his window and the castle fell to Parliament. Fairfax set up headquarters at Tiverton, and was joined in December by Oliver Cromwell who later moved on to attack Plymouth

Talbot and the remaining garrison were taken prisoner. Sadler was captured, and it emerged that he had originally been a Parliamentarian who had defected to the King’s cause. Knowing he faced death for deserting, Sadler escaped to Exeter. The Royalist town did not prove to be the safe haven he had hoped for though, and he was executed by commanders there for deserting his post at Tiverton.
Caption Image 1:
Tiverton Castle.
“Tiverton Castle” by James Taylor is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Stormed; After Naseby; Sir Thomas Fairfax; Edward Massey; Turncoats and treachery; Churches at war

Headline: The Pierrepont family supported their King, but it cost them their home.
Body Text: Tong Castle was home to the Pierrepont family during the Civil War. The Pierrepont’s declared for King Charles I and installed a Royalist garrison in the castle. On 28th December 1643, Parliamentarian troops from nearby Eccleshall commanded by Captain Stone, took the castle after a short series of assaults.
Tags: Stormed; Family homes

Headline: A Royalist raiding party from Newark took the castle at Torksey in a sneak attack.
Body Text: Torksey Castle guarded a vital crossing of the Fossdyke and as a vital strategic point, changed hands several times during the First Civil War. By August 1645, the castle was under Parliamentarian control. The nearby Royalist town of Newark sent out a force to take the stronghold. The attackers waited until the commander of the garrison was away and scaled the castle walls, taking the Parliamentarians completely by surprise. The Royalists managed to take 140 prisoners, and then retreated before Parliamentarian reinforcements arrived.
Tags: Taken by surprise; Newark's ring

Headline: Cannons made all the difference in clan warfare.
Body Text: Toward Castle was held by Sir James Lamont, who supported King Charles I. Lamont used the castle as a base from which to launch raiding parties against the Campbell Clan, a strong Parliamentarian presence in the area. Furious, the Campbells retaliated, besieging Toward Castle in May 1646. On 1st June, the Campbells had brought in cannons to bombard the castle. Just two days later Sir James Lamont surrendered on the condition that he and his garrison could go free.
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Scotland and Ireland

Headline: The castle and town of Tutbury were divided as they declared for opposing sides.
Body Text:
The town of Tutbury declared for Parliament at the start of the First Civil War, but the castle was held for the King. Parliamentarian forces tried to take the castle in April 1643, but the brief siege was not successful, and the castle’s garrison continued to fight for the King.

In April 1646, as hope for a Royalist victory was all but lost, the castle surrendered after a three week siege. It was a condition of surrender that the castle should be slighted, and this process began in 1647.
Caption Image 1:
Tutbury Castle.
“Tutbury Castle ruins” by Thomas Quine is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Slighted

Headline: Switching sides to support the King proved to be a fatal mistake for Henry Lilburn.
Body Text: Tynemouth Castle initially declared for the King, but was captured on 27th October 1644 by a Scottish army under the command of General Alexander Leslie. Keen to keep control, the Parliamentarian commander in the north of England, Sir Arthur Haselrig, ordered that a garrison should be maintained at the castle. The job was given to the staunch Parliamentarian Henry Lilburn. Lilburn’s allegiance though, was not as clear cut as it seemed. In October 1648, four years after it had been taken by the Parliamentarians, the castle was declared for the King when Lilburn changed sides. Furious, Haselrig besieged the castle, taking it swiftly in a night time attack. Lilburn was captured and beheaded. Haselrig displayed his head outside the castle walls as a deterrent to any other Parliamentarians thinking of changing sides.
Caption Image 1:
Tynemouth Castle.
“Castle” by Jacqui is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Stormed; Turncoats and treachery

Headline: Despite heavily outnumbering their attackers, the Royalist defences at Wakefield were no match for Fairfax’s army.
Body Text: The town of Wakefield declared for the King at the outbreak of the Civil War in 1642. With weak defences, it soon became a target for the Parliamentarians. On 21st May 1643, Sir Thomas Fairfax arrived with 1,500 men to take the town, but was faced with a Royalist garrison of 3,000. Despite being heavily outnumbered, the lack of defences meant the Royalists were driven back and quickly captured. 1,400 prisoners were taken and a Parliamentarian garrison was established.
Caption Image 1:
Sir Thomas Fairfax.
“Thomas Fairfax” by William Marshall, licensed by National Portrait Gallery.
Tags: Stormed; Sir Thomas Fairfax

Headline: Not even a slap in the face from the King could shake Colonel Thomas Blagge’s loyalty to the Royalist cause.
Body Text:
At the outbreak of the First Civil War, the town of Wallingford sided with the King. A Royalist garrison was established under the command of Colonel Thomas Blagge. Blagge had strong connections with the Royal family; Queen Henrietta Maria and Prince Rupert were Godparents to his children, but Blagge’s relations with Royalty were not always easy. On one of his visits to Wallingford, King Charles reportedly struck Blagge for not providing enough soldiers. That didn’t stop Blagge fortifying the town for the King, transforming one of the bridges across the Thames into a drawbridge and garrisoning troops in local churches.

With the tide of the war turning in their favour, Parliamentarian soldiers under the command of Sir Thomas Fairfax laid siege to Wallingford in May 1646 and bombarded the Royalists for six weeks. Colonel Blagge refused to surrender without instructions from the King. On 27th June 1646, almost two months after King Charles was arrested, permission was granted and Blagge was persuaded to surrender.
Caption Image 1:
Sir Thomas Fairfax.
“Thomas Fairfax” by William Marshall, licensed by National Portrait Gallery.
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Oxford's ring; Sir Thomas Fairfax

Headline: The siege at Walmer Castle was put on hold while Colonel Rich waited for a mortar.
Body Text:
Built by Henry VIII, Walmer Castle was taken by Parliamentarian forces at the start of the First Civil War, but saw little military action after that. At the outbreak of the Second Civil War in 1648, the castle was taken by Royalists as part of a resurgence of support for the King in Kent.

Fearing that such a significant coastal fortress might be used to send supplies to Royalists all over the country, the Parliamentarian high command tasked Colonel Rich with the job of retaking the castle.

Rich arrived at Walmer, but had to wait a week for a mortar to arrive so that he could bombard the castle. When the mortar eventually arrived, there was no engineer to help operate it and it couldn’t be used. It didn’t really make that much difference. The Roundheads had enough artillery to bombard the castle into submission. On 12th July, the garrison surrendered.
Caption Image 1:
Walmer Castle.
“Walmer Castle & Gardens” by Dongyi Liu is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Ports and the sea

Headline: The Cotton family’s loss was a sailor’s gain at Warblington Castle.
Body Text: The fortified Tudor manor at Warblington was the seat of the Cotton family, who supported King Charles I.  Warblington was garrisoned by soldiers under the command of Lord Hopton. In January 1643, Parliamentarian forces led by Colonel Norton besieged Warblington. The attackers bombarded the manor and launched a 160 man assault, overwhelming the garrison. The Roundhead’s slighted the house, demolishing most of the building. They left one turret standing, which served as a landmark to help ships navigate Langstone channel.
Tags: Stormed; Slighted

Headline: Put that light out! A soldier’s stray match accidently destroyed his commanding officer’s house at Wardour Castle.
Body Text:
The Arundell family were Catholic landowners and supporters of the Royalist cause. In April 1643, Thomas Arundell was away from home on the King’s business. He left Blanche, his 61 year old wife, with a garrison of 25 trained fighting men to defend Wardour Castle. On 2nd May 1643, Parliamentarian commanders Sir Edward Hungerford and Colonel Edmund Ludlow demanded entry to the castle to search for Royalists.  They were refused admittance and set about besieging the castle with a force of 1,300 Roundhead soldiers. The castle’s walls were bombarded with cannon and mines were dug under the walls. The castle endured the onslaught for eight days. Eventually Lady Arundell agreed to surrender.  The castle was placed under the command of Colonel Edmund Ludlow.
Lord Arundell was injured at the Battle of Stratton and died of his wounds. In December 1643, Arundell’s son, Henry laid siege to his own castle, determined to reoccupy his family home. The siege lasted several months. Cannon fire broke windows and gouged the walls. The castle held out until March, 1644, when Arundell ordered his men to lay mines. The Royalist mines devastated the castle. It was thought that one of Ludlow's men unwittingly tossed a match into the tunnel where a mine lay hidden. The resulting explosion ripped a gaping wound in the rear of the building, destroying the upper floors of the castle. General Ludlow, asleep at the time, was forced to single-handedly defend what was left of his bedchamber, until his men could reach him. After four days, the threat of more mining combined with the defenders increasing hunger, forced the Parliamentarians to admit defeat. Ludlow surrendered and was taken prisoner.  Arundell, had regained control of his castle, but his home had been inadvertently destroyed in the fray.
When Parliament won the war the castle reverted back to Roundhead control. Arundell eventually retrieved his family home when Charles II was restored to the English throne but never got round to rebuilding the damaged castle.
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Mines and petards; Family homes

Headline: A Royalist commander’s threat to burn down the town he was supposed to be defending might have been effective, but it lost him a lot of support from the people who lived there.
Body Text:
In November 1642, after an unsuccessful attempt to take Manchester, the Earl of Derby established a Royalist garrison in Warrington. Mud walls and defensive earthworks were hastily built. In April 1643, Sir William Brereton arrived with a Parliamentarian army and laid siege to the town. The siege lasted three days before Derby began to set fire to Warrington, threatening to burn the whole place down rather than surrender. His gamble paid off. The Parliamentarians withdrew.

On 22nd May 1643, Brereton returned to attack the town. The Royalists, now under the command of Colonel Edward Norris, immediately fled to the Parish Church to mount a defence. The siege raged for six days. By 28th May, the Parliamentarians had entered the town. Unsurprisingly the attackers were welcomed by the townsfolk.
Tags: Stormed; Sir William Brereton; Churches at war; Townspeople
