Headline: A furious Marquis of Montrose wreaked havoc in Weem.
Body Text: Weem Castle, also known as Castle Menzies, was home to the Menzies Clan. During the First Civil War, despite strong links to the Stuart dynasty, Clan Menzies opposed King Charles. The foremost Royalist commander in Scotland, the Marquis of Montrose, tried to get them to change their mind and sent a messenger to Weem Castle. Somehow, the messenger was wounded, and a furious Montrose sought revenge. On 29th August 1644, Montrose led a Royalist army to Weem, where they burnt much of the village and surrounding countryside. Try as they might though, the Royalists could not take the castle and marched away the same day.
Caption Image 1:
Weem Castle.
“Menzies Castle” by Rob Harris is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Besiegers gave up; Scotland and Ireland

Headline: Three wealthy sisters survived in an enemy occupied house.
Body Text:
Welbeck Abbey was one of the many homes of William Cavendish, Earl of Newcastle, the Royalist commander in the north of England.  Following his defeat at the Battle of Marston Moor, William Cavendish fled the country and went into voluntary exile. Taking his sons and a few servants with him Cavendish abandoned the Royal garrison at Welbeck Abbey, leaving his home, his money and possessions to the care of his three daughters.  A  Parliamentarian force, led by the Earl of Manchester besieged Welbeck Abbey. On 4th August 1644 the Abbey surrendered and Parliament occupied the house. During this time the three Cavendish sisters remained at the house and protected the family silver, wrote, and even managed to juggle their absent father’s finances in such a way as to send him money to fund his self-imposed exile.

On 16th July 1645, Welbeck was retaken by Royalist troops. On 13th October 1645, King Charles I held a council of war at Welbeck. As Parliaments’ forces began to encircle Newark in preparation for the town’s final siege, they arrived at Welbeck. The Royalist Governor Colonel Frecheville negotiated surrender terms with the Roundhead General Sydenham Poyntz. Welbeck was surrendered to Parliament in November 1645.  The three Cavendish sisters were finally forced to leave their family home.
Caption Image 1:
Sydnam Poyntz.
“Major General Poyntz”, licensed by National Civil War Centre - Newark Museum.
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Newark's ring; After Marston Moor; Family homes

Headline: Women saved the day when they fought alongside the men of the town, buying the defenders of Wem precious time.
Body Text:
Wem was the first town in Shropshire to declare for Parliament. A small garrison was established. An earth rampart was thrown up to fortify the town and houses, and buildings outside the town’s wall were burned down to prevent the enemy using them for shelter.

In the summer of 1643, the King sent 4000 men, three cannon, and a mortar capable of firing a 30lb shot, to storm Wem. Lord Capel commander of the Royalist forces intended to attack Wem before its defensive works were finished. However, Sir William Brereton, who had been sent by Parliament to establish a stronghold in the nearby town of Nantwich, moved his forces closer to Wem to defend it. Instead of attacking Wem, Lord Capel ordered his men to plunder the villages around Nantwich instead. Brereton and most of Wem’s defending garrison hurried out toward Nantwich.  The attack on Nantwich was a trick designed to draw Brereton’s soldiers away from Wem. Wem was the real target and had been left with only 300 soldiers to defend it. When the news that Wem was under siege reached the Parliamentarian army, they didn’t think that the town would be able to withstand a Royalist attack. Parliament came exceedingly close to staying where they were and abandoning Wem to the Royalists. In the end though, they turned around and hurried back to defend the town. The Royalist’s launched a huge offensive at Drayton Gate, but the spirited resistance put up by the townsfolk bought the defenders enough time for the Roundhead army to return from Nantwich, forcing the Royalists to withdraw to Shrewsbury. The feat that was commemorated in verse;

?The women of Wem and a few musketeers
beat Lord Capel and all his cavaliers.?
Tags: Relieved; Sir William Brereton; Townspeople

Headline: The Royalists at Westbury on Severn found themselves garrisoned in a Church, trying to survive the Parliamentarian bombardment.
Body Text:
Westbury on Severn had initially declared for Parliament at the outbreak on the First Civil War and established a garrison in the Church of St Mary, Peter and Paul. In early 1644, a Royalist force led by Colonel Winter took the church for the King.

This was much to the annoyance of the Parliamentarian commander, Colonel Massey, who was travelling through Gloucestershire at the time. On 7th May, Massey decided to retake the garrison, using grenadoes to bombard the defenders into submission. His plan worked, and Westbury on Severn fell back into Parliamentarian hands.
Caption Image 1:
St Mary, Peter & Paul Church, Westbury on Severn.
“St Peter & St Paul, Westbury” by Robert Cutts is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0

Headline: Furious at a last minute attempt to change the terms of surrender, Cromwell made no attempt to prevent the slaughter of soldiers and civilians at Wexford.
Body Text:
After the fall of Drogheda in September 1649, Oliver Cromwell planned to march south from Dublin and capture the seaports of Leinster and Munster before winter set in. Cromwell wanted to capture Wexford; a port where Royalist supporters from Europe landed and a place where privateers launched raids on English shipping. Cromwell left Dublin on 23rd September. He marched along the Leinster coastline accompanied by a support fleet of twenty ships. The Parliamentarians arrived at Wexford on 1st October 1649. Before Cromwell’s arrival the Marquis of Ormond had reinforced the Wexford garrison with 1,000 men. The garrison was commanded by Colonel David Synnott.
The speed of Cromwell’s advance took the garrison at Wexford by surprise. On 2nd October, Cromwell captured a garrison at Rosslare allowing the Roundhead fleet to enter Wexford Bay and unload heavy siege artillery. Cromwell set up his cannon to concentrate fire on Wexford Castle. On 3rd October, Cromwell invited Wexford to surrender. He offered lenient terms hoping that he could secure Wexford without destroying it and use it as a place for his soldiers to stay during the winter. The mayor, the aldermen and many of the citizens of Wexford were prepared to surrender, but Colonel Synnott played for time. Negotiations continued until 10th October when Cromwell's patience finally ran out. He ordered his artillery to bombard the castle walls. The next day, Synnott and the aldermen of Wexford agreed to accept Cromwell's terms of surrender. When a delegation met Cromwell to finalise the surrender, at the last minute, a further set of proposals were presented for negotiation. The terms were unacceptable to Cromwell and the negotiations broke down.
On 11th October, Cromwell’s cannon had blasted two wide breaches in the castle’s wall.  Captain Stafford, the commander of Wexford Castle had agreed to surrender before an assault was launched.  Cromwell's troops appeared on the battlements and turned the castle’s guns on Wexford. The Royalists’ guarding the south wall of the town lost heart and fled. The Parliamentarians scaled the abandoned castle walls, opened the gates and stormed into the town. The Royalists made a stand in the market square, but were quickly overwhelmed. Cromwell and his officers made no attempt to restrain their soldiers. The Roundheads slaughtered the defenders and plundered the town. Around 2,000 Royalist soldiers were killed or scattered. Hundreds of civilians were shot or drowned as they fled across the River Slaney. Colonel Synnott was among the dead.  Parliament lost only twenty or thirty soldiers in the assault.
Cromwell justified the massacre as judgment upon the perpetrators of a Catholic uprising in 1641. He expressed no remorse for the many civilians killed at Wexford.
Caption Image 1:
Oliver Cromwell.
“Oliver Cromwell” by Robert Walker, licensed by National Portrait Gallery.
Tags: Stormed; No quarter; Ports and the sea; Scotland and Ireland; Oliver Cromwell; Townspeople

Headline: It took the Parliamentarians several attempts to hit their target of Whorlton Castle.
Body Text: Whorlton Castle was home to the Bruce family, who held it for the King. Parliamentarian soldiers who sought to take the castle decided to bombard the garrison into submission. They mounted artillery on Whol Hill but soon realised they were overshooting and missing their target. The attackers moved to Toft Hill where they were able to fire far more accurately, destroying much of the castle and eventually taking it for Parliament.
Caption Image 1:
Whorlton Castle.
“North Entrance” by summonedbyfells is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0

Headline: Outclassed and outnumbered, the garrison at Wigan allowed the Parliamentarians to take the town.
Body Text: At the outbreak of the Civil War, the town of Wigan declared for the King. Unfortunately for the townsfolk, this made them a target for Ralph Assheton, a Parliamentarian commander. In 1643, Assheton was marching through Lancashire and after a victory at Whalley, marched on Wigan on 22nd April. Under the command of Colonel Tyldesley, Wigan had a garrison half the size of Assheton’s 2,200 strong army, and was in no position to resist. The defenders fell back and Assheton marched into the town. The Parliamentarian forces demolished all the fortifications at Wigan, burned the town gates and made the townsfolk swear not to fight for the King.
Tags: Stormed; Slighted; Townspeople

Headline: The garrison at Wilne Ferry found themselves on the receiving end of some unusual, but nonetheless effective Parliamentarian tactics
Tags: Stormed

Headline: A plan to punish his nephew for refusing to fight backfired spectacularly for a Royalist governor.
Body Text:
At the outbreak of the First Civil War, many were quick to pledge their allegiance to either the Royalists or Parliamentarians. Some people though, were more worried about staying out of the conflict, like Sir John Brydges. Brydges, the owner of Wilton Castle, refused to support either side and instead volunteered for military duties in Ireland.

In 1645, he returned to Royalist controlled Hereford, and found himself under increasing pressure to join in the fight for the King. Pressure was especially strong from his uncle, Barnabus Scudamore, the governor of Hereford. Still, Brydges refused to be swayed, much to the fury of his uncle. In anger, Scudamore ordered Brydges’ house, which was within the castle walls, to be destroyed. When the family were at Church, Royalist soldiers set the house alight.

If Scudamore had hoped to intimidate Brydges into fighting for the King, his plan backfired spectacularly. On returning home to see his house destroyed, Brydges promptly joined the Parliamentarian forces in Gloucester, and helped take Hereford for Parliament, unseating his uncle.

Headline: The Royalist city of Winchester was no match for Cromwell and his relentless artillery.
Body Text:
Parliament had originally occupied Winchester but moved out of the city in September 1643. On 18th September, the Royalist Colonel Sir Edward Ford marched into the city with his entire regiment.
Two years later in 1645, Oliver Cromwell marched on the city with his main force.  At the time, Winchester was defended by a Royalist garrison of 700 men under the command of Lord Ogle.  On 28th September, Cromwell requested the city surrender. The Mayor of Winchester, William Longland pleaded for time to persuade Ogle to give up the town. Ogle and the Royalist garrison withdrew into Winchester Castle. Cromwell’s cannon fired warning shots at the castle but still Lord Ogle refused to surrender.  The Roundhead bombardment began on 4th October 1645 and continued relentlessly throughout the following day. When a breach opened in the castle defences, Lord Ogle lost heart and requested a treaty. On 5th October, the castle surrendered. The Parliamentarian troops captured a large supply of weapons and ammunition.

Parliament decided that the castle should remain garrisoned in case of another Royalist rising. Thomas Bettesworth was made the castle’s governor. In 1651 though, due to fears of a Royalist invasion from France led by the exiled Royalist commander Prince Rupert, Winchester Castle was eventually demolished.
Caption Image 1:
Oliver Cromwell.
“Oliver Cromwell” by Robert Walker, licensed by National Portrait Gallery.
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Slighted; After Naseby; Oliver Cromwell

Headline: The strategic value of Wingfield Manor ensured fearsome fighting over who would get to control it.
Body Text:
At the outbreak of the Civil War, Wingfield Manor was owned by John Talbot, 10th Earl of Shrewsbury, a supporter of Parliament. Located in what was then a strategic position near a main north/south artery of the country, the manor became a target for nearby Royalists. The Earl of Newcastle’s forces took the manor in December 1643 following a three day siege.

Now in Royalist control, 200 men were garrisoned in the manor and it was used as a base for raids against Parliamentarians in the area.  The Royalists lost the manor after a short siege on 20th March 1644, but soon regained it.  The valuable position of the manor it seemed, was too attractive to give up. In August another Parliamentary force led by Lord Grey of Groby and Sir John Gall of Hopton approached. The assault began when four heavy siege guns were brought up.  A 32 pounder soon opened a considerable breach in the wall before the manor surrendered. It was reported that Colonel Dalby, the Governor, had disguised himself as a common soldier in order to escape, but was recognised while walking through the stables and was shot in the face.
Caption Image 1:
Wingfield Manor.
[Untitled] by steve p2008 is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Surrendered on terms

Headline: The castle at Witton le Wear survived the war thanks to the deep pockets of its owner, but that’s more than can be said for the contents.
Body Text: The castle at Witton le Wear was owned by Sir William Darcy and was garrisoned for the King during the Civil War. Parliamentarian soldiers under the command of Sir Arthur Haslerigg attacked the stronghold later in the war, forcing the Royalists to surrender. Rather than lose his home, Darcy paid a fine of £1000 to keep his estate. Haslerigg kept the promise to return the castle to its owner, but not before he had looted the contents, leaving only the structure intact.
Caption Image 1:
Witton le Wear Castle.
“Witton Castle” by jimsumo999 is taken from Flickr and licensed under CC BY 2.0
Tags: Surrendered on terms

Headline: The Governor of Wiverton Hall was persuaded by his wife to surrender without a fight.
Body Text:
Wiverton Hall was the home of Royalist Sir John Chaworth, the second Viscount of Armagh.  The hall was fortified and became an outpost of the Royalist stronghold of Newark. During the war, Wiverton Hall received a number of Royal visitors, including Queen Henrietta Maria, Prince Rupert, the King’s nephew, and his brother Maurice.

When Parliament besieged Newark it began to target Newark’s surrounding Royalist outposts. On 3rd November 1645, Shelford Manor was captured and many of its defenders massacred. Soon after, Parliament turned its attention to Wiverton Hall. The defending governor, Sir Robert Therrill, was prepared to fight, but Therrill’s wife worried about her husband’s safety. She feared that he would be killed like Shelford’s defenders.  Therrill’s wife wasn’t staying at Wiverton when the Parliamentarians arrived to besiege it. She had to obtain permission from the attackers to pass through the Parliamentarian lines in order to attempt to talk her husband into surrendering the hall.  On 9th November, Parliamentarian troops were on the point of storming Wiverton and Therrill was finally convinced to surrender. The next day, the defenders marched out without their weapons. Wiverton and his men left behind “150 firearms, 40 pikes, three barrels of powder, bullets, match, three great vessels of strong beer and a good store of beef”.  With the exception of the gatehouse, Wiverton Hall was destroyed. The hall remained in a ruinous state for 200 years until the present Wiverton Hall was created from the surviving gate house.
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Newark's ring

Headline: A Royalist clergyman survived a fall from the battlements, but his ordeal was far from over.
Body Text:
After the First Civil War, many Royalists continued to support the King in the hope of returning him to the throne. Woodcroft Castle was still loyal to the King, which made it a safe haven for Royalists in the area. This was the case for Michael Hudson, a former Chaplain to the Charles I, who lived in nearby Woodgate Castle. In 1648, keen to damage the Parliamentarian cause, Hudson had organised a group of men to launch a surprise attack on a small group of soldiers. The plan failed, and Hudson was forced to retreat. Hudson chose to go to the relative safety of Woodcroft Castle, a well defended stronghold with a moat. Unfortunately for Hudson, the attacking Parliamentarians overcame the moat by using bundles of branches to form a path.

Before long the Parliamentarians were in the castle. The castle was overrun and fell into Parliamentarian hands. Hudson was chased up to the battlements and forced over the edge. Dangling by his fingertips, the Roundhead soldiers hacked at his hands, sending him plummeting into the moat below. It was reported that Hudson survived the fall, but was pulled from the moat, killed, and had his tongue cut out as a trophy for the Parliamentarian soldiers.
Tags: Stormed

Headline: The home of England’s first porcupine became a house of chickens as cowardly Royalists surrendered without a fight.
Body Text:
The site at Woodstock has been visited by Royalty as far back as Ethelred the Unready over 1,000 years ago. When King Henry I built walls on the site to create an enclosed park, he kept lions, camels and England’s first porcupine. Henry II built the palace. Henry VII ordered major rebuilding work in the 16th century, not realising that his granddaughter, the future Elizabeth I, would be imprisoned in the palace by her sister Mary I.

Charles I was a regular visitor to Woodstock. So, it was no surprise that the palace was garrisoned for the King at the start of the Civil War. In July 1643, during the conflict, the King visited Woodstock with his wife Queen Henrietta Maria to escape an outbreak of the plague in Oxford.  On 17th July 1644, the Palace surrendered to Parliament without a fight, but the Parliamentarians departed soon after and the Royalists reclaimed the garrison.

Parliament was trying to take Oxford.  Woodstock was providing Oxford with supplies and therefore had to be taken. In April 1646, Colonel Thomas Rainsborough arrived with an army of 2,000 men. On 15th April, the garrison managed to fight off a major offensive but surrendered on the 26th after a three week siege. The palace had suffered heavily during the conflict. Damage from bombardment, looting and the decline of hunting contributed to Woodstock’s deterioration. Woodstock ceased to host Royal visits and fell into disrepair.
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Oxford's ring

Headline: The Parliamentarian victors at Woolsthorpe desecrated and then destroyed the town church.
Body Text:
The town of Woolsthorpe was an outpost of Royalist Belvoir during the Civil War. As the war went on, the Parliamentarians secured much of Lincolnshire, leaving outposts like Woolsthorpe very vulnerable.

Parliamentarian forces finally arrived in the village in 1646. They proceeded to bombard the church into submission. The village surrendered soon after. The Roundhead soldiers stayed overnight, using the damaged church to stable their horses. When they left the next morning, they set fire to the straw and burned down the church. The Royalist stronghold of Belvoir fell soon after.
Tags: Surrendered on terms; Newark's ring; Churches at war

Headline: The Fleetwood family were unable to withstand the might of “Cromwell’s Battery”.
Body Text: Wootton Lodge was the home of Sir Richard Fleetwood and his family during the Civil War, and was held for the Royalists. In summer 1643, Oliver Cromwell arrived with an army to take the house. Artillery was set up in the grounds of the house, on a slope still called “Cromwell’s Battery”, and the bombardment began. The Fleetwood family and their garrison lasted for two days before they surrendered. The house was taken, and Sir Richard and his two sons were tied up and taken to Derby along with 70 other prisoners.

Headline: Worcester’s loyalty to the King was so impressive, it inspired even the Parliamentarians to commend it.
Body Text:
Parliamentarians, under the command of the Earl of Essex had originally occupied the Worcester, but the Royalists took the town in November 1642 and held it until July 1646. Worcester was known as the "Faithful City", due to its unwavering support and loyalty to the King.
On 29th June 1643, the Roundhead General Sir William Waller bombarded the city for a day before moving on. When Waller left, 400 women from Worcester hurried out of the city with shovels and spades. They demolished the siege works and levelled the ditches and trenches left by the Parliamentarians. General Waller was so impressed by the women’s efforts he wrote a letter to the citizens of Worcester commending the courage of the women involved.
By 1646, the Royalist cause was in a state of collapse. In May 1646, the city was besieged by Parliamentarian forces, commanded by Colonel Edward Whalley who brought up heavy artillery to bombard the city.  The Royalist Governor, Colonel Henry Washington, commanded over 1500 troops, 28 cannon and some lighter guns. By early July though, morale was low among the defending Royalists.  King Charles I was a prisoner and the Royalist capital Oxford had fallen. Money and food were running out.  A truce between attackers and defenders came to nothing. On 9th July, Colonel Thomas Rainsborough replaced Colonel Whalley as commander of the besieging forces.  By moving gun batteries closer to the walls, Rainsborough immediately increased pressure on the city.  A second truce allowed the Parliamentarians to gather intelligence about the state of the town’s defences, and they discovered that Worcester’s gunpowder would soon be reduced to a single day’s supply.  With the defenders position looking increasingly desperate Rainsborough offered the city terms for the surrender. On 23rd July 1646 Worcester surrendered.
In 1651, during the Third Civil War, King Charles II attempted to fortify his position at Worcester. Repairs were made to the existing fortifications, in particular the earthwork known as Fort Royal which stood just beyond the city wall. On 3rd September 1651, the Battle of Worcester was fought outside the city. It would be the final battle of the Civil Wars.  Oliver Cromwell’s New Model Army defeated the forces of Charles II. The Royalists were forced back into Worcester. Parliament captured Fort Royal and turned the Royalist guns on the city. The Parliamentarians entered the town and the final stage of the battle was defined by confused street fighting. Panic set in amongst the defenders and the city was sacked. The possessions of the townsfolk were either looted or destroyed. King Charles II escaped, eluding capture for 45 days until he was able to slip away to France.

Headline: The Royalists defended Wormleighton House against a Parliamentarian bombardment, only to burn it down a year later.
Body Text: In the summer of 1644, Parliamentarian troops bombarded the Royalist garrison at Wormleighton.  The bombardment didn’t last very long but was intense enough to force the defenders to surrender. When they retook the garrison in 1645, the Royalists burnt Wormleighton Manor down so that Parliament wouldn’t be able to use as a fortress.

Headline: Homes under the hammer.
Body Text: On the 21st November 1643, the Roundhead Captain Adams laid siege to the home of Royalist Robert Tatton.  For three months Tatton and 50 servants resisted Parliament but a cannon ball that smashed part of Tatton’s dining room brought the siege to an end. Three of Tatton’s men had been killed in the siege. Captain Adams had also lost three men. After the siege Parliament allowed Robert Tatton to buy his house back for £707.

Headline: Church steeples were shot off, mines were flooded and the Battle of Marston Moor interrupted the siege of York.
Body Text:
York was considered the Royalist capital in the North of England and was a vital stronghold, but it soon became apparent that the city’s defences needed to be vastly improved.  In 1642, York increased its supply of ammunition and stockpiled three months’ worth of food. Sconces were built, 20 cannons were positioned around the city and the Medieval walls were strengthened with earth.

On the 16th April 1644, the Earl of Newcastle assumed command of the city and less than a week later on 22nd April, a 2,000 strong Parliamentarian army led by Lord Fairfax and the Earl of Levan besieged York.  Parliament managed to capture some of Royalist outposts in the early fighting and by June, had received enough extra soldiers to completely surround York. Parliament’s first major assault was directed at Walmgate, one of the old Medieval entrances to the city. The attackers dug siege mines under the gate, only for them to be flooded by the defenders. Violent hand-to-hand fighting raged around the Bootham Bar gateway and the steeple of St Sampson’s Church was blasted off by a cannonball weighing 63lb. Newcastle requested a halt in the fighting so that he could negotiate with the attackers, but was a trick to buy more time until help arrived. Parliament weren’t fooled and carried on fighting.

Towards the end of June, Parliament received word that Prince Rupert was on his way to York. The besieging forces left York to fight the Royalist army. The result was the Battle of Marston Moor, where the Royalists suffered one of their worst ever defeats. After the battle, Royalist survivors and victorious Parliamentarians made their way back to York and on the 5th July, the siege began again. After Marston Moor, the Earl of Newcastle had abandoned the Royalist cause and left England for Germany, leaving the defence of York in the hands of Sir Thomas Glemham. On the 16th of July, Glemham negotiated favourable terms of surrender. The Royalists were allowed to leave York and despite a little light looting were treated well by their enemies.
